When one is reborn in the next life, the causes of birth are joined again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the path of transmigration ends; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the path of transmigration continues again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the cycle of birth and death is interrupted; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the cycle of birth and death resumes again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the continuity of existence is broken; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the continuity of existence is linked again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the seeds of future existence are destroyed; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the seeds of future existence sprout again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the conditions for rebirth are eliminated; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the conditions for rebirth are assembled again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the realm of suffering is left behind; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the realm of suffering is encountered again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the state of delusion is abandoned; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the state of delusion arises again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the bonds of attachment are severed; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the bonds of attachment are tied again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the fetters are loosened; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the fetters are fastened again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the stream of existence is cut off; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the stream of existence flows again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the wheel of samsara stops; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the wheel of samsara turns again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the ocean of birth and death is crossed; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the ocean of birth and death is entered again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the mountain of ignorance is climbed down; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the mountain of ignorance is climbed up again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the darkness of ignorance is dispelled; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the darkness of ignorance descends again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the fire of craving is extinguished; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the fire of craving blazes up again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the wind of karma ceases; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the wind of karma blows again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the net of views is torn; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the net of views is woven again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the prison of the three realms is escaped; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the prison of the three realms is entered again; this is like that which was non-existent suddenly becoming existent. Furthermore, when a person dies, the gate of liberation is opened; this is like that which was existent suddenly becoming non-existent. When one is reborn in the next life, the gate of bondage is closed again; this is like that which was non-existent

Once one fails to awaken for a single thought-moment and enters the womb, there arise the hundred bones, the four great elements, the five aggregates, and the nine apertures—this is like tying a handkerchief into the shapes of a rabbit or a horse.
As soon as a single breath ceases, it transforms once into putrid decay, and transforms again into dust and filth;
even a single finger, a single claw, a single hair, or a single strand of hair [is no longer to be found].
To seek that which exists but cannot be found is like a magician who has dissolved his illusions of rabbits and horses back into emptiness.
Since one fails to perceive or awaken to this, one remains attached to illusory and inverted states, regarding them as truly existent.

At all places and at all times, the preceding thought follows upon the succeeding thought, and the succeeding thought follows upon the preceding thought; it is entirely nothing but the delusions of worldly toil.

When one’s thoughts and emotions consist of ten thousand points of inverted discrimination and conceptualization, how can one at such a time awaken to principle, see one's nature, turn away from birth and death, and attain liberation in nirvana? Thus, Guifeng said:
"From the beginning, you have not understood phenomena and thus your deluded thoughts are not liberated; now that you still do not comprehend them, how can you attain liberation?"

"O Deliverer, we pray that you will provide skillful means for all sentient beings of the future age, so that they may practice in gradual stages and cause all beings to forever leave behind all illusions.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground; thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again until it was finished.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

You have been able to provide for all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age the expedient means and gradual stages for practicing the 'Illusion-like Samādhi' of bodhisattvas, so as to enable all sentient beings to become free from all illusions. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you. At that time, Samantabhadra...
The virtuous Bodhisattva, having received the instruction with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

[This indicates] the formal request for permission to listen. Regarding the phrase "Illusion-like Samādhi": it is like an illusion and is unreal; this was explained previously in the section on metaphors. As for "samādhi," here it is translated as "right reception" (*samyak-samāpatti*).
The commentary states that because one does not receive any further sensations, it is called "right reception. "Reception" (*vedanā*) refers to the act of perceiving.
To take "receiving" as the meaning: it is like a bright mirror placed upon a stand;

within the mirror there are originally no signs of blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, large, small, wide, or narrow. Although the mirror does not receive these, it is not obstructed by them as they manifest their brilliance.
It is the same for a Bodhisattva practicing the illusion-like samādhi within the awakening of equality.
In the supreme state of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), there is no enlightenment to be sought; below, there are no sentient beings to be delivered;

and in between, there are no myriad practices to be cultivated. Although there may be seeking, delivering, and cultivating, these do not obstruct the benefit of sentient beings, the bringing of welfare and happiness to all classes of beings, or the universal cultivation of the myriad practices for the sake of liberating sentient beings—provided they are understood to be like dreams and illusions. For example:
To see an ant falling into water and not see anyone capable of saving it, nor the object being saved—
this is called practicing the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*). Furthermore, for one who studies the Way, during the twelve periods of the day,
when walking they must not conceptualize "walking," and when standing they must not conceptualize "standing," and so on, even up to sitting and lying down.
When reading scriptures, prostrating, practicing compassion, or employing skillful means, one must not harbor even a single thread of emotional views or attachment to existence;
only then will it not hinder one’s walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. Thus it is said: "Cultivate the myriad practices as flowers in the sky;
sit in meditation within a moon-in-water dharma-hall; subdue the army of demons within a mirror; and accomplish the Buddha-work within a dream."
"Good son, the various illusory transformations of all sentient beings all arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment.
The answer consists of four parts; here, first, it establishes that illusion arises from enlightenment as the fundamental principle. "Sentient beings" refers generally to the great multitude.
"Various illusory transformations" refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*); all of these are existent.

The Dharma of the outflows (*āsrava*) is the Tathāgata, who is precisely the Buddha. "Perfect" (*yuan*) means being free from characteristics and non-biased; "enlightened" (*jue*) means being empty yet not empty;
"wondrous" (*miao*) means being defiled yet not defiled. "Mind" (*xin*): in Sanskrit it is *citta*, which here means "solid and real.
This mind is not the same as the mind of discursive thought or the mind that arises through accumulation. Now, this single character "mind" shall be explained according to the five teachings.

The provisional teaching of "one mind" for the foolish refers to those of the Hīnayāna who, not knowing that there are no phenomena external to the mind, cling to the existence of objects outside the mind.
The Initial Teaching takes the eighth *ālayavijñāna* as "one mind," because it holds that there are no objects external to the mind.
The Final Teaching takes the *tathāgatagarbha* as "one mind," because it maintains the non-duality of principle and phenomena. As for the Sudden Teaching...
The Teaching School (Jiao) teaches that by extinguishing both defilement and purity, there is but the One Mind, for it shatters all numerical categories.

The Complete Teaching School (Yuan) maintains that the whole encompasses the myriad existences as the One Mind, because principle and phenomena, the fundamental and the derivative, are without distinction.
Now, this mind is precisely the mind of the "extinguishing of defilement and purity as being but the One Mind"; it is what this Sudden School (Dun) critiques regarding the Teaching School.
I exhort you to abandon the perception of marks so that the mind is extinguished; where the mind is extinguished, delusion does not arise, and this non-arising is itself Buddhahood.

Do not rely further upon the gradual stages of the spiritual grounds. This means that within the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements of all sentient beings—whether it be the single body or the myriad things outside, or any phenomenon subject to outflows—all arise from the vast [wisdom] of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
This arises upon the Great Void, the Wondrous Mind of Clarity; this is the delusion arising from the True.

Within this lies the "Three Subtleties and Six Coarsenesses" of the *Awakening of Faith*. Question: Since the wondrous mind of Perfect Enlightenment is equal for both ordinary beings and sages, why does this scripture not speak of the "wondrous mind of sentient beings"?
Answer: Because the Buddhas have already realized it, whereas sentient beings possess it by nature.
Therefore, it is for this reason that the Buddha alone is singled out.
It is like flowers in the sky that arise from space; though the illusory flowers vanish, the nature of space is not destroyed.

The following two sections clarify that when illusion is exhausted, awakening is fulfilled, thereby resolving the preceding doubt. Of these three parts, the first presents a metaphor to provide an explanation.
The various illusory transformations previously described all arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*vimala-bodhicitta*).
This is like a person who, due to an eye ailment, falsely perceives flowers in the sky; thus it is said: "One film over the eye causes a thousand flowers to disarray the sky;
one delusion in the mind causes the sands of the Ganges to undergo birth and extinction. If the film over the eye is removed, the flowers in the sky immediately vanish. And so it is with this...
The nature of the vast void is fundamentally indestructible; as it is said, "when the cataract is cured, the flowers vanish, and sentient beings are themselves the Buddha.
Thus, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "All objective realms exist only through the differentiation of deluded thought;
if one is free from delusion, then the characteristics of all objective realms do not exist. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "Thoroughly understand that the three realms depend [upon deluded thought]."
The mind possesses the twelve links of dependent origination, and it is likewise so; birth and death are all created by the mind.
When the mind ceases, birth and death are exhausted.
The illusory minds of sentient beings must be extinguished by relying on illusion itself; when all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind remains unmoving.
Regarding the second point, the synthesis of the fundamental meaning: the illusory mind is itself delusion; the extinction of illusion is wisdom.

This means that since sentient beings have already given rise to false attachments—the illusory mind that pursues the shadows of the four great elements and the six sense objects—how can this be removed?
It must be extinguished by relying upon that which possesses awareness, the mind of illusory wisdom. This is called "clarity" (ming).
Coming to obscure the wisdom gives rise to delusion; their disappearance is like the rising and falling of the two ends of a scale.

Although the preceding deluded and illusory mind has been extinguished, the perceiving wisdom-mind that recognizes the illusion still remains. You must further sweep away both the delusions and the illusory wisdom itself.
Only when all illusions have reached their end will you finally behold the original, perfect, and wondrous mind of *bodhi*.
Without going and without coming, it is tranquil and unmoving; it is like waves arising from water—when the waves subside, the water remains.
Illusion arises from awakening; when the illusion ceases, awakening is fulfilled. Only then has one reached the end of the waters and sat beneath the rising clouds.
Upon reaching such a field, one may then shift the body and turn the steps; the ten directions intersect and the myriad transformations unfold in a thousand ways.
Regarding the passage "and yet there is no end to the wedge," this section concerns what was previously asked by Samantabhadra: "How does one cultivate illusion within illusion?
The present answer states that it is not at all problematic to use illusion to cultivate illusion; it is just like using one wedge to extract another, or using sound to bring silence to sound.
To speak of awakening based on illusion is also called illusion; if one says there is awakening, one has not yet escaped illusion, and to say there is no awakening is likewise so.
Therefore, the extinction of illusion is called immovability.
Third, regarding the simultaneous sweeping away of both delusion and awakening, there are three layers to this sweeping away:
First, if one claims that there is a mind of awakening spoken of in contrast to false delusion, this is a duality-based method;
even this very mind capable of awakening is itself an illusion. Second, if one claims that the awakening mentioned previously was an awakening in contrast to delusion, but [now...]

If one gives rise to the thought that there is a true awareness distinct from illusory awareness, yet has not yet departed from illusion, this is no different from the previous case of positing awareness based on illusion;
whereas the former was a gross error, this is a subtle error.
Thirdly, if one further claims that what was previously described as a distinct awareness is itself the attachment to existence, this is now combined with the present [error].
To say that one possesses all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) while claiming that this very mind which lacks anything is itself an illusion—
why would one say this? If one were to claim that within one's own portion there exists this extraordinary and marvelous matter,

filling the six voids and pervading the entire Dharma-realm, this would be to superimpose an additional "existence" upon the nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), thereby creating a duality.
If these two were to claim that even this extraordinary and preeminent matter does not exist, they would again be adding an "absence" to the nature of perfect enlightenment;
thus, there are two. Therefore it is said: "To abandon one while grasping at another will never reach an end.
This is because the delusion of viewing the mind as a mere object is profound; as it is further said, "Abandoning existence to cling to emptiness is itself a sickness."
It is likewise like avoiding drowning only to throw oneself into fire. Yunmen’s "The light does not penetrate" has two kinds of illnesses:
first, when one is entirely ignorant and there is something directly before one's face;
second, when one has penetrated that all phenomena are empty, yet there is still a lingering sense that something exists—this too is the light not penetrating. It is thus.
One cannot help but be thus, yet one must not remain so; how, then, should one ultimately apply the mind?

Simply take that mind which previously spoke of "illusion" and "awakening," that mind which did not speak of "awakening," and that mind which spoke of "no awakening"—sweep away all these illusions at once.
Only after this is it that one is unstained by the two extremes, pure, and free from coming or going.

It is the awakened nature that neither arises nor ceases; thus the *Vajra* says, "Suchness is immovable," and also says, "The place where both existence and non-existence have departed is the excellent realm of heaven and earth."
Good son, all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age should distance themselves from all illusory and false realms.
Because they maintain a mind of detachment, they distance themselves even from that which is like an illusion.

They distance themselves from detachment itself, and they also distance themselves from the very act of distancing oneself from illusion. They distance themselves even from this distancing from distancing from illusion.
Below this, there are four successive stages for departing from illusion to reveal awakening; the text contains four layers: first, departing from delusion;

second, departing from awakening; third, the removal of the former; and fourth, the removal of the latter. The first two constitute the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*), while the latter two constitute the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
From the words "Good son" up to "illusory objects," this is the first layer: departing from delusion. This refers to the World-Honored One calling [the assembly].
Samantabhadra and all sentient beings who practice the path should, as I have instructed,

exhort one another throughout the twelve periods of the day to remain far removed from the illusory, false, and unreal realms of the five aggregates (*skandhas*), the twelve bases (*āyatanas*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātus*)— that is,
to transcend the realm of yin and yang, of creative transformation, and of physical forms and numerical measures.
To apply the mind in this way is due to firm attachment; even when one reaches the point of distancing oneself from it, this constitutes the second stage of distancing from awakening.
Although all delusive phenomena have been abandoned, one still firmly clings to the mind that is capable of awakening and certainly does not relinquish it.
Yet this very mind capable of awakening is itself a false and unreal mind, and it too must be abandoned.
"To distance oneself from illusion and also to distance oneself from that distancing—this is the third successive removal.
Nevertheless, although one has attained the mind capable of awakening through distancing, the mind capable of distancing itself has not yet been forgotten; this remains a subtle affliction.
This very mind capable of distancing must also be removed once more. 'To distance oneself from distancing illusion and also to distance oneself [from that]' means:"

This is the fourth successive elimination. Although one has attained the mind capable of eliminating [the object], there still remains a subtle mind capable of eliminating that has not yet been forgotten;
this very mind capable of eliminating must also be further eliminated.
Eliminate it again and again until there is no more to eliminate. It is like encountering an enemy: simply do not dwell with them.

One immediately attains freedom from affliction. Generally speaking, for one who studies the Way, throughout the twelve periods of the day, they must constantly employ contemplative wisdom (guan-hui) without ceasing for even a single thought-moment.
It is like a hen brooding her eggs: the warm breath must be maintained without interruption. Furthermore, one must recognize the presence of subtle ailments;
when one is trapped within emotional attachments and unable to let them go, this is called the "obstruction in the breast" (ai-ying).
Regarding why Baoshan told Li Ao: "Great Governor, if you wish to attain assurance in this matter, you must stand atop the highest peak and walk upon the deepest ocean floor.
If you cannot relinquish things within the inner chambers, they will all become leaks.
Therefore it is said: 'In studying the Way, one must first minutely discern the mind; the most subtle of the subtle is paramount.'"
By seeking within the state of seeking until one reaches the state of non-seeking, one finally believes that the ordinary mind is the Buddha-mind.
Upon attaining that which is beyond separation, all illusions are eliminated;

thereafter, the true awakening is secretly revealed. It is said to be "secretly revealed" because the word "awakening" (jue) does not appear in the scripture; thus, the above constitutes the fourth [section].

After the illusory phenomena of the heavy burden have been entirely cast away at once, they nevertheless reappear as before—vividly active, shaking the earth, and emitting light everywhere, such that one cannot avoid them in any place.
Only at this point is the nature of original true awakening fully revealed in its entirety, with not even a single hair’s breadth of external objects remaining; this is the realm reached here.
The devas held flowers, yet there was no path; the non-Buddhists peered secretly but could not see it. Guifeng said:
"Spiritually aware of itself, there is originally nothing; supported by external conditions, it is entirely empty. Bai Juyi said:

"When the past and future limits are severed and not a single thought arises, if one gives rise to a mind again, movement of thought immediately deviates from the Dharma-body and loses right mindfulness."
It is like drilling for fire: two pieces of wood act as the cause, fire emerges, the wood is exhausted, and the ashes fly while the smoke vanishes.

This is the illustration. The wood is a metaphor for delusion; the fire is a metaphor for awakening; the ashes are a metaphor for detachment; and the smoke is a metaphor for the process of elimination.

When combined, it means that after the smoke has vanished, the ashes then fly away. This was a reversal made by the translator, who [misinterpreted] the preceding text’s four stages of "detaching from delusion" and "detaching from awakening" as being the "elimination" (quán).

The metaphor for the intention of departing from and dispelling [delusion] is like this: when wood grows from the great earth and fire is produced through the mutual influence of the wood's nature and conditions, as soon as it breaks out, it burns away the wooden stake.
Once the wood is burned, although ashes remain, they are blown away by the wind and the smoke is extinguished;
yet the great earth itself has never been moved. Thus, the great earth is used as a metaphor for Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*).
"Nature-gold has no arising or ceasing. Longya said, "Studying the Way is like drilling for fire: when you see smoke, do not stop;
only when the sparks appear have you finally reached home. Banzhi said, "The night is still and the water cold, so the fish do not bite;
the boat returns empty, carrying only the bright moon."
Using illusion to cultivate illusion is likewise so; although all illusions are exhausted, they do not enter into annihilation.

This is the combined metaphor. "Illusion" refers to the second instance of "wisdom-illusion" in the preceding Mañjuśrī chapter, while "using wisdom-illusion to cultivate illusory phenomena" refers to the first instance of "delusory illusion" in the preceding Mañjuśrī chapter.
The meaning is that when one employs wisdom-illusion to cultivate delusory illusions at that time—

It is also like people in the world drilling for fire: the fire arises through the mutual dependence of two pieces of wood; once the fire emerges, the wood is consumed, the ashes fly away, and the smoke vanishes.
Although one uses wisdom to dispel illusions, when the illusions are gone, the illusion of wisdom still remains. One must then simultaneously dispel even this illusion of wisdom;
only after that, the state where nothing further can be dispelled is truly empty and vast, unlike the void of the nihilistic non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas).

Regarding the view that there is nothing: it is said that when delusion arises, awakening is present; when delusion ceases, awakening ceases, and with the cessation of both awakening and delusion, one enters True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Question: If everything is extinguished, then there is no mind. Answer: Although all illusions may come to an end, they do not enter into total annihilation.
"Good son, if one knows illusion, one is immediately detached from it; no expedient means need be employed. Once detached from illusion, one is enlightened;
there is likewise no gradual progression. All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who practice according to this will thus be able to forever leave all illusions behind."
The fourth section, "Discerning that Illusion and Awakening Are Not Coexistent," responds to his request.
Previously, Samantabhadra asked what expedient means should be used for subsequent cultivation so that all sentient beings may forever leave behind all illusions. Now, the answer is given:
"One should simply contemplate and see that the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and all contaminated phenomena are illusory and delusory, and not real. This is because—
Once one is free from illusion, there is no further need for expedient means. It is like a person in the world who dreams of a sore on their body and seeks out medicines by every possible means;
yet as soon as they wake up, this sore is fundamentally non-existent—what medicine would they seek then?
For those who study the Way, once they can leave behind illusory phenomena, that very illusion is itself true awakening; there are no further stages or levels.

Regarding the reason for the gradual stages, it is said that sudden enlightenment in a single thought is like Avalokiteśvara snapping his fingers to cause a change of heart, thereby establishing one as Wondrous Virtue (*Guṇākara*).
Once the snow has melted, spring will naturally arrive. Furthermore, he exhorted them, saying:
"All Bodhisattvas and those sentient beings of the final age with sudden capacity need only rely upon my teachings and practice accordingly."
Forever transcending dreams and illusions, one shall emerge from saṃsāra and proceed directly toward the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood, bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

Samantabhadra, you should know that the beginningless illusory ignorance of all sentient beings is established from the Perfect Enlightenment Mind of all Tathāgatas, just as flowers in the sky exist by depending on space.
If these illusory flowers were to vanish, the space itself would remain fundamentally unmoved;
so too, illusion arises from Perfect Enlightenment. When the illusion ceases, Enlightenment is fulfilled, for the mind of Enlightenment is inherently unmoving.
If those bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age constantly distance themselves from illusions, they will leave all illusions behind;
just as fire produced within wood is extinguished when the wood is exhausted, so too is awakening—there is no gradual sequence, and expedient means are likewise thus.
The Universal Worthy Chapter concludes.
*Yuanjue jing lüejie*, Volume One, End;
*Yuanjue jing lüejie*, Volume Two, Beginning.
The Sūtra begins the "Chapter on the Universal Eye" (*Puyan-zhang*).

From here below, it extensively clarifies the aspects of practice through nine chapters. Of these, the first four generally clarify the contemplative practices for the realization and cultivation of those with superior faculties;
now, this "Universal Eye" chapter reveals the gateway of contemplation that is identical to that of the Buddha. As for the term "Universal Eye":
By means of this dharma-gate, one contemplates that body and mind lack inherent substance;

that the faculties, consciousnesses, objects, and realms—whether mundane or supramundane, one's own body or the bodies of others—are all pure, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*, and universally identical to all Buddhas.

When this contemplative practice is perfected, one suddenly perceives such a realm as this, which is the true Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*). This encompasses both compassion and wisdom, meaning that one universally beholds all beings.
The purity of the Dharma is the Great Wisdom Universal Eye that universally perceives all sentient beings attaining Buddhahood; this is the Great Compassion Universal Eye.
This chapter, based on Mañjuśrī’s understanding and Samantabhadra’s practice, enters the contemplation of the two emptinesses and performs the cultivation of the Dharmadhātu Contemplation.
Thus, the topical outline refers to it as the "Universal Illumination Contemplation," which generally applies to individuals of the three capacities.
To clarify further, the practitioners of contemplation are distinguished by their three grades of faculties—superior, middling, and inferior—which differ from one another.

These differing faculties constitute the "sudden" capacity. Nevertheless, the Commentary states that regarding these various chapters, each preceding one does not depend upon those that follow, while each subsequent one must necessarily build upon what precedes it.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "O World-Honored One of Great Compassion,
we pray that you will expound for the sake of the bodhisattvas in this assembly and for all sentient beings of the final age, the gradual stages of a bodhisattva’s practice."
We reflect upon how to sustain sentient beings and what skillful means should be employed to cause all who have not yet awakened to do so.

World-Honored One, if those sentient beings lack correct skillful means and correct reflection, they will become confused and distressed upon hearing the Buddha, the Tathāgata, speak of this samādhi, and thus will be unable to enter into the realization of Perfect Enlightenment. We pray that you will grant us your compassion for our sake.

For the sake of sentient beings in the final age, having spoken these words as a provisional skillful means, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and made this request three times, beginning again from the end.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You all..."

"You are able to ask the Tathāgata on behalf of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age concerning the gradual stages of cultivation, contemplation, and maintenance, as well as the various provisional skillful means.
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain them for you.
At that time, Universal Eye Bodhisattva received the instruction with joy, and together with the great assembly, listened in silence.
In the opening of this inquiry, the request to explain the gradual stages of practice is first set forth.

This is because in the preceding chapter, the questions posed by Samantabhadra were profound and far-reaching, and the World-Honored One’s response likewise addressed the underlying principle. He first eliminated the maladies of the mind, and only thereafter did he teach the simultaneous cultivation of the myriad practices.

Furthermore, there was concern that what had been heard previously might lead one to think that the World-Honored One taught that "knowing illusion as it is constitutes detachment" and that one need not act.
Skillful means also have no gradual progression; one might say that merely knowing this is sufficient, so why must one further practice?

Now, Puyan wishes to ensure that the gateway of the teaching is complete and perfect, and thus makes this inquiry. "Contemplation" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); "abiding and maintaining" refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*);

and "waiting to listen," and so forth, refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). This is the process of entering the holy from the mundane, returning to the true by reversing delusion. It is necessary.
Relying upon the three types of wisdom, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "One enters samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Now, the question is asked:

if those sentient beings lack correct means (*upāya*) and correct reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*), and their minds become confused and distressed upon hearing the Buddha, the Tathāgata, speak of this samādhi, they will be unable to awaken to and enter into Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). The meaning is that [awakening] must necessarily depend upon such means and so forth.

Regarding "attaining entry," the *Sū* (Commentary) states that this serves as a counter-illumination of the request. This refers to those who have opened up the understanding and practice within the chapters on Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra;
this samādhi is precisely the "Dharma-gate of Detaching from Illusion" in the chapter on Samantabhadra. If one is deluded, one does not awaken; if one is dazed, one does not enter.
According to the two terms "awakening" and "entering," their depths differ: to be suddenly and clearly enlightened is called "awakening."

The realization, cultivation, and verification of the Dharma-seal is called "entry" (*praveśa*); thus, it is said that through the Great Opening, the crooked is revealed, marking the initial awakening, cultivation, and entry.
The structural divisions such as the "restatement of the request" and so forth can be understood from the preceding sections.
"Good son, those newly initiated bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age who wish to seek the Tathāgata’s pure and perfect *bodhi*"...
The mind should maintain right mindfulness and remain far removed from all illusions.
The answer consists of four parts: first, the skillful means for initiating practice. "Right mindfulness" refers to the chapter on Mañjuśrī’s elucidation of understanding;

"remaining far removed from all illusions" refers to the chapter on Samantabhadra’s initiation of practice. Therefore, it was previously stated that the third is the Bodhisattva Universal Eye (*Samantanetra*).
Based on Mañjuśrī’s understanding and entering the contemplation of Samantabhadra’s conduct, [the Master] pointed to this text, asking:
"What is called right mindfulness? It is non-mindfulness that is called right mindfulness; to have mindfulness is the work of Māra. Non-mindfulness is the Dharma-seal.

When discrimination flourishes, the armies of Māra blaze; when the functioning of the mind is forgotten, the Buddha-way thrives. He further said: "One who is free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space."
This means that all dharmas exist with distinctions only because of deluded thoughts; if one is free from deluded thoughts, then no objective realms exist at all.
Thus, one knows that non-thought is right mindfulness. If one examines the various sutras, each has its own skillful means:
for instance, in the *Avataṃsaka*, the cultivation of various gates of practice takes "non-attainment" as its skillful means, while in the *Vajra*... [text truncated]
The Chan gate takes non-abiding as its expedient means, while this sutra takes right mindfulness as its expedient means;
this is because if one maintains even a single dharma externally, conceptual thoughts will arise internally, and if there are conceptual thoughts internally, one will perceive dharmas externally.
To remain far removed from all illusions is the passage on the fourfold successive negation from the "Universal Good" chapter.
First, relying on the Tathāgata’s practice of *śamatha*, one firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts and settles the assembly in quiet chambers for seated meditation.
Second is the practice of *vipaśyanā*. This text has two sections; first is the section on morality (*śīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding *śamatha*—which is translated here as "cessation" (*zhi*)—"cessation" is the meaning of concentration. What is meant by cessation? It is the halting of all discursive thoughts and the contemplation of the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).

How does one know this regarding emptiness? The *Awakening of Faith* states: "If one practices *śamatha*, one dwells in a quiet place, sits upright with a correct mind, not relying on the breath, not relying on forms and colors, not relying on space, and even not relying on earth, water, fire, or wind;
not relying on seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing—all conceptualizations are removed as they arise, and that which removes them is likewise removed."
The mind is what is called *śamatha*. One who firmly maintains the prohibitions and precepts is said to be single-mindedly cutting off conditions;

not violating them is called "upright maintenance. Guarding the sense bases refers to the precepts of restraint, while the precepts of body and speech refer to the precepts of prohibition. These precepts prevent what is improper and stop evil.
The term "Śrāmaṇera" (Rulai) is used specifically to distinguish this from the practitioners of *śamatha* in the Lesser Vehicle and the Bodhisattvas.
Regarding this concentration, for the most part, those who study the Way do not fail to achieve the fruit of sainthood through the three trainings of the untainted (trīṇy-āśravakṣayāṇi).
This has already been fully set forth: *śamatha* is concentration; firmly maintaining the prohibitive precepts is morality (*śīla*);

and the two lower contemplations on emptiness are wisdom (*prajñā*). If one maintains the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, one will escape the three miserable realms and be reborn among humans or devas. If...
One who cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*) transcends the six realms of desire; one who cultivates wisdom (*prajñā*) emerges from the three realms, such as those of the Two Vehicles.
An ancient saying states: "Precepts deliver one from the three miserable paths; concentration transcends the six realms of desire; wisdom delivers one from the three realms. It is further said:

"By studying concentration and wisdom equally, one clearly perceives the Buddha-nature. This is explained according to the Dharma. To explain it by way of analogy: the precepts are like grasping [the object].
Question: All other sutras speak of *śīla* (precepts), *samādhi* (concentration), and *prajñā* (wisdom);

why does this sutra speak of *samādhi*, *śīla*, and *prajñā*? Answer: There are two reasons. First, if a practitioner maintains the precepts with a distracted mind, they will be incapable of entering this gate of contemplation;
therefore, concentration is mentioned first, followed by the precepts. Second, this is the teaching of this specific sutra.

A person first realizes the awakened nature (*bodhicitta*) and subsequently cultivates the practices of a bodhisattva; therefore, the observance of precepts and abiding in meditative concentration precede this. Regarding "settling the assembly":
this refers to a group of people who share the same views, the same teachings, and study together to deliberate upon the Buddha-dharma.

"Dwelling in silence" means to remain quiet. The "quiet chamber" is a metaphor for the meaning of Perfect Enlightenment (*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*); it implies that if a practitioner wishes to enter these two [states], [they must first establish a foundation].

When practicing the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one must first rely upon the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the ethical precepts (*śīla*) of the Buddhas of the ten directions to restrain the body, speech, and the six sense faculties.
While it is easy to subdue fierce beasts, it is difficult to subjugate the minute mind;
thus, although a practitioner of the Way may initially possess the gate of awakening, the seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*) accumulated over immeasurable eons still remain.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, one should use the pure precepts of all Buddhas as a defense to prevent others from trampling upon the crops of the Dharma;
only then can one dwell in peace whether in public or private life. Among fellow students, one’s inner ground should remain silent and still, as if always in a quiet chamber.
Guifeng said: "Sitting is for the purpose of restraining the body; when the body is settled, the mind becomes calm."
In leisure, the environment is tranquil. As the Sūtra says: "The entire ocean of karmic obstructions all arises from deluded thoughts.
If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Seeing [the Buddha] depicted in the full lotus posture, even Māra is struck with awe;
how much more so for a person on the Path who sits upright without wavering? A later passage in the Sūtra states: "Unobstructed and pure wisdom all stems from dhyāna."
It is an inevitable principle that wisdom arises from meditative concentration.

One should constantly maintain this reflection: "This body of mine is a composite of the four great elements—namely, hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities—which all belong to the earth element;
as well as saliva, mucus, pus, blood, lymph, phlegm, foam, sputum, and tears."
The vital essence, as well as the excretions of feces and urine, all return to water; warmth returns to fire; movement and transformation return to wind.
When these four great elements have each separated, where then does this deluded body reside?
The second is the contemplation of wisdom. Furthermore, there are two chapters; first, the contemplation of the two emptinesses.

From this point forward, we first contemplate the emptiness of the self (*ātman-śūnyatā*). The World-Honored One taught practitioners to constantly engage in the correct mindfulness of seeking and investigation during walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, contemplating:
"This single physical form of mine is entirely a borrowed thing from heaven and earth."
The elements of earth, water, fire, and wind combine to form this physical shape; reflect deeply upon this, and in the end, which among them is your true self?
Thus, Zhuangzi said: "The hundred limbs, nine apertures, five viscera, and six bowels all exist together in confusion—who among these would I call my own kin?
Do you delight in them all equally, or do you harbor partiality toward some? Now, regarding this passage:
The same applies to the text. At the beginning, it says, "This body of mine is a composite of the four great elements," which is a general statement.
What follows next—namely, the subsequent text—is all specific enumeration. The phrase "so-called" (*yīsuǒ*) is a term used for evaluation; this evaluation refers to everything upon this present body:
the hair of the head, the hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities—all of these are [the elements].
Objects characterized by solidity and obstruction shall naturally return to the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*).

Furthermore, hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, marrow, brain, blood, lymph, saliva, mucus, phlegm, tears, semen, vital energy, and the excretions of both large and small intestines—all of which are moist substances—shall naturally return to the water element (*ap-mahābhūta*).
All the warmth present upon the body shall naturally return [to the fire element].

Furthermore, within the twelve periods of the day, as the fire element turns upward and downward, twists and turns, bends and stretches, and moves in rising and sitting, it naturally returns to the wind element.
Thus, the four elements are a provisional combination where none can be missing:
if there were only the earth element without water and fire, it would be like grasping dry ash—it could never form a ball. If there were only...
If there were the element of water without the element of earth, it would be like oil or water, lacking any solidity.
If there were only the elements of earth and water without the element of fire, it would be like a mass of flesh in the shade during the summer months;
in the absence of the sun's light, it would immediately rot and decay. If there were only the elements of earth, water, and fire without the element of wind, they could not come into being.
As for growth, why is it that wind is able to cause the myriad things to flourish? Since the four great elements each have their own respective domains,
when you, all sentient beings, consider which of these belongs to you— whether it be the earth element, the water element, the fire element,
or the wind element— if you hold such a view, then earth and water shall return to water.
Fire returns to fire and wind returns to wind; when the four great elements each depart, their departure is the meaning of emptiness.
At that time, one no longer knows where the previously falsely grasped body could possibly be. This is when the "shell-and-leak" child of the four elements is captured and defeated;
being unfooled by this illusory phantom is precisely what constitutes right mindfulness and right practice.
One immediately realizes that this body is ultimately without substance; its appearance as a composite is truly like an illusion or a transformation.

This occurs because, through the preceding entry into the contemplation of investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*), one observes that the delusory body composed of the four great elements is entirely devoid of reality, and only then does one perceive the true principle of *tathatā*.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When the Buddha was in the world, there was a man traveling alone on a long journey..."
While staying overnight in an empty house, a ghost suddenly appeared in the middle of the night carrying a dead person and placed it before him.
Another ghost then pursued them, shouting angrily, "This dead person is my property! Why have you carried him here? The first ghost replied, "This is my property;
I myself carried him here. Each ghost seized one hand and one foot, and they struggled over the corpse.
The first ghost said, "There is someone here; we may question him together. The second ghost then asked, "Who brought this dead man here?
The man thought to himself, "These two ghosts possess great power. Whether my words are true or false, I cannot escape death in any case.
It would be better not to speak the truth. He then said, "The first ghost brought him here. The second ghost became furious and seized him.
One of the ghosts pulled it out by hand before it touched the ground; the other, pitying its haste, took an arm from a corpse and attached it, which immediately adhered.
In this manner, two arms, two legs, two hands, a head, and both sides were replaced; thus, the entire body was exchanged.
Thereupon, the two ghosts took the newly acquired human body, sat facing each other, ate together, wiped their lips, and departed. By inferring from this:
One immediately realizes that the bodies of all sentient beings ultimately lack any substantial reality;
they are all but the corpses of the dead, which are merely patched together when they decay. Are these not, therefore, illusory, deceptive, and unreal things? As Zhuangzi said:
"They entrust themselves to strange things to form their bodies"—is this not precisely so?

Through the provisional conjunction of the four conditions, the six sense organs falsely arise. These six sense organs and the four great elements combine internally and externally to produce a false "conditioning energy" that accumulates within;
this appears as a semblance of a conditioning mark, which is provisionally named "mind."
The former is the contemplation that the body is without self; this is the contemplation that the mind is without self.
As for the "four conditions," these are earth, water, fire, and wind; the six sense organs constitute the external, and the four great elements constitute the internal condition.

Regarding "vital energy" (*qi*), this refers to the mind that arises upon the six sense objects as a faculty capable of grasping and discerning. This mind is a portion of the true mind, being the vital energy associated with the true mind.
The convergence of the constituent elements (dhātu) is what is meant by "one body"; it is merely a provisional combination of the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind.
Since within this there are falsely conceived to be the four great elements, externally there are falsely conceived to be the six sense faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya).

Given that there are six sense faculties, there must necessarily be the six sense objects (ṣaḍ-viṣaya). Once the six sense objects exist, they entice and provoke the intermediate discrimination and conditions.
The deluded mind of *qi* (vital energy) accumulates between the four great elements and the six sense organs, appearing as if it possessed a physical form;
thus, he refutes this by saying that it is merely a provisional combination that constitutes the mind, rather than a true, substantial mind.

This is the means by which one investigates and penetrates the inverted, delusory thoughts of攀緣 (*pānyuán*, clinging to objects) accumulated over immeasurable kalpas; therefore, at the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, [the Buddha] bestowed [this teaching].
He joyfully clings to this mind, yet it lacks any foundation; he is bewildered and at a loss regarding the seven locations. The World-Honored One told Ānanda: "Alas! This is not your mind.
This is the deluded, inverted false discrimination of external objects; it is not your true mind.
This is in agreement with the present meaning.
Good son, if this deluded mind were without the six sense objects, it could not exist;

when the four great elements are analyzed and dispersed, no sense objects can be found, and within them, the conditions for the objects each dissolve and vanish, so that ultimately no perceiving mind can be seen.
This "deluded mind" refers back to the aforementioned mind that conditions sensory objects; it is this deluded mind capable of discrimination.
If there were no external six sense-objects—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—then within [the mind] there would be no discriminating mind. Thus, Master Fu said:
"There has never been a mind without its objects, nor has there ever been an object without a mind. When one observes correctly, the four great elements...
Upon analyzing [the body] into its constituent elements, the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are found to be unobtainable.

Within this state, after the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the six sense objects have each dispersed and returned to emptiness, ultimately and fundamentally, even the mind that performs the discernment of the object cannot be perceived. As the previous chapter stated:

"One falsely identifies the four great elements as the characteristics of one's own body. Having reached this contemplation of the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), the scriptural text proceeds from the constant...
Having formed this thought, one simultaneously shatters it at the point where it is realized that [the self] is truly identical to an illusion;

furthermore, when one mistakenly identifies the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristics of one's own mind, one simultaneously shatters this from the passage in the sutra beginning with "a false combination of the four conditions" up to "there is no mind of conditions to be seen.
Thus, both the deluded body and the deluded mind are found to be identical to the true reality (dharmatā).
Good son, because that sentient being’s illusory body ceases, the illusory mind also ceases; because the illusory mind ceases, the illusory objects also cease;
and because the illusory objects cease, the cessation of illusion itself also ceases.
The former refers to the contemplation of the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); this refers to the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

That [phrase] points back to the preceding section on how sentient beings who have awakened through understanding initiate practice and, upon reaching this point, enter the contemplation of the emptiness of the self. Subsequently, one realizes that the illusory body composed of the four great elements is entirely empty;

it is not only the body that is empty, but the illusory mind—which arises from the intermediate conditions of vital energy—is also empty. The phrase "Because the illusory mind is extinguished" is a restatement (*nirdeśa*) of this point.

When the superior arises, the inferior is not merely the emptiness of the illusory mind; when the illusory objects are empty, they too are empty. These six sense-objects belong to the category of dharmas;
thus, not only are the dharmas empty, but the extinction of the illusion is also extinguished. Since this wisdom is also empty, the *Heart Sūtra* says:
"No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma... even no wisdom and no attainment. — Panshan.
It is said: "The mind is like the moon, solitary and full, its light encompassing the myriad forms. The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist;
when both light and objects have vanished, what is it then?
Because illusion is extinguished through extinction, that which is not illusion is not extinguished."
The preceding section refuted attachments in order to reveal the principle of the True Suchness of the two kinds of emptiness; this passage also has two parts, and this [section] cites the phenomena.

Since the practitioner previously cultivated the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness to destroy the two attachments to self and phenomena, once these attachments are exhausted and views are eliminated, they realize the true principle of the two kinds of emptiness within Perfect Enlightenment;
therefore it is said, "That which is not illusion does not perish. This is not the same as the aforementioned body and mind.
How could the illusion of the various strata of dharma-knowledge ever be extinguished? If one claims it can be extinguished, one falls into the view of annihilationism. As the ancients said:
"When both mind and dharmas are simultaneously absent, the nature is itself the Truth"—this is precisely that essential point.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the impurities are exhausted, its brilliance appears.
This is the illustration. Because the preceding explanation using Dharma-terminology might be difficult for people to clarify, worldly objects that can be perceived are employed as metaphors:

"impurity" represents the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa*), "polishing" represents investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*), and "appearance" represents the manifestation of the [truth of] self and phenomena.

Second, the analogy of polishing a mirror to clarify the principle of the two emptinesses that realize *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti-mātratā*. Although the original intent was to show that polishing a mirror is fundamentally for the removal of dust, here we adopt the phrasing for the sake of textual consistency.
This means that when the preceding explanation of destroying the two attachments to self and phenomena is complete, these attachments are exhausted and views are eliminated;

thus, the true reality (*tattva*) manifests. This is like a worldly person using medicinal ash to wipe dust from a mirror: once the dust and grime are entirely gone, the luminosity within the mirror is revealed.

Generally speaking, the two characters "polishing" (*mo*) and "dust" (*chen*) have many interpretations. Some say it refers to drawing near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and hearing the Mahāyāna to repent and eliminate karmic obstructions;
others say it refers to counteracting afflictions (*kleśa*); or to sitting in the full lotus posture of right concentration (*samādhi*); or to the mind and dharmas becoming one object;

or to reviling desire and abandoning the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). All of these are forms of "polishing the dust. The preceding passages all concern the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*); hereafter follows [the discussion of] the subsequent sections.
The scriptural passage is the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* (Contemplation of the Dharma Realm).
"Good son, you should know that both body and mind are illusory defilements; when the characteristics of these defilements are eternally extinguished, the ten directions are pure.
This serves to confirm what preceded and reveal what follows. "You should know that both body and mind are illusory defilements" confirms what preceded.
"The marks of defilement are eternally extinguished, and the ten directions are pure" reveals what follows. "Illusion" means that which is illusory and lacks substantial reality;
"defilement" has the meaning of being smeared and polluted by dust. The Buddha addressed Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, saying:

"You all must realize and know that this false body composed of the four great elements, as well as the deluded mind that can perceive and differentiate—the shadows of conditions—are both [illusory]."
These are illusory and unreal phenomena, like dust and grime that defile the true body and the true mind.
Once one understands that these are illusions and no longer clings to persons or dharmas, the signs of defilement are forever extinguished. How is this known?

Because clinging to a person is called a sign of defilement, and clinging to dharmas is likewise called a sign of defilement; since the self is empty and dharmas are quiescent, what is there not [extinguished]?
Upon clearing the bowels, one sees that the worlds of the ten directions are all inherently present, free from characteristics and untainted—
this is the wondrous awakening wherein "mountains, rivers, and the great earth are entirely revealed as the body of the Dharma King."
Good son, it is like a pure maṇi jewel that reflects five colors, appearing differently according to the direction;
those who are ignorant see that maṇi as actually possessing those five colors.
This is an illustration. *Maṇi* here is translated as "rain-jewel," referring to the worldly *maṇi* gem.
It is perfectly luminous and pure within, originally devoid of form or color, yet it manifests variously according to the direction.
If this gem is placed suddenly in the eastern direction, a blue color immediately appears within that gem; if it is placed suddenly in the central direction, within that gem...
If it suddenly appears in the west, a white color immediately manifests within that pearl;

if it suddenly appears in the north, a black color immediately manifests within that pearl. Yet the substance of the pearl is round, bright, and translucent, fundamentally devoid of such color-forms as blue, yellow, red, white, or black;
they merely appear according to their respective locations. Thus, in the world...
There are foolish people who cannot distinguish east from west or north from south, yet they truly claim that within the *maṇi* jewel there actually exist these five colors.
This is explained by way of analogy; if explained according to the Dharma, the five colors represent the five destinies:
blue represents the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), yellow represents the human realm, red represents the animal realm, and white represents the heavenly realm.
Question: Is the black [mirror] the same as or different from the mirror and the jewel? Answer: It is different.

This is because the previous mention of polishing a mirror was merely a metaphor for cultivating the contemplation of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) to destroy the two attachments and manifest the principle of the two emptinesses;
whereas the present mention of the *maṇi* jewel is used to serve as the central theme for the three successive layers of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and thus they are not the same.
How do we know this? Furthermore, the essence of a pearl is inherently round, luminous, and pure, entirely free from even a trace of defilement;
it is called "true emptiness beyond all signs. When one contemplates the various images manifested within the pearl, the images do not obstruct the pearl, nor does the pearl obstruct the images.
This is called the contemplation of the non-obstruction of phenomena (*dharmāpratigha*). Without departing from these various images, the images are entirely the pearl.
This refers to the contemplation of the non-obstruction of phenomena (dharmadharmāpratighāta). If these are correlated with the three natures (*trisvabhāva*):
the analogy of the *maṇi* jewel represents the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is the principle of the two kinds of emptiness that is revealed;

the appearance of various colors represents the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which refers to the various illusions described as being grasped by deluded people as truly existent; and the five colors represent the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

What was previously described refers to the defilements of dust and grime. However, one day the World-Honored One held up a jewel and asked the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions, "What color is this jewel?
At that time, the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions each spoke of it as being a different color.

The fifteenth is that all actions of body, speech, and mind follow the movement of wisdom.
The sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth are that one knows the three periods of time—past, future, and present—through wisdom, penetrating them all without obstruction.

Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*), "assistance" means to provide support, for they assist the Right Path; the "Path" is itself the cause, which is called *śamatha* (calm abiding).

those who fear "cultivating what has already been cultivated" or "accomplishing what has already been accomplished" are like those who would place a head upon a head or build a house atop another house. If there were truly cultivation and accomplishment, then there would be two [levels].

It is because one wishes to reveal that the practitioner, while within contemplation, suddenly becomes identical to the Buddha. This is because the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) is identical to the Buddha;

whether it be hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions—these are all small numbers compared to the great number of *asaṃkhyeya*, here translated as "innumerable" *kalpas*. There are also "unspeakable" *Ganges-sands*;
