In this process of mutual dependence, there is nowhere for them to go when they simultaneously fall into error. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"You are all people who are doubly deluded. And again: "When observing appearances, they are fundamentally false and cannot be pointed out;
it is like seeking to produce empty fruits from empty flowers. How true these words are! How could one not engrave them upon the heart?
"Good son, a deluded and floating mind with many clever views cannot achieve the skillful means of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
This refers to the three doubts prior to Vajragarbha’s [realization], all of which have been conditioned by inverted, delusive thoughts and discriminations for immeasurable kalpas;
being empty, groundless, and unreal, they give rise to clever and artificial views that can ultimately never be severed."
This is the dharma-gate of the skillful means for dispelling hindrances, resolving doubts, and realizing entry into the vast and perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
To analyze it in such a manner is not a correct question.
These three doubts constitute a question that is neither authentic nor appropriate within the Buddha's Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Vajragarbha, you should know that the nature of the Tathāgata’s quiescence is such that it has never had beginning or end.
If one contemplates it with a mind of saṃsāra, one merely revolves back again and reaches only the limit of saṃsāra, unable to enter the Buddha-realm. It is like refining gold ore:
because the gold is not destroyed by the refining, although it was originally gold, it is only through the process of refining that it achieves the state of being a single mass of pure gold.
Do not again treat the cycle of birth and death and nirvana as substantial; for both ordinary beings and Buddhas are alike like flowers in the sky.
Contemplation is like a magical illusion—how much more so the pursuit of what is false? If you can understand this mind, only then should you seek perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

The verse says: "For example, like refining gold; it is not because of refining that [gold exists]"—these two lines explain the primordially existent dharma as an antidote to the attachment to the existence of gold in ore.
"Though gold is present from the beginning, it is ultimately accomplished through refining"—these two lines serve as an antidote to the attachment to non-existence through cultivation.
"Contemplating [all things] as like illusions and transformations"—this verse corresponds to the section on "cultivated contemplation" within the prose commentary.
"From the arising of the mind until it has become like a flower in the sky—how much more so when one interrogates what is illusory?

This verse uses this contemplation to discern the realm of the Buddha; that is to say, if the very mind of prior contemplation is itself illusory and a magical manifestation, how much more so when one uses this illusory mind to interrogate, discern, and differentiate the perfectly enlightened realm of *pariniṣpanna-jñāna*? Such is the nature of such differentiation.
This, too, was not correct. Thereupon,
Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
This is a profound investigation into the root of saṃsāra. "Maitreya" means "The Kindly One" (Cishi) in Chinese; this is his clan name.

It is because through this gate one profoundly investigates the root of craving, eradicates subtle delusions, exhausts its successive origins, and deduces its fivefold differentiated natures that "Maitreya" represents an Equal-Enlightenment Bodhisattva (*samyaksambuddha-bodhisattva*) who is in his final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
To eliminate subtle afflictions, it is generally taught within the scriptures that one attains the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) only after severing four matters.

These four matters are: first, inferior outflow-free states (*anāsrava*); second, subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); third, both分段生死 (*bheda-saṃsāra*, delimited birth-and-death) and 變易生死 (*pariṇāma-saṃsāra*, transformative birth-and-death);

and fourth, the internal and external transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Only by severing these four matters does one enter the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi*). Therefore, this shall be addressed when Maitreya poses his inquiry.

The World-Honored One of Great Compassion extensively reveals the secret treasury for the sake of bodhisattvas, causing the great assembly to deeply awaken to saṃsāra and distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox;
he bestows upon all sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) era the fearless eye of the Way,
engenders resolute faith in Great Nirvāṇa, and ensures they no longer follow the realms of cyclic existence or give rise to views of transmigration.
Profoundly awakening to saṃsāra is the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*); discriminating between the heterodox and the orthodox is the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*).

Furthermore, the eye of wisdom realizes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while the dharma-eye masters conventional phenomena (*saṃv�ri-ti-satya*). Moreover, the eye of wisdom is fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*), whereas the dharma-eye is subsequently attained gnosis (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
However, Tiantai regards fundamental gnosis as "clumsy wisdom" (*zhuo-zhi*), for it merely realizes one's own nature; it is through subsequently attained gnosis that...

"Wisdom" refers to the capacity to discern capacities and adapt the teaching, distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox, preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, and speaking of the Path;
this "Eye of the Way" is precisely the aforementioned two eyes combined. "Decisive faith" is the wisdom that is able to believe;
"Great Nirvana" is the Dharma that is believed. "No longer following the cycle of rebirth" refers back to the previous analogy of the moving clouds and the revolving moon.
Furthermore,
World-Honored One, if bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age wish to roam within the Tathāgata’s great ocean of quiescent extinction,
how should they sever the root of saṃsāra? How many natures are there within these various cycles of rebirth?
This passage sets forth the Dharma to request that one first sever saṃsāra. "Great" refers to the nature of absolute non-reliance;
its inherent stillness is called *śānti* (quiescence), and its inherent cessation is called *nirvāṇa*. The "ocean" is a metaphor:

like the great ocean, its substance is deep and its function is vast, possessing merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. That "the traveler does not dwell" refers to the Great Nirvāṇa of Non-abiding.

Regarding the necessity of severing the root of saṃsāra: Previously, in the "Chapter on Vajragarbha," we heard the Buddha teach that sentient beings in the末法 (mofa) age must first sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra. We now inquire: what exactly is that root, and how is it to be severed?
Furthermore, among the six realms of saṃsāra, how many types of spiritual dispositions (gotra) of persons are there?
Furthermore,

how many distinct levels of differentiation are there in cultivating the Bodhi of the Buddha, and how many kinds of skillful means for teaching and transforming should be established to enter into the realm of worldly afflictions and deliver all sentient beings?

This requests compassion and wisdom. Regarding the various distinctions in the cultivation of the Buddha’s Bodhi: this corresponds to Great Wisdom returning to enter the realm of afflictions for the sake of sentient beings;

this corresponds to Great Compassion. Furthermore, the first is the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional, while the second is the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness.
Moreover, the first is the vow to learn boundless Dharma-gates, while the second is [the vow to save] boundless [sentient beings].
Regarding the vow to deliver all sentient beings, the preceding text asks: "How should one sever the root of saṃsāra?
This refers to the vow to sever boundless afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, although the Buddhas possess immeasurable and boundless gateways (*mukha*), one must also study them.
What are these boundless Dharma-gateways? For instance, within the teachings of a single lifetime, there are the various Dharma-gateways for practice.
Regarding the various methods by which the venerable masters of the Chan school throughout the land engage with people, each possesses a distinct wisdom.

Once one has known the gateways of all dharmas, one must rely on the texts to interpret their meaning; only after awakening to the principle and realizing one's nature does this constitute the boundless practice of self-cultivation.
Thereafter, it is essential to carry out the practice of benefiting others. Why is it essential to carry this out?
The practice of benefiting others takes conditions as its root;

if one understands only matters pertaining to oneself, this is called "solitary principle and meager affairs," which can never achieve perfect penetration. How could a single wing or a solitary wheel ever fly or move?
It is like water that cannot harmonize its flavor by itself, wood that cannot form a great mansion alone, or a single garment that cannot suffice for a multitude.
A single substance cannot cure diverse ailments; a single thread cannot form a patterned embroidery; a single note cannot harmonize the lute and zither;
a single word cannot encourage manifold virtues; and a single precept cannot prevent numerous transgressions.
It is just as when the Great Ocean Dragon King at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* established ten thousand intermediate kalpas, and Samantabhadra further extended them to two hundred.
Regarding this doubt—if one encounters such an opportunity, what should one do?

For this reason, the Elder Śākyamuni, possessing the wisdom attained subsequent to enlightenment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), opened for the Dragon King the eighty thousand gates of affliction (*kleśa*) and provided answers to the two thousand eloquent expositions of the Great Being Samantabhadra.
Now, those who wish to examine the capacities of others and preach the Dharma to practice altruistic conduct should likewise act in this manner.
One must simply understand that within that which is beyond verbal expression, one provisionally employs speech; within that which is without expedient means, one establishes expedient means;

and within that which is without analogy, one establishes analogies. Moment by moment, with loving-kindness and compassion, one practices unconditioned loving-kindness (*apratihata-maitrī*) as an uninvited friend, extensively opening up expedient means to benefit sentient beings and bring peace and happiness to all classes of beings.

Inferring from this, the "subsequently attained wisdom" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is truly skillful wisdom. Therefore, in the Way of the Chan School, practitioners who investigate the profound must possess two eyes:
first, the "eye of self" (*svacakṣus*) which clarifies the fundamental principle; second, the "eye of wisdom" (*jñānacakṣus*) which discerns delusion.

As the Preface states: "The Buddha called it 'all-seed wisdom' (*sarvabījaka-jñāna*); its cultivation relies upon extensive learning. Furthermore, Master Shou said: "Though the hundred rivers provide moisture, how [can they compare to the ocean?]"
"It does not obstruct the vastness of the great ocean that contains the Five Peaks; nor does its own loftiness hinder the universal illumination of the great sun.

I only pray that you will not abandon your great compassion for saving the world, so that the wisdom-eye of all practicing Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age may be cleared and purified, illuminating the mirror of the mind to achieve the perfect realization of the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed knowledge and vision. Having spoken these words, [he prostrated].
Having prostrated with the five limbs touching the ground, he made this request three times, beginning again and again.

"The Eye of Wisdom" (*prajñā-cakṣus*) is that which is able to illuminate. "Solemnly purifying" means that all conditions, images, and objective spheres are entirely free from confusion or corruption.
"Illumination" refers to that which is illuminated. "Mind" is the subject of the teaching, while "mirror" is the metaphor; it is intended to mean...
If practitioners of later ages can, throughout the twelve periods of the day, ensure that the wisdom which illuminates and the objects illuminated are like a mirror facing its reflection—
neither deceiving one another, neither accepting nor rejecting, such that things are reflected as they arrive and forgotten as they depart,
responding infinitely and acting with sovereign ease— then, if they can do so, this is perfection.
It is the full realization of the unsurpassed wisdom and vision of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions. "Perfect realization" means that there is neither subject nor object;
because no worldly phenomenon can precede it, it is called "unsurpassed. Now, this "unsurpassed knowledge and vision" refers to seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing.
This mentions the beginning and the end to encompass the middle. What, then, is meant by "unsurpassed knowledge and vision"?
The ancients said: "There is that which is known and that which is not known; there is that which is not known and that which is not unknown.
There is that which is seen and that which is not seen; there is that which is not seen and that which is not unseen.

Now, as for having that which is seen and that which is not seen, it is like holding a candle at night: there is that which is illuminated and that which is not illuminated. As for having that which is not seen and... [the text continues].
That which is not seen is like the sun rising in the sky, whereby all under heaven becomes brilliantly illuminated.

Furthermore, if while walking one perceives the state of walking, one does not see the state of standing; if while sitting one perceives the state of sitting, one does not see the state of lying down.
It is simply that while walking, one does not see walking; while standing, one does not see standing; and this extends to sitting and lying down.
At that time, one does not see the bottom of sitting or reclining, nor even seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing;

at all places and at all times, it does not obstruct walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, nor seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing. Amidst the thousand differences and myriad distinctions, everything is simultaneously cut off in a single sitting.

Wherever the eyes touch or the senses encounter objects, there is nothing that is not ascending into the pure Dharma-palace of liberation, and nothing that is not the realization of Great Perfection (Mahāpariniṣpanna).
To awaken to this wondrously adorned realm is what is called unsurpassed knowledge and vision;
how could any worldly, illusory phenomena surpass this Dharma? Only those who understand it in this way will begin to derive great benefit.
Thus, the ancients said: "Without a [discriminating] mind, the Buddhas of the ten directions share the same wind at a thousand li; with [discriminating] knowledge, the ten directions..."
The Buddhas face to face are as distant as Hu and Yue; yet Laozi, having attained this principle, said: "Without stepping out of his door, one knows all under heaven;

without looking through the window, one perceives the Way of Heaven. If we correlate this according to the School of Provisional Teaching, the unsurpassed knowledge and vision, the holy *nirvāṇa*-nature, and *bodhi* are precisely the Dharma of *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

You have been able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the profound, secret, subtle, and wondrous meaning, so as to cause the bodhisattvas to purify their eyes of wisdom and to cause all sentient beings of the final age to forever sever [their afflictions]."
“When you have awakened to the true nature of the mind within saṃsāra and attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, having received these instructions with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.

The mind awakens to the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and this true reality is endowed with the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). As for "true reality," it is immovable amidst all phenomena; it is the characteristic of formlessness.
If one brings forth its essence, it is perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). There are five types of patience:

the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*) in the stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*); the patience of faith (*adhimukti-kṣānti*) at the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); and [the patience of] cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) at the second... [stage].

From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the sixth stage is called "Patience in Accordance" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), the stage of penetration. From the seventh stage up to the ninth stage is called "Patience regarding Non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

From the tenth stage up to Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) is called "Patience of Quiescent Extinction" (*nirvāṇa-kṣānti*). Among these five patiences, it refers here to the patience regarding non-arising;
as stated in the preceding chapter, all sentient beings have not yet awakened, and through deluded vision, they give rise to the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
Now that you have realized the true nature (*dharmatā*) and understood that the deluded mind does not arise, saṃsāra is forever severed;
this may thus be called the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Good son, all sentient beings, from the beginningless past, have been bound by various forms of affection, love, and craving.
There is saṃsāra.

In the answer, within the specific explanation of the root of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is indicated by way of desire; this refers to the various kinds of the four modes of birth and nine classes of beings.
These include the kindness of kinship, such as that of parents and so forth, or the kindness of things experienced, or that which occurs spontaneously.
The arising of affection may be due to respect, or affection may be formed through kindness; thus, kindness and affection are of various kinds.
Here, "greed" refers specifically to sexual desire.
Throughout all worlds, whether beings are born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation, they all arise because of sexual desire.
Regarding the rectification of one's nature and destiny, one should know that the root of saṃsāra is craving.

Second, in terms of taking birth, this refers to the six heavens of the desire realm and the five realms of mixed habitation; "rectification" here refers to the act of receiving birth. As the ancients said:
"If craving is not heavy, one will not be born in Saṃsāra; if mindfulness is not singular, one will not be born in the Pure Land. To be born in Saṃsāra...
The elders all say that this is because the mind of craving and desire is heavy. For instance, in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, embracing constitutes the practice of desire;
in the Tuṣita Heaven, holding hands constitutes the practice of desire; in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, playful laughter constitutes the practice of desire;
and in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, gazing at one another constitutes the practice of desire—down even to the crows, which transmit breath with their beaks.
The magpie uses a branch to pass [the fire] around; all such things are due to receiving a physical life because of lustful desire.

Generally, when people of the world approach the end of their lives, if they are those who practiced wholesome dharmas throughout their lifetime, the cold first begins from the bottom and ascends to the navel;
the warmth above the crown of the head is the last to vanish, and they will then be reborn in the human realm. If the heat reaches the head and face first...
If this heat is exhausted, such a person will be reborn in the heavenly realms. Conversely, if one has committed the ten evil deeds throughout a lifetime, then:
if the heat from the top of the body down to the waist is exhausted last, one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts;
if the heat from the waist down to the knees is exhausted last, one falls among the animals; and if the heat from below the knees down to the feet is exhausted last...
Those who fall into hell and those who enter nirvana among those beyond training (aśaikṣa) may have their "warmth" in the heart or in the crown of the head.
Furthermore, after death, if one has accumulated much merit from wholesome dharmas in a single lifetime, they will be reborn in a good realm;

if their evil karma is heavy, they will fall into an evil destiny. As for those whose wholesome and unwholesome deeds are balanced and remain undetermined, they will consequently dwell in a state of obscurity.
Regarding the place [of rebirth], it refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). One must determine for oneself that this lasts forty-nine days, much like weighing an object on a scale.

If wholesome karma is slightly superior, one first experiences birth in a happy realm; if unwholesome karma is slightly superior, one first experiences the retribution of an evil state and subsequently receives the reward of a happy state.
After this period is fulfilled, one returns to take birth once more. At the time of undergoing such birth:
Although all places where one is born may be far away, by the power of karma, they appear before one's eyes.
Those with merit may hear the sounds of the masses singing and dancing, or the sounds of bells, gongs, and various drums, as well as various peaceful, exquisite, and pleasing sounds;
those without merit may hear the sounds of wind, rain, thunder, lightning, or the surging of great rivers.
Amidst the sounds of swelling waves and various chaotic, unpleasant noises, one may then falsely perceive oneself entering a terrace, pavilion, or palace;
or one may see oneself entering a thicket of thorns or amidst reeds and lotuses.
If one has been transformed into a male, then within the mother’s womb, a manly desire immediately arises, and one turns one's back toward the exterior.
Facing inward, if it transforms into a female, she faces outward with her back toward the interior,
resting against the father's right flank; at that time, as the father’s semen and the mother’s blood unite,
the individual spirit feels joy and takes conception there, dwelling within the mother’s abdomen above the internal organs.
The hot organs are below and the cold organs are above. When the mother eats a bowl of hot food, her body feels as if it were in a cauldron of boiling water;
when she drinks a bowl of cold water, her body feels as if it were pierced by ice.
When she is full, she is so cramped that the pain in her body is beyond description; when she is hungry, her belly feels as if it were being overturned.
"Their suffering is suspended without measure. This refers to birth from eggs or wombs; it is not so for the two types of birth from moisture or by transformation (*saṃsvedaja* and *upapāduka*).
Those born from moisture merely become stained by fragrance; when they reach the place of birth, this fragrance may be pure or impure, depending on what is induced by their past karma.
As for those born by transformation, they merely take delight in their place of reliance, or—
Whether good or evil, these are also experienced as the result of past karma. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"In the realm of inverted desire, beings born from moisture or transformation are defiled by odors. Generally, while in the womb, one remains for thirty-eight weeks before finally being born.

During the first week, the embryo is like curd; during the second week, it is like solidified butter (*navanīta*); during the third week, it is like a medicinal pestle; during the fourth week, it is like a warm stone; and during the fifth [week]...

In the seventh week, the physical form gradually appears; in the sixth and seventh weeks, the elbows and knees appear; in the seventh week, the hands and feet are produced; in the eighth week, the twenty fingers and toes appear;
in the ninth week, the eyes, ears, and other organs are produced; in the seventeenth week, it is like a floating bag; in the eleventh week, the bodily apertures become permeable;
in the twelfth week, the intestines and bones are produced; in the thirteenth week, the sensation of hunger and thirst arises; in the fourteenth week, the sinews are produced.
In the fifth week, the various channels are produced; in the sixteenth week, the various apertures emit breath; in the seventeenth week, the eyes, nose, and so forth become clear and pure;
in the eighteenth week, the sense organs grow; in the nineteenth week, the three faculties are complete; in the twenty-seventh week, the various bones are produced;
in the twenty-first week, flesh is produced; in the twenty-second week, blood is produced; in the twenty-third week, skin is produced. II.
In the fourteenth week, the skin is produced; in the twenty-fifth week, the flesh grows; in the twenty-sixth week, hair, body hair, and nails grow;
in the twenty-seventh week, each according to their wholesome or unwholesome karma, they individually perceive the marks of suffering;
in the twenty-eighth week, inverted perceptions arise; in the twenty-ninth week, physical form and color manifest; and in the thirty-seventh week, the hair and nails [are fully formed].
During the thirty-first seven-day period, the marks of a great man are fully formed;
during the thirty-sixth seven-day period, the thought of wearying detachment arises; during the thirty-seventh seven-day period, five kinds of evil thoughts arise;

and during the thirty-eighth seven-day period, when the child is about to be born, winds arise within the mother’s womb, moving the child’s body upward or downward to cause it to hang upside down with its head facing [the birth canal].

The birth canal is like two rocks squeezing a mountain; those whose bodies possess merit think to themselves at that time, "I am plunging into a bathing pool to sport in the water, as if falling onto a high bed in a place of flowers and incense.
Those without merit think to themselves at that time, "I am falling from a high mountain down a precipice into a ditch, a pit, or a latrine, or as if onto the bare ground."
Upon the prison bars, the thorns, and the brambles, as well as amidst the wilds, the stones, and the midst of spears and halberds, there is immeasurable sorrow and anxiety.
Furthermore, at the time of birth, the mother is endangered and the child is terrified;

when one is born and falls upon the grass, the body is so delicate and soft that the wind blowing through the grass touches it like treading upon blades of swords and halberds, causing one to suddenly lose voice and cry out in great agony.
Furthermore, within seven days after birth, eighty thousand types of parasites arise within the body;
by this one may infer that among the four modes of birth and nine categories of beings, there is none that does not receive its physical form through sexual desire.
That they wander aimlessly through the five destinies and crawl about through the four modes of birth, having no means of liberation, is entirely due to craving and desire.
The roots are used as the basis for the analogy, while the roots themselves are the basis for the dharma being illustrated. How is this known?

It can be taken as proof that if one cuts down a tree without exhausting its roots, the tree will repeatedly grow back; likewise, if one severs craving without exhausting its root, suffering will repeatedly arise.
Because the various desires assist in the arousal of the nature of craving, they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death.
Desires act as the auxiliary cause; "auxiliary" means a supporting condition. The various desires are the external objects, while the nature of craving is the seed accumulated over immeasurable eons.
Because these external sensory objects draw forth the seeds of the mind of craving, throughout the twelve periods of the day—

The silken cords of affection are knotted ten thousand times, and the nets of emotion are layered a thousandfold. Because of this loving heart and its greedy desires, one creates karma; because one creates karma, one undergoes retribution.
Thus, the cycle of birth and death is never severed, as causes and conditions pull one another along, like a magnet attracting a needle.
The needle belongs to the north and is made of iron; this [magnet] belongs to the south and is made of stone. The south corresponds to Yang, while the north corresponds to Yin. Due to this Yin...
It is simply that the yang [principle] resonates with its counterpart. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "I love your form; you cherish my mind.
Because of these causes and conditions, for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of births, we remain constantly bound. Zhaoran says:
"The reason sentient beings have long wandered in saṃsāra is entirely due to their attachment to desire. If desire ceases within the mind, there will be no further birth and death."
Desire is the cause of craving for life, and craving for life is the cause of existence; sentient beings’ craving for life, in turn, relies upon the root of desire.
Desire serves as the cause and craving for life serves as the fruit.
This clarifies that because of desire, cause and effect revolve and depend upon one another in succession without interruption. "Desire" here refers to lustful greed.
"Life" refers to the life-force of the body; if there were no craving and desire, this body would not be born.
One should know that for all sentient beings, desire arises from the mind of attachment.

Since one already possessed lustful desire in past causes and thereby obtained this body, in the present life one again gives rise toward this very body to a mind of cherishing, protecting, and greedy attachment.
Because one cherishes this body, and because one relies upon and clings to this body as the cause for the arising of sensual desire in future lives,
one consequently experiences the karmic retribution of birth and death in those future existences. As these states thus revolve and continue in succession without end,
it is said that "cherishing life" constitutes the fruit.

Because of sensual objects, various favorable and unfavorable conditions arise; through aversion toward the unpleasant and attachment to the pleasant, one generates hatred, jealousy, and various types of karma.
For this reason, one is reborn again in the hells or as a hungry ghost.
These evil karmas bring about the retribution of suffering. "Unfavorable" refers to what is disagreeable to the mind, while "favorable" refers to what is agreeable; both arise from craving for them.
When objects do not accord with one's mind, it gives rise to feverish affliction, resentment, and envy;
because of the arousal of anger, one commits various evil karmas such as killing, harming, beating, reviling, or insulting.

Or, when objects accord with one's desires, one gives rise to defiled attachment, committing various evil karmas such as sexual misconduct, theft, drinking and eating [forbidden things], plundering, and frivolous speech. If one acts in this manner throughout the twelve periods of the day...
Those who harbor such thoughts will consequently experience the retribution of the three miserable realms: if they give rise to anger, they will experience the retribution of the hells;
if they give rise to delusion, they will experience the retribution of animals; and if they give rise to greed, they will experience the retribution of hungry ghosts.

The reason animals are not explicitly mentioned here is due to two meanings: first, to maintain the symmetry of the phrasing; second, to include the intermediate category by citing only the first and the last.
Knowing that desire is to be reviled, one becomes weary of craving and the paths of karma; abandoning evil and delighting in the good, one again appears as a deva or human.

This means that while the preceding text described how sentient beings—without knowing or perceiving—give rise to delusions and create karma to fall into the evil realms, they now know and awaken to the fact that they previously gave rise to a mind of greed and desire.

This is not the path of goodness; it is deeply loathsome and should be abandoned. Moment by moment, one should feel weary of and detest the paths of evil karma leading to the three miserable realms, and thus cast them off.
One should abandon the mind that creates the ten non-virtuous actions and instead give rise to a mind that delights in the merit of the ten virtuous dharmas.
By cultivating faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, one attains the dharma of the ten virtues. If one acts thus throughout the twelve periods of the day...
By applying the mind in this way, one eventually attains the karmic rewards of human existence and the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Nevertheless, even so, this is not yet considered truly virtuous. Why? Because for humans there are the eight sufferings, and in the heavens there are the five signs of decay.

As for the eight sufferings: first, the suffering of birth; second, the suffering of old age; third, the suffering of illness; fourth, the suffering of death; fifth, the suffering of separation from what is loved; sixth, the suffering of enmity and hatred... [and so forth].

The seven sufferings of the assembly are: first, the suffering of birth; second, the suffering of aging; third, the suffering of illness; fourth, the suffering of death; fifth, the suffering of meeting those one dislikes; sixth, the suffering of parting from those one loves; seventh, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; eighth, the suffering of the five aggregates being in a state of intense burning.

Regarding the five signs of decline (*pañca-vyasanāni*): first, the clothes become soiled with grime; second, the flower garlands wither and fade; third, sweat flows from both armpits; fourth, the body becomes foul-smelling and filthy; fifth, one finds no pleasure in one's own seat.
For a detailed exposition of these five signs of decline and eight sufferings, see the Chapter on Mañjuśrī.

Furthermore, because one knows that all cravings are loathsome, one abandons craving and delights in equanimity (*upekṣā*); yet, this merely nourishes the root of craving and results in the superior wholesome fruits of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

This is the "immovable karma" (*āniñjya-karman*) that brings about rebirth in the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*). Regarding the environmental retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*), it is said that one does not understand that the aforementioned actions were produced by craving.

Whether it be the mind that commits evil or the mind that cultivates goodness through attachment, as long as one has not yet escaped the wheel of suffering, one must eventually abandon that heart of attachment and the desire to cultivate goodness;

both are discarded at once. Furthermore, if one does not realize that this mind of renunciation is identical in nature to that heart of attachment, and thus continues to nourish the root of attachment as before, then such a way of employing the mind is merely conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
The mind attains the form realm, which gradually increases until the formless realm is fully realized as the primary retribution.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The bodies of the Brahmā kings in the heavens are ten yojanas in height; the bodies of the gods in the formless realm are thirty-six yojanas in height.
Regarding "immovable karma" (*aniñjya-karman*): it refers to causes that are immovable resulting in fruits that are immovable. Thus, the cause is not subject to the lower realm of desire.
The fruit moved by the objects of the realms is not moved by the meditative concentration of the mind of the fourth dhyāna;
just as the first dhyāna is not moved by the objects of the desire realm, the second dhyāna is not moved by the objects of the first dhyāna,
and the third dhyāna is not moved by the objects of the second dhyāna, so it gradually increases until—
These are the deities of the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because they all remain within saṃsāra, they do not achieve the Noble Path.
This is the summary. For this reason, as explained above, because the mind of craving and desire is not severed, one undergoes the three miserable destinies (*durgati*).
As for the retribution of abandoning the mind [of craving], one does not cease to receive the retribution of the two upper realms;

these are all matters of birth and death within the three realms and transmigration through the six paths. Those who wish to emerge from this cycle must first rely on what the Buddha taught to sever the mind of lustful desire and the mind that gives rise to craving and thirst.
"Craving" (āśā) is a metaphor for the longing for water; as for the matter of karmic retribution, when it arises, it is certain to occur.
Since the retribution of the mind must necessarily follow from its actions, one may observe one's actions through their consequences and thus transform them;
or one may examine the mind through its actions and thus reverse it.

This is like a person in the world who wishes to dry up a stream, which must first have its source exhausted, or who wishes to prevent a pot of soup from boiling, which must first have the fire removed. Therefore, the ancients said: "To block..."
To stem the flow is not as effective as blocking its source; to stir the boiling water is not as effective as extinguishing the fire.

Since the source of water originates from the spring, if the source is not blocked, the water will be inexhaustible; since the fire boils the water, if the fire is not extinguished, who can stop the boiling?
Therefore, there are guests who block the source and do not need to dam the flow for it to dry up of itself, and there are guests who extinguish the fire.

It is like trying to stop boiling water by merely ladling it out; through such analogies, the matter can be understood in detail. To weary oneself with the fruit [of suffering] is not as effective as severing its cause;
to fear the suffering itself is not as effective as being deterred from the evil causes. Since the fruit increases from the cause, if the cause is not severed, the fruit will never end.
Evil arises from suffering; if the evil is not punished, how can the suffering cease? Therefore, one must bring about their total cessation.
Because those who seek the cause do not weary of the fruit and thus perish themselves, and the sages who punish evil do not fear suffering and thus distance themselves from it;
may all you gentlemen record this as a warning! Thus, the fundamental root of the saṃsāra of all sentient beings is simply these three characters:
greed, desire, and attachment. In the preceding Mañjuśrī Chapter, ignorance was identified as the root of birth and death.
Based on this, it is the initiation of karma; now, in the Chapter on Maitreya, craving is identified as the root of saṃsāra, which is the moistening of karma.
While various sūtras may speak of the initiation of karma, none are as concise yet comprehensive as the text of this sūtra.
Good son, when Bodhisattvas manifest transformations within the world, they do not take unlovely things as their basis;
rather, through compassion, they cause others to relinquish attachment, and by making use of various forms of desire, they enter into birth and death.

This [explanation] addresses the potential objection that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can only bestow happiness while compassion (*karuṇā*) can only extract suffering, and that such fears might hinder the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Consider, for instance, Layman Pang: could he truly have been preoccupied with worldly matters such as caring for his wife, raising his sons, and nurturing his daughters?
Furthermore, figures such as Monk Zhoutou were all manifestations of Bodhisattvas; they merely displayed these appearances.
Their taking of birth is the same as that of ordinary beings, for the purpose of benefiting, subduing, gathering, and transforming all sentient beings.
If all sentient beings in the final age can renounce all desires, eliminate hatred and attachment, and forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra, [they shall attain liberation].
By diligently seeking the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*), one attains awakening within the pure mind;

this reveals the nature of awakening. As for the passage stating that "all sentient beings who can renounce all desires, eliminate increased craving, and forever sever the cycle of rebirth," this section is explained according to the Chan school: it means to let the familiar place become unfamiliar.

Next, those who diligently seek the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment and thereby attain awakening within the pure mind are like those who release [the ore] from its place of origin and refine it until it is matured;
this is explained according to the doctrinal school. This refers to first extracting the ore and subsequently forming gold.
The above scriptural passage provides a general answer to Maitreya’s prior question regarding the desire to travel upon the Great Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Quiescent Extinction (*mahāśānti-nirvāṇa*).
"What must be severed to cut off the root of saṃsāra? I now reply: it is the two words "craving and desire.
Son of good family, all sentient beings, due to their fundamental craving and desire, manifest and bring forth the five distinct natures;
these differences arise unequally, appearing as deep or shallow according to two kinds of obstructions.

Second, within the clarification of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), there is a general indication of the causal basis for its manifestation. "Manifestation" (*xian*) refers to the unfolding, while "unfolding" (*hui*) refers to the dispersal.

This means that when ignorance—the fundamental affliction—is manifested, unfolded, and dispersed, it is because all sentient beings, due to turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the sensory dust, give rise to craving and desire;
consequently, they manifest, unfold, and disperse fundamental ignorance. At that time, the nature of the *śrāvaka* and the *pratyekabuddha* is revealed.
The natures of Bodhisattvas, the natures of externalists, and the indeterminate nature are each distinct and different. Why is this so?
It is because those who initially encounter and follow the teachings of false teachers firmly cling to and do not relinquish the two selves—the self of persons and the self of phenomena.
This obstacle is profound when compared to the Two Vehicles; however, if they encounter the teachings of the Two Vehicles that explain the emptiness of persons, [they may progress].
Although one has already understood the emptiness of persons, if one has not yet forgotten attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), then compared to a false teacher, this [understanding] is shallow;
yet if one encounters the teaching of a Bodhisattva, even compared to that of the Two Vehicles, it is still shallow.
However, upon the awakened nature of these sentient beings, there is fundamentally no barrier of depth or shallowness; it merely follows what they have been habituated to through conditioning.

What are the two obstacles? First is the obstacle of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*), which obstructs right knowledge and vision; second is the obstacle of phenomena (*vastu-āvaraṇa*), which continues the cycle of birth and death.

These are the two obstacles upon which [the self] relies. Ordinary beings possess the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*); because they previously falsely identified the four great elements as their own physical form, this is called the "obstacle of phenomena.
Consequently, they wander aimlessly through the four modes of birth and crawl about within the six realms of existence. As for the followers of the Two Vehicles...
Because of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), it is called the "obstruction to principle" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); thus, one possesses wisdom but lacks compassion.

Regarding these two obstructions, the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* refers to them as attachment to self (*ātmagrāha*) and attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Specifically, the *Awakening of Faith* explains that first, from within fundamental awakening (*mūlapratibhāsa*), a single moment of non-awakening causes the mind to stir, which constitutes the "mark of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*);
having something perceived constitutes the "mark of transformation" (*pariṇatilakṣaṇa*); and the manifestation of objective realms constitutes the "mark of manifestation" (*pratibhāsalakṣaṇa*).
The arising of a discriminating mind constitutes the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*); the non-interruption of this mind constitutes the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*).
These five are all called the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). The arising of a mind that gives rise to attachment constitutes the characteristic of attachment (*abhiniveśa-lakṣaṇa*);

to conceptually construct names for the objects of such attachment constitutes the characteristic of calculating names (*nāma-kalpanā-lakṣaṇa*). These two characteristics belong to the grasping at self (*ātma-grāha*). In the context of Yogācāra, these are termed...

The afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): the afflictive hindrance obstructs the mind, so that the mind is not liberated; the cognitive hindrance obstructs wisdom, so that wisdom is not liberated.
In this sutra, these are termed the hindrance of principle (*li-zhang*) and the hindrance of phenomena (*shi-zhang*).
