The second chapter, "On Samantabhadra," states: "For example, when drilling for fire, fire emerges from the mutual friction of two pieces of wood;
once the wood is exhausted, the ashes fly away and the smoke is extinguished. This is a metaphor drawn from distant objects.
"This is like the eye not being able to see itself"—this is a metaphor drawn from one's own body, taken from what is near. Those who study the books of the sages must understand these principles.
This is the principle.

Sentient beings, deluded and inverted, have not yet been able to eliminate all illusory transformations; thus, within the midst of their false efforts—whether cessation has occurred or not—they manifest various distinctions.

This clarifies that when speaking to those of specific capacities regarding the realization [of truth], there is no distinction between sentient beings who are deluded about themselves and those who pursue external objects through inversion;
this very delusion and inversion constitute the three subtleties and six coarsenesses.
Because their delusion is so profound, they do not realize that all phenomena—the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements—are entirely illusory and unreal.
To grasp at [the mind] as truly existent, perceiving the preceding thought but not perceiving the subsequent thought—this refers to persons in the three stages of ordinary beings, sages, and saints.
Regarding "within the false application of effort," this refers to Bodhisattvas from the seventh stage downward within the stage of sainthood;
they all cultivate the path within dreams, whereas it is only upon reaching this stage that one exclusively practices the formless (*animitta*).

When one contemplates the canopy and attains perfect clarity and realization, one first knows that afflictions are fundamentally non-existent; thus, the function of the wisdom that can sever them is already seen to be illusory.
It is like using medicine to cure a disease within a dream: once the dream has ended and one has awakened, both the medicine and the disease are gone.
Therefore, it is said that this is the realm of deluded functions.
If one attains the Tathāgata’s quiescence that accords with reality, wherein there is truly neither quiescence nor one who is quiescent—
then this realization of the fruit-position, which accords with the single-minded quiescence of all Buddhas of the ten directions without contradiction,
is not merely the non-perception of a dharma of quiescence that is realized; it is also the absence of a subject capable of realizing quiescence.
When such a person reaches this state, it is called "the two extremes"; they do not linger therein, for subject and object are both severed.
They are fully pervasive and freely flowing in all places; they are subtle and dense, encompassing the eight directions to their furthest reaches.

Lofty and majestic, there is nowhere throughout the great trichiliocosm that they do not pervade, and no land where they are not seen. Thus it is said: "Look beyond the heavens— who is this kind of person? This is the ultimate.
This is a general indication that the four stages—the ordinary person, the worthy, the sage, and the fruit—are not different;

it is only in the following text that these four stages are opened up: first, the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), which extinguishes the characteristic of stillness; second, the stage of worthiness (*ārya*), which extinguishes the characteristic of difference; third, the stage of sagehood (*ārya*), which extinguishes the characteristic of abiding;
and fourth, the stage of fruition (*phala*), which extinguishes the characteristic of arising. For the most part, this corresponds to the four stages in the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Good son, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been driven by the delusion of "self" and that which "loves the self";
because they have never known that these arise and perish moment by moment, they give rise to increased craving and become attached to the five desires.
Regarding these ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), there are two types: first, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who fully possess greed, anger, and delusion;
second, ordinary beings at the stage of the ten faiths. Herein is the first [type]. This section of text refers to those who have not yet entered the stage of faith.

The reason this text exists is that if one does not rely on the delusion of ordinary beings, there would be no stage of faith; therefore, it is first explained that "sentient beings" (*sattva*) refers to the four [categories of beings].
Regarding the birth of the nine classes of beings: that which is called "the self" due to deluded thought is the substance of what is grasped;

that which is called "loving the self" is the view of the grasper. This means that all sentient beings of the nine classes, since beginningless vast kalpas ago, because of a single moment of non-awakening, have mistakenly entered the parents' wombs through deluded thought, being [conceived] by the father's semen and the mother's...
Blood envelops the nature of one's own solitary spirit; through the conjunction of the three conditions, this body is produced.

This is the "self" that is grasped and clung to. Now, I do not know the cause from which it arises, yet upon this illusory body, I further give rise to views of attachment, saying, "This is my eye," "This is my..."
"The ears, the eyes, the nose—this is my hand, my foot, my body, my clan, and my name. Nowhere can one find a fixed "self" upon which to rely.
We contend with others over this notion of self, yet we have never once truly awakened to it.

Throughout the twelve periods of the day, the preceding thought continues into the succeeding thought, and the succeeding thought continues into the preceding thought; every thought arises and perishes like a flame.
Like the blazing of a lamp or the trickling of a stream, the myriad manifestations of the passions and deluded thoughts— whether they accord with me and I love them,
or oppose me and I hate them— are all merely the five desires of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena to which one is deeply attached.
If one encounters a virtuous friend who instructs and awakens them,
this is precisely the permeation by hearing that purifies the nature of perfect enlightenment.

This refers to internal permeation (*antar-vāsanā*). It is fundamentally empty and quiescent, like a mirror that is bright and pure: when objects come, they appear; when objects depart, it is cleansed, entirely free from obstruction.
The Patriarch said: "In the nature of mind, there is originally no nature; this was spoken to counter those who seek [something external].
Since there is nothing to be attained within the Dharma, why harbor doubts about what is or is not resolved?"
He elucidates the arising and ceasing [of thoughts].

When wisdom shines forth clearly, the nature of the mind is revealed; the delusive habits from beginningless time are all simultaneously awakened to and manifested, just as one realizes a dream upon waking.
Because deluded thoughts arise and cease at the very moment of delusion, and because these delusive thoughts take "self" as their object, the delusive thoughts themselves cannot see themselves.
Delusive thoughts are like the eye, which cannot see itself. Now that you have attained awakening, the mind is in profound accord with true enlightenment;
because you no longer take delusive thoughts as the self, you employ the wisdom of this profound accord to illuminate thoughts as they arise and cease.
You know each thought at its arising and its ceasing, whereas previously you were entirely unaware of the arising and ceasing of every moment of thought.
One immediately realizes that the nature of this life is inherently weary and anxious.
When this mind of arising and ceasing deludes the nature, the nature itself gives rise to false thoughts of arising and ceasing;

these deluded thoughts in turn exhaust and enslave the mind’s deliberations with a thousand schemes and ten thousand plans, never ceasing for a single moment. This clarifies that while one must still the delusions and follow the truth, such [delusions] nonetheless exist.
If there is truth, there is delusion; if there is no delusion, there is no truth. Those who weary themselves with their own reflections are precisely those caught in this state.
When the scholar Zhang Zhuo visited Shishuang and attained realization of the Way, he said: "Luminous and quiescent illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges;

all beings, whether ordinary or holy, are one family. When a single thought does not arise, the entire body is revealed; as soon as the six sense-faculties move, they are shrouded by clouds. He cut off [all conceptualization] right there.
To eliminate afflictions while further increasing illness and yet claim one is approaching True Suchness is also a perverse adherence.
To follow worldly conditions without hindrance while regarding nirvana and birth-and-death as flowers in the sky—
if someone should sever their wearisome anxieties and attain the purity of the Dharma-realm, that very understanding of purity becomes an obstacle to themselves.
Therefore, regarding Perfect Enlightenment (Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra), one does not attain mastery; this is called an ordinary person conforming to the nature of enlightenment.
Once they realize that thoughts of arising and ceasing are detrimental to the Way, they cease the mind of striving and contriving.

Because the deluded mind is stilled and delusion no longer arises, they attain the purity of the Dharma-realm. There are two aspects to the Dharma-realm: first, the Dharma-realm of principle (*li*); [the second is the Dharma-realm of phenomena].
Regarding the two aspects of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*): if the dharma-realm is pure, then within its original nature, it is primordially free from characteristics and transcends names;
there is nothing to be differentiated, and neither the six sense objects nor the realms of mental toil arise.
If the phenomenal dharma-realm is pure, then beyond the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements, as well as the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—
The grasses, trees, thickets, and all phenomena are, in their very essence, empty. This is because when the mind is pure, they are pure;

when the mind is defiled, they are defiled. As it has been said: "When the mind is void, the environment is tranquil; when thoughts arise, phenomena flow forth. When the water is turbid, the waves are murky;

when the pool is clear, the moon shines bright. Thus, once coarse thoughts are eliminated, one attains peaceful purity. Within this peaceful purity, one maintains the mind and gives rise to love for it, thereby forming the notion of purity.
Views are spontaneously pierced through by the very mark of pure understanding, as if one’s own nostrils were being bored; it does not come from external sensory objects to disturb one.
Therefore, it is said that within the great, perfectly enlightened state of non-action and quiescent illumination, one cannot attain unimpeded mastery.
As the ancients said: "Do not seek amidst the depths of white clouds; take care to avoid cold ashes."
"Burning to death" refers to those ordinary beings of the ten stages of faith who are constantly in accord with the nature of original enlightenment and do not turn their backs upon it. Good son,
although all Bodhisattvas perceive that views constitute an obstacle, even after they have severed the obstacle of views, they still abide in the awareness of the awareness of views.
To perceive hindrances as hindrances yet not to be subject to them—this is called the Bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stages (bhūmi) conforming to the nature of awakening.
These thirty positions of the ten stages of faith, the ten practices, and the ten dedications belong to those of the Three Sages; this is termed the stage of equipment (sambhāra-mārga).
However, because the views and understandings of those in the Three Sages are superior to those in the ten stages of faith, they subsequently awaken to the ten...
When a person of faith perceives their own understanding as an object of obstruction, they then sever their attachment to the notion of purity.

Although they have attained the removal of the notion of purity, there still remains a mind capable of seeing and awakening; thus, they dwell in attachment to this capacity for awakening and do not know how to relinquish it.
This very mind of awakening is itself an obstruction; therefore, regarding perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), [one must let go].

Within unconditioned quiescent illumination, one cannot attain self-mastery; this refers to those bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) who have not yet entered the first stage, yet whose minds are in accord with the nature of awakening.
"Noble son, both 'illumination' (zhào) and 'awakening' (jué) are termed obstacles.
Therefore, for the Bodhisattva, these ten stages of the sages— where 'illumination' refers to those in the preceding stage of faith (xìn-wei) who possess pure understanding,
and 'awakening' refers to those in the preceding stage of worthiness (xián-wei) who possess the awakening of insight— both of these are obstacles."
This is what is called awakening. The visions perceived by those in the two preceding stages are both incorrect.
For example, when Bodhidharma was about to return to the West, he commanded his disciples to each present their own realization.

At that time, Dao Fu came forward and said, "As I see it, I do not cling to words and letters, yet I do not depart from words and letters, but take them as the functioning of the Way. Bodhidharma said to him:
Dewei Pini’s dhāraṇī was: "What I now understand is like Qingxi seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha;
upon one seeing, it is never seen again. Damo said: "You have obtained my skin. Daoyu said:
"The four great elements are fundamentally empty, and the five aggregates do not exist; in my vision, there is not a single dharma that can be apprehended. Damo said: "You have obtained [my flesh]."
"My bones [belong to me], yet these three Great Beings all possess illumination and awareness; their attachment to dharmas has not yet been removed.
Therefore, a Bodhisattva dwells constantly in awareness, yet does not abide in illumination—for illumination and the illuminator are simultaneously extinguished."
"Constant awakening" (*nitya-bodha*) means "constant," which is a designation for that which is eternally unchanging; it refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

"Illumination" (*prakāśaka*) refers to the wisdom that is capable of illuminating. "The illuminator" (*prakāśaka*) refers to the objective realm being illuminated. "Cessation" (*śānti*) has the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This means that the Bodhisattva who has entered the stages (*bhūmi*) does not dwell in or cling to the wisdom that illuminates, nor to that which is about to be illuminated.
In this realm where both subject and object are empty and the two attachments are simultaneously abandoned—

namely, that which from the very beginning has been free from the marks of mental objects, free from the marks of words, free from the marks of discrimination, and free from the marks of subject and object—
it is said that one takes the markless realm as an object with markless wisdom; it is like water poured into water, resembling space.
When merged with emptiness, there is no trace remaining. How is this known? The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"When, regarding the object of cognition, the intellect perceives nothing at all, at that time one abides in consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), because one is free from the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper.
Thus, Panshan said: "Light does not illuminate objects, and objects do not exist; when both light and objects are forgotten, what is it then? This refers to the realm [of suchness].
The winds of the elements cannot blow it away; water cannot wet it. It is clear and vast, pure and bright, liberated beyond the realm of right and wrong.
Master Benren said to Qingjing: "At the summit of a high mountain, there is nothing with which to speak.
It is like the Second Patriarch, who, having finished his prostrations, stood in his place. Bodhidharma said: 'You have attained my essence.'"
As for the marrow, only the Second Patriarch was one who both illuminated and that which is illuminated were simultaneously extinguished in stillness.
It is like a person who cuts off their own head; once the head is severed, there is no longer anyone capable of cutting.
This illustration is like the case of ordinary people: before one's head has been severed, the head is the object (*karman*) and the hand is the agent (*kartṛ*).
Once one has personally used a sword to cut it off, the head becomes the object severed and the hand becomes the agent that severs.
Now that one’s own head has already been severed, how could there still be a distinction between the hand that severs and the head that is severed? It is certainly not so.
There is no such principle [of a subject that ceases]. As Master Dongpo said: "Once the head is severed, there is no further one who can sever;
when ice melts, how can it again know 'ice'?
Thus, the obstructing mind extinguishes itself; once all obstructions have been severed and extinguished, there is no longer any one who obstructs.
This is the union. That which obstructs the mind is precisely the awareness that perceives the obstruction; those various obstructions are precisely the obstructions that are perceived.
Since one uses the obstructing mind of the perceiver to awaken away the awareness of the perceived obstructions, one should further sweep away the perceiving mind all at once.
Thus, there is no longer a mind capable of extinguishing obstructions, for both the subject and the object have vanished.

From "forgetting both the scriptural text" to "dwelling in constant awakening," all of this clarifies that Bodhisattvas on the stages do not dwell in or cling to either the subject that realizes or the object realized.
The teachings of the Sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon; if one sees the moon, one understands that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon itself.

The following section clarifies non-abiding in tranquility. Herein, first, the metaphor is presented: the Sanskrit term *sūtra* is translated here as "Scripture" (*qi jing*), which serves as the general title for the teachings of the entire lifetime of the Buddha.
The Commentary states: "Now, the establishment of words and images is intended for the realization of the meaning;

yet there are those who, lacking the realization of the meaning, become deluded and confused by clinging to words and images, thereby losing sight of the Truth. Therefore, the finger pointing at the moon is used as a metaphor for [the scriptures]."

"Verbal teaching" means that to see the moon one must rely on the tip of a finger, and to awaken to the mind one must rely on the Buddha's teachings. By using the finger to see the moon, once the moon is seen, the finger is forgotten;
by using the teaching to explain the mind, once the mind is awakened, the teaching is forgotten. To retain the finger while seeking the true moon is to lose the true moon;

to cling to the teaching while seeking the fundamental mind is to lose the fundamental mind. Zhaolun says: "One who is skilled at speaking seeks that which words cannot express; one who is skilled at leaving traces..."
Regarding "traces," it means that one cannot trace them by following after traces. The Patriarch said: "The Tathāgata [teaches] all dharmas to eliminate the 'self' from all minds;
since I have no 'self' in any mind, what need is there for any dharmas? The Buddha said:

"My teaching of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures is like an empty fist used to deceive small children, or like yellow leaves used to stop a child's crying; they are merely semblances. How do we know this?
Master Pang said: "When a child is crying, the mother says, 'I will give you gold. She takes a yellow leaf and holds it up, and the crying immediately stops. Chan said:
"Upon meeting people, one must discard the objects used for knocking at the gate; having attained [the Way], one must further forget the name of the watchtower.
In general, those who have not yet entered the ground must rely on the teachings and practice cultivation; once they enter the ground, they see [for themselves].
Once one has subsequently ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*) and realized the principle, one no longer relies upon the teachings.
It is likewise with the various verbal explanations and instructions given by all Tathāgatas to bodhisattvas.

This is the harmony of the Dharma; that is to say, the various skillful means, various verbal explanations, and various parables employed by the Buddhas of the ten directions to reveal and instruct all Bodhisattvas and all sentient beings are like a finger pointing at the moon.
This is because the teachings of the entire lifetime of the Buddha were all expedient means provided out of necessity for the sake of sentient beings.

To expound and clarify the original nature: if one who has realized this nature understands that all verbal expressions are ultimately not the nature itself, they will naturally no longer cling to written characters or language. As a sutra says:
"The realization of dharmas does not reside in words," and again: "One grasps the nostrils but loses the mouth. Huìtáng said: "Five thousand [words]..."
Words serve only as pointers; one uses the finger to observe the moon in the sky, and once the moon is seen, the finger is forgotten—there is no other matter involved.
Whether intoxicated and sleeping or sober and sitting, one simply follows conditions. As Zhuangzi said: "The fish-trap exists for the sake of the fish;

once the fish is caught, forget the trap. The snare exists for the sake of the rabbit; once the rabbit is caught, forget the snare. Words exist for the sake of the meaning; once the meaning is attained, forget the words."
To say that the scriptures state, "There are only words and no real meaning," is not so; for if one merely carries empty words while seeking the Way, one is far removed from the Way.

If one treats the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as something merely marvelous, it is much like a fierce tiger entering a cage or a spiritual phoenix falling into a trap—what joy is there in such things? Have you not seen what Dongshan said?
If one is an "upward-streamer" (ūrdhvasrotas), one should not affix the words and teachings of the patriarchs and Buddhas to one's forehead;
for if they are so affixed, it is like a tortoise carrying a map—it portends its own destruction.
This is called a bodhisattva who has already entered the stages (bhūmi) conforming to the nature of awakening.
This concludes the preceding discussion on non-abiding realization and non-abiding instruction; this is how a bodhisattva who has entered the stages corresponds with the nature of awakening.
Good son, all obstacles are ultimate awakening; mindfulness and forgetfulness are nothing other than liberation;

dharmas that are established and dharmas that are destroyed are both called nirvāṇa; wisdom and folly are both universally termed prajñā; the dharmas accomplished by bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists are equally bodhi;
ignorance and suchness are no different in their realm; and all precepts, concentrations, and wisdoms—
Lust, anger, and ignorance are all the Brahma-conduct; the realms of sentient beings are of one and the same Dharma-nature ground; the hells and celestial palaces are all pure lands;
sentient beings and non-sentient things alike achieve the Buddha-way; and all afflictions are ultimately liberated.
This refers to the stage of the fruit of Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment. The former—those of the ten stages of sainthood—merely change their bones and wash their entrails;
they are utterly pure and untainted, proceeding exclusively in this manner, yet they do not understand how to come back in this manner.

This is what is called "being able to exit the realm of Māra but unable to enter the realm of Māra. One cannot call such a person one who has left behind things or transcended people; they are merely collapsing amidst good and bad fortune.
Only by beating out the impurities of the external world and holding a child so that it does not cry can one reach the stage of fruition.
It is not only a matter of knowing how to go thus, but also knowing how to come thus; not only is one able to emerge from the realm of demons, but one is also able to enter the realm of demons.
Reaching this point, whether in heaven or hell, in a tiger’s den or a demon’s palace, under the moon or before the wind, in a brothel or a tavern—[one remains free].
The mountain of knives and the forest of swords are all places where one may find rest and establish one’s life;
thus, the Chan school says, "To turn one's body is to enter the realm of demons, and to shift one's feet is to wander onto the path of the heterodox.

Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states, "Without leaving afflictions, one attains nirvana," and the celestial maiden says, "One does not exit the realm of demons to enter the realm of Buddhas. This section of the scripture contains ten pairs [of opposites].
1. The pair of consciousness and cognition; 2. The pair of establishment and refutation; 3. The pair of delusion and wisdom; 4. The pair of the heterodox and the orthodox;

5. The pair of the real and the false; 6. The pair of defilement and purity; 7. The pair of the dependent and the primary; 8. The pair of suffering and joy; 9. The pair of existence and non-existence; 10. The pair of bondage and liberation.
"That all obstacles are ultimate enlightenment"—these two phrases constitute the general heading that introduces what follows.

The distinction between the ten pairs refers to the fact that upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, wisdom merges with Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), such that there is no longer any mind of discrimination regarding superiority or inferiority.
Therefore, the dharmas of the ten subsequent pairs are all identical to the single nature of reality (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, if one perceives that there are obstructions to be severed, and then, having severed them, calls this "enlightenment," such enlightenment is not ultimate; for it still perceives the existence of obstructions to be severed.

When hindrances are awakened to, they are then called the ultimate; the attainment of mindfulness is itself wisdom. This means that when right mindfulness manifests during the twelve periods of the day, the first five consciousnesses become the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*); the sixth mental consciousness becomes the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*); the seventh consciousness becomes the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*); and the eighth, the *ālayavijñāna*— [The text continues: —becomes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-mahājñāna*). Thus, the four wisdoms are fully perfected within the eight consciousnesses. Furthermore, because these four wisdoms are fundamentally non-dual with the dharmadhātu, they are collectively termed the "Dharma-realm Wisdom" (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*). Therefore, it is said that the eight consciousnesses are the four wisdoms, and the four wisdoms are the eight consciousnesses. They are neither one nor different. It is only by awakening to this principle that one realizes Buddhahood. This is what is meant by the statement: "If one does not awaken to the mind, one wanders through birth and death; if one awakens to the mind, one attains Buddhahood. It is also said: "The mind-ground is originally pure; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it is defiled. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally luminous; it is only due to adventitious afflictions that it is obscured. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally tranquil; it is only due to false thoughts that it is disturbed. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally empty; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it is grasped. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally still; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it moves. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally unborn; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it arises. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally unconditioned; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it is conditioned. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally free from outflows; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it has outflows. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without form; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it has form. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without characteristics; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it has characteristics. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without action; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it acts. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without obstruction; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it is obstructed. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without increase or decrease; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it increases or decreases. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without coming or going; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it comes and goes. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without birth or death; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it is born and dies. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without defilement or purity; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it is defiled or pure. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without bondage or liberation; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it is bound or liberated. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without gain or loss; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it is gained or lost. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without increase or decrease; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it increases or decreases. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without change or transformation; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it changes and transforms. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without movement or stillness; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it moves or is still. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without arising or ceasing; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it arises and ceases. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without beginning or end; it is only due to deluded thoughts that it has a beginning and an end. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without self or other; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is self and other. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without subject or object; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is subject and object. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without duality or non-duality; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is duality or non-duality. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without existence or non-existence; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is existence or non-existence. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without being or non-being; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is being or non-being. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without permanence or impermanence; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is permanence or impermanence. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without pleasure or pain; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is pleasure or pain. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without emptiness or non-emptiness; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is emptiness or non-emptiness. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without oneness or manyness; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is oneness or manyness. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without distance or proximity; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is distance or proximity. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without high or low; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is high or low. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without inside or outside; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is inside or outside. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without center or periphery; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is center or periphery. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without near or far; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is near or far. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without light or dark; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is light or dark. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without sound or silence; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is sound or silence. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without color or form; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is color or form. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without fragrance or odor; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is fragrance or odor. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without taste or flavor; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is taste or flavor. It is also said: "The nature of the mind is originally without touch or sensation; it is only due to deluded thoughts that there is touch or sensation. This is a gate of awakening found even within this place of clamor.

The principle underlying these penetrations is that both subject and object are states of obstruction. To understand is the "subject" (the mind), and the body is the "object.
As soon as subject and object exist, both the true and the false are obstructive phenomena. That which lacks cognition is called the "mind," while the periphery of the mind is called "knowledge";
that which touches the body is called "awareness. Once one realizes that both subject and object are obstructive phenomena, [one transcends them].

If one enters this contemplation, the realm of experience becomes such that there is no longer a knower, nothing known, and no object of awareness. Since neither subject nor object exists, there is only this single mind.
This single mind is luminously clear and never obscured; it is ever-awakened and knows all things, abiding eternally without extinction throughout the bounds of the future.
Thus it is said: "The moon of the mind shines alone, illuminating heaven and earth as one; this is its radiance."
The single character "One" (之) precisely reveals the wondrous, absolute, and peerless essence.

If one wishes to call it empty and still, it is not like the great void; if one wishes to speak of its characteristics and functions, they are not...

It is called the Way (*dharma*) because it is deep below and unfathomable, encompassing heaven and earth in its vastness while penetrating the Avīci Hell in its subtlety.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. He made this request three times, beginning and ending the cycle. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Bianyin:

The Bodhisattva said, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! That you are able, for the sake of this great assembly and for the sentient beings of the future age, to question the Tathāgata regarding such cultivation—listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vibhūṣaṇa, having received the instruction with joy, along with the entire great assembly, listened in silence.
Because it is the mark of the markless, it is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); its essential nature is precisely Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Good son, all Tathāgatas are pure in their Perfect Enlightenment and fundamentally possess neither cultivation nor a cultivator.
All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon the power of illusion due to their lack of awakening; at that time, [cultivation] then comes to exist.
The twenty-five kinds of the wheel of pure meditative concentration:
this response cites the intent to indicate the number. As for "all Tathāgatas," this refers to the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the Buddhas of the ten directions;
within the vast, luminous, and perfectly awakened pure essence, there is fundamentally nothing to be cultivated.

Since this person has neither cultivation nor realization, for what reason do all the teachings speak of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age as having both cultivation and realization?

It is simply because, based on the single thought of non-awakening within original enlightenment, one becomes deluded regarding the truth, turns away from the profound stillness, loses the fundamental nature, and undergoes saṃsāra; that which is taught by all Buddhas is merely based upon this non-awakening.
Therefore, it is said that through the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*), when cultivation is practiced, there is indeed cultivation and realization.

This cultivation, being adapted to the capacities of sentient beings, consists of twenty-five kinds of pure wheels of meditative concentration (*viśuddha-samādhi-cakra*). These wheels possess the sense of "skillful means" (*upāya*), meaning they are able to crush the obstacles of affliction so as to bring forth the wheel of right knowledge;
thus they are called "wheels. Regarding these twenty-five wheels, first, the initial three:
In Master Miako’s commentary on the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*, twenty-five contemplations are each given a name based on metaphors;

these are fully utilized in Guifeng’s commentary to organize the scriptural text and make the meditative practices clearly manifest. Specifically, there are twenty-one cycles for the sequential cultivation of single contemplations, one cycle for the interlaced cultivation of multiple contemplations, and one final cycle for the perfected cultivation of the three contemplations.
If bodhisattvas grasp only at extreme tranquility and, by the power of that tranquility,
permanently sever the afflictions and ultimately achieve fulfillment such that they enter nirvana without rising from their seats, these bodhisattvas are said to practice śamatha alone.

Regarding the twenty-five wheels listed below this section for the Bodhisattvas and others, each should also be individually identified as "Awakening to Pure Perfect Enlightenment as the Fundamental Basis for Initiating Practice.

However, since they were already identified and listed previously, I have omitted them here to avoid excessive textual prolixity. Furthermore, the characteristics of these three contemplative practices [were discussed] previously.

This has already been fully explained; now, it is simply to be divided into twenty-five categories to correspond with twenty-five types of capacities and to reveal the characteristics of the single and the manifold, which is why the previous details have been omitted here.
This present stage is the contemplation of clarifying the turbid and ceasing activity.
This contemplation is like murky water: first one must clarify it to make it pure, and once it is pure, one can then [perceive] within it.
Just as one perceives objects in the present, practicing this tranquil contemplation (*śamatha*) is likewise so:

it means that since the practitioner has come from immeasurable kalpas past, they have used nothing but this mind of ignorance, afflictions, all karmic obstructions, delusive thoughts, inversions, and discursive攀缘 (pān-yuan) discrimination, never ceasing for even a moment;
now that they have entered this contemplation, they should bring it to rest through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regulate the breath and subdue it so that it does not arise again, like a person holding a staff watching cattle so they do not damage the crops.

Seek only the ultimate stillness; this clarifies that one-pointed, tranquil mindfulness no longer relies upon form or color, nor upon earth, water, fire, or wind, nor upon seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
Through the power of this tranquil mindfulness and profound contemplation, one subsequently perceives the body.
The mind is entirely empty and quiescent; since even a fleeting thought lacks affliction, how could it possibly exist?
Since afflictions do not arise, it is entirely the awakened mind. Thus it is said that "ultimate accomplishment" means entering nirvana without rising from one's seat;
this refers to entering the state of all Buddhas without rising from the very seat of the emptiness of the essence of phenomena.
Quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*) is the principle of suchness (*tathatā*).

If bodhisattvas contemplate all things as being like illusions, then by the power of the Buddha, they manifest various functions within transformed worlds and fully practice the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva;
through these dhāraṇīs, they do not lose their quiescent mindfulness or their various tranquil wisdoms.
This Bodhisattva practices what is called the "Single Cultivation of Samāpatti.
This is the "Culinary One’s Unrestrained Blade Contemplation," which originally appears in the "Nourishing Life" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*.
That text is a parable concerning a man surnamed Pao and named Ding, who served as a butcher for the Lord of Wenhui; it describes what he saw three years prior.
There was nothing that was not an ox; after three years, he no longer saw the whole ox.
His butcher’s knife, though used for nineteen years, had never suffered even the slightest wear, as if it were a fresh blade just emerged from the whetstone.
Indeed, the hundred limbs of the ox have their separations and unions, their curves and straightness, their apertures and cavities—yet, as for [the knife]...
Even at the tip of a single hair, there is no place where a dharma-realm does not exist; how much more so for the spaces between the fine bones—how could they alone lack orderly arrangement?

Furthermore, where there is a separation, one follows that separation to separate them; where there is a union, one follows that union to join them; where there is curvature, one arranges them crosswise;
where there is straightness, one follows it to connect them. Where there is a cavity, they pass through; where there is no cavity, they stop. If...
Now, when the dissection of the ox reaches this point, it is as if disassembling earth; once movement begins, the hundred parts are already divided.
What further effort could there be in between? If this is so, then the ox is not harmed and the blade remains as it was.
For the ox is a metaphor for things, and the blade is a metaphor for life. Thus, the ox dissected by one who is skilled at dissection, though—

Though the multitude [of things] is encountered, the blade is not diminished in the least; for one who meets with things skillfully, although the objects encountered may be numerous, the source of life remains unharmed.
"Ten" is a yin number and "nine" is a yang number; this shows that the passing of years has already been long.
That he saw the ox three years ago indicates that he did not see the Dao, but saw only the thing. Three.
That after three years he no longer saw the "whole ox" means that he saw the Way and did not see the object.
Now, if one passes a lifetime amidst infinite changes and events, unless one nourishes and sustains oneself by following the nature of destiny and the reality of one's being,
then one will ruin one’s life, injure one’s nature, diminish one’s virtue, and shorten one’s lifespan, standing as a neighbor to death.
One can endure for a long time without the spirit being exhausted and the *hun* and *po* souls being fatigued.

According to the intent of Zhuangzi, the ox represents all the illusory and unreal things of this world—high reputation, substantial profit, glory, wealth, honor, rank, wine, beauty, riches, and vital energy.
The knife represents one's own body; with this body, one accords with the myriad things.

If one entrusts affairs to spontaneity (*ziran*) and does not transgress the principle of one's allotted nature (*xingfen*), then one can nurture the person, remain far from calamities and hardships, and live out their natural span to the full extent of their longevity, avoiding an untimely end by the axe. This is the meaning of abiding in the Middle Way and following the intent of the scriptures;
it is not otherwise. To take the ox as a metaphor for the myriad practices (*wanxing*) and the knife as a metaphor for the numinous clarity (*lingming*)—this is the contemplation.
Wisdom is likened to a Bodhisattva who, upon entering this contemplation, benefits sentient beings and extensively cultivates the myriad practices;

though engaging with the mundane through various activities according to conditions, it remains ever luminous and ever distinct upon the foundation of one’s own numinous, enlightened wisdom, manifesting in its entirety and alone without the slightest deficiency.
Even for a single thought-moment when one is not at home [in this state], it is already so.

Because it blunts the blade of one’s own wisdom, it is illustrated by the analogy of Cook Ding who wields his knife with ease. The Sūtra states that "the power of the Buddha" refers to the power of awakening;
"fully practicing the pure and wondrous conduct of a Bodhisattva" refers to precept (śīla); "extensively delivering all classes of beings" refers to [compassion];
"fully studying the Dharma-gates without losing silent mindfulness" refers to concentration (samādhi); and "all various still wisdoms" refers to wisdom (prajñā).

If bodhisattvas merely extinguish all illusions without engaging in their functions, severing afflictions alone until afflictions are completely exhausted without relying on various practices—this is precisely the meaning of being "absolutely beyond dependence. This is the realization of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Such a bodhisattva is called one who "practices *dhyāna* exclusively."

Regarding the observation that sound emerges from obstruction and that prior stillness is observed, it is said: "It is like the resonance of a bell within a vessel, where the sound issues forth externally.

Master Ke’s Commentary states: "It is like a ten-thousand-jun bronze bell; though the star-studded tower obstructs it, a single strike of the mallet causes its sound to vibrate throughout the universe.
Since its own essence encompasses others, it cannot be hindered or obstructed. How could the tower constrain the form of the bell such that the resonance would fail to emerge?"
To "penetrate" means to allow form and obstruction to pass through pipes and strings; it refers to that which prevents sound from being transparent.

Only by extinguishing all illusions and not grasping at activity can one do so, for illusory phenomena are boundless and difficult to exhaustively investigate. Thus, it is said simply: "extinguish, extinguish," which means the severing of thought.
Furthermore, because activity and purposeful action obstruct meditative stillness (*śamatha*), it is said: "do not grasp. This refers to the solitary severance of afflictions (*kleśa*).
When one merely accords with the fundamental awakening of the numinous mind, afflictions naturally cease to exist.

Since that which is to be severed is empty and non-existent, this very state is itself realization. Regarding the three contemplations—quiescence (*śamatha*), illusion (*māyā*), and stillness (*śānti*)—these are practiced individually;
however, how do quiescence and stillness differ? Quiescence is the realm of the two vehicles, while stillness is the realm of the Buddhas. Furthermore...
"Quietude" (*śamatha*) refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), while "stillness" (*nirvāṇa*) refers to liberation;
therefore, they are not the same. Next, the twenty-one wheels are divided into three categories, with seven wheels in each category.

In the first category, one first takes quiet contemplation as the primary practice, while concurrently cultivating illusory contemplation and still contemplation; thus, there are two types: that which is practiced first and that which is practiced later.

Regarding the first cycle, there are two wheels: the preliminary cultivation, the intermediate cultivation, and the subsequent cultivation; and the wheel of non-cultivation and simultaneous cultivation, followed by the subsequent cultivation—these three wheels together constitute seven wheels.
In the second cycle, taking the illusory contemplation as the primary focus while concurrently practicing tranquility, there are again two wheels:

the preliminary cultivation, the intermediate cultivation, and the subsequent cultivation; and the three wheels of preliminary cultivation, simultaneous cultivation, and subsequent cultivation—these together likewise constitute seven wheels.
The third stage again takes quiescent contemplation as the primary focus, practicing both quiescence and insight in the sequence previously described;
thus, they together constitute twenty-one cycles (three times seven). Now, we shall address the first stage, which takes quiescent contemplation as the primary focus.
If bodhisattvas first attain profound stillness and, with a mind of still wisdom, illuminate all illusions,
thereby initiating bodhisattva practice therein, these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated śamatha and subsequently cultivated samāpatti.

The first is the Contemplation of the Ferrying Boat that Simultaneously Saves Others. This means that when this Bodhisattva cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to transcend the mundane world, it is like setting sail;
when he brings forth wisdom (*prajñā*) to transform sentient beings, it is "simultaneous salvation. "First, attaining ultimate stillness" indicates the beginning:

by reaching the utmost emptiness, one maintains stillness with earnest devotion. Therefore, this Contemplation of Stillness is established as the primary focus, using a mind of still-wisdom to follow the traces of stillness step by step.
To initiate practice is like setting the sail; the mind of tranquil wisdom is the boat itself. To illuminate all illusions is to give rise to the bodhisattva practices therein.
This involves the simultaneous cultivation of the contemplation of illusion. If there were no tranquility, one would oneself dwell within the realm of illusion;
how then could one illuminate illusions to deliver others? It would be like a boat that sinks by itself—how could it rescue those drowning? Thus it is.
A Bodhisattva is one who first cultivates śamatha and subsequently cultivates samāpatti;
this combination of prior and subsequent cultivation constitutes the first cycle.
If bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom, realize the nature of tranquility and thereby sever the afflictions to emerge forever from birth and death,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated śamatha and subsequently cultivated dhyāna.
Second is the Contemplation of the Tranquil Sea Clarifying the Void. Regarding the tranquil sea, the waves do not stir; this is first using still contemplation to reverse the flow.
Regarding the void clarifying the water-nature, the nature of water becomes clear and bright; this is subsequently using silent contemplation to manifest the nature.

If Bodhisattvas, by means of still wisdom, attain stillness, they realize the nature of ultimate stillness; since the nature is itself quiescence, they tread upon stillness while concurrently cultivating quiescence.

Thus, one cuts off afflictions and forever emerges from birth and death. The function of these two contemplations consists of cutting off afflictions as the cause and emerging from birth and death as the result;
yet when the cause perishes, the result is lost. This Bodhisattva is said to first practice *śamatha* and subsequently practice *dhyāna*.
This is the second cycle concerning what is practiced first and what is practiced later.
If Bodhisattvas, by means of tranquil wisdom, further manifest various transformations through the power of illusion to deliver sentient beings,
and subsequently sever their afflictions to enter into quiescent extinction, these Bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *śamatha*,
then cultivated *samāpatti*, and finally cultivated *dhyāna*.
The three contemplations of Maheśvara’s three eyes: these three contemplations are cultivated together like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara.

First, when Bodhisattvas use tranquil wisdom to bring about stillness, this is "stillness" (寂). Second, they further manifest various transformations through the power of illusion to deliver all sentient beings;
this is "illusion" (幻). Finally, they sever afflictions and enter into quiescent extinction; this is "quiescence" (寂). This is the Bodhi... [text ends]
"Sā" refers to first practicing *śamatha*, then practicing *samāpatti*, and finally practicing *dhyāna*;
this is termed "the single wheel of first, middle, and final practice."
If Bodhisattvas, having severed afflictions through the power of ultimate stillness, subsequently give rise to the pure and wondrous conduct of a Bodhisattva to deliver all sentient beings,
these Bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *śamatha*, then practiced *dhyāna*,
and finally practiced *samāpatti*.
"Fourth, the simultaneous cultivation of the three contemplations. Regarding the "three points," this refers to the Sanskrit letter *i* (𑖮𑖿). The *Jiao shu* (Commentary on the Essentials) states:
"When a single person cultivates the three contemplations together, it is called 'simultaneous' (*qi*); it does not mean they occur at the same moment.

It refers to when Bodhisattvas, through the power of ultimate stillness—having first attained 'stillness' (*jing*) by severing afflictions and subsequently attained 'tranquility' (*ji*)—thereafter initiate the pure and wondrous practices of a Bodhisattva."

To deliver all sentient beings is an illusion; since afflictions have been exhausted and attachment and views have perished, the practices they initiate are without exception pure and sublime, capable of untying the bonds of others.
This Bodhisattva is one who first practiced the middle wheel and subsequently practiced the third wheel.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of ultimate stillness, sever afflictions with the mind, and further deliver sentient beings while establishing worlds,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *śamatha* and then practiced *samāpatti* and *dhyāna* in equal measure.
The five grades consist of single and dual contemplations. The first is the single, quiescent contemplation as described above;
the latter is the dual clarification of stillness and illusion as shown by the two subsequent mouths. Therefore, they are called "single and dual.

If Bodhisattvas, through the power of ultimate stillness, quiet their minds, sever afflictions, further deliver sentient beings, and establish worlds—such Bodhisattvas are said to have "previously cultivated" [the path].
To cultivate śamatha and samāpatti-samādhi in equal measure is to cultivate both the illusory and the tranquil simultaneously;

the first phrase refers to stillness, while the latter two phrases refer to the illusory and the tranquil. This constitutes first practicing simultaneous cultivation and subsequently practicing the first cycle.
If a bodhisattva, having first aroused transformative power through the force of supreme tranquility and subsequently severed the afflictions,
is called a bodhisattva who practices śamatha and samāpatti together and subsequently cultivates dhyāna.
Sixth is the contemplation of the two-headed, single-legged being. In the *Bai Ze Tu*, there is a mountain spirit whose head is like a drum and has two faces, visible both front and back.
This is a metaphor for the simultaneous illumination of stillness and transformation, where the two benefits operate in unison, like the two heads;
the solitary, tranquil contemplation is like the single leg. If bodhisattvas employ the power of ultimate stillness to support and stimulate their transformative manifestations...
By simultaneously marking stillness and illusion, one employs the power of ultimate stillness to assist and stimulate the power of transformation in order to deliver sentient beings;
subsequently, one cuts off afflictions. This Bodhisattva is said to practice *śamatha* and *samāpatti* together first, followed by *dhyāna*;
this refers to "quiescence" (*jì*). Because the two prior benefits are complete, one enters the Middle Way. This is the section [in question].
This differs from the preceding section of the sutra. In the former, stillness alone constitutes the beginning, while at the end, both stillness and illusion are practiced;

here, stillness and illusion are treated as equal from the start, and one begins by practicing stillness alone. To make this easy to see: in the former, the upper [part] is single and the lower is dual;
here, the upper is dual and the lower is single. This represents simultaneous cultivation, whereas the latter begins with the second [stage].
It is like a wheel.
If bodhisattvas employ the power of ultimate stillness to support their state of cessation before initiating activity to transform worlds,
such bodhisattvas are said to practice śamatha and dhyāna together first, followed by the practice of samāpatti.

The seventh is the contemplation of the falling fruit and blooming flowers: having already used the tree of meditative concentration to produce the fruit of the Middle Way of cessation, one now uses the subsequent blooming of flowers to enter the realm of sentient beings through the contemplation of illusion, delivering all beings so that they may likewise attain the fruit of nirvana.
If bodhisattvas employ the power of ultimate stillness to support cessation, they bring about simultaneous extinction.

Furthermore, when one subsequently brings forth the function to transform the world, this Bodhisattva is said to be practicing *śamatha* and *dhyāna* in equal measure, followed by the practice of *samāpatti*, which includes the illusory (*māyā*). This is the third cycle of equal cultivation.
Next, in each of the seven cycles, "illusory" is first designated as the primary focus, while the other two are practiced concurrently.
If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of transformation, takes up profound stillness through various forms of conformity,
this bodhisattva is said to have first practiced *samāpatti* and subsequently practiced *śamatha*.
Now, first is the observation of "military followed by civil":

this refers to King Wu, who first raised his armies to conquer King Zhou, then turned his weapons upside down, returned the horses to the southern slopes of Mount Hua, released the oxen into the wilds of Taolin, and melted down his spears and halberds to forge agricultural tools—thus laying down arms and cultivating culture.
This serves as a metaphor for this Bodhisattva, who first manifests transformations and sows seeds.
Having first practiced in accordance with the liberation of sentient beings, one subsequently enters into quiet contemplation (*śamatha*).

If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of transformation, adapts to various manifestations of this "phantasm" (*māyā*) and thereby attains ultimate stillness, such a bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated *samāpatti* (meditative attainment) and subsequently cultivated *śamatha*. This is the first cycle of sequential practice.
If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of transformation, attains quiescence through various objective realms,
this bodhisattva is said to have first cultivated samāpatti and subsequently cultivated dhyāna.

The second is the contemplation of retiring upon the completion of one's merit. This is illustrated by the analogy of a scholar who, after passing the imperial examinations, establishes great merit and achieves great fame at court;
yet when his merit is accomplished and his success realized, he withdraws from office and returns to seclusion, remaining as he was before—merely the same scholar of old.
This illustrates how a Bodhisattva, having generated wisdom to benefit others and deliver sentient beings, immediately [withdraws] once the task is finished.
When this merit is perfected and one practices quiescence through internal cultivation, it is called "retirement.

If various bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, encounter diverse realms that are like illusions and yet attain nirvana, these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated *samāpatti* and subsequently cultivated *dhyāna*, combining both quiescence and insight; this is the second cycle of sequential practice.
If bodhisattvas perform buddha-work through the power of transformation, abiding in tranquility while severing afflictions,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced samāpatti, then cultivated śamatha, and finally cultivated dhyāna.
The third is the illusionist’s mastery of the art of dissolution: first one initiates transformations by performing magical feats, and subsequently returns to the tranquil essence of stillness;
therefore, it is called "dissolving the art of illusion into stillness. This constitutes the first cycle of the beginning, middle, and end.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation and unimpeded activity, sever the afflictions and abide in ultimate tranquility,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first practiced *samāpatti* and cultivated *dhyāna*, followed by cultivating *śamatha*.

The fourth, the contemplation of the hidden sea of the divine dragons, means that the arising of illusory transformations is like divine dragons spreading clouds and rain, while returning to the essence and entering stillness is like hiding in the sea;
this is the second wheel, consisting of the prior, middle, and subsequent stages.
If a bodhisattva, through the power of transformation and skillful means, acts in such a way that both [the phenomenal and the quiescent] accord with ultimate stillness and extinction,
this bodhisattva is said to have previously cultivated samāpatti while practicing śamatha and dhyāna in unison.
The fifth is Nāgārjuna, who realized the True Contemplation (*tathatā-darśana*). This means that he first employed *māyā* (illusory arts) and subsequently returned to profound stillness.

It is said that when Nāgārjuna first practiced illusory arts, he extensively converted those following heterodox paths; later, he studied the True Vehicle (*saddharma-yāna*) and personally attained the fruit of sainthood. Regarding his name, "Nāgārjuna," the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) states:
"To the north of a great city in Western India, there was a large tree whose shade sheltered five hundred great *nāgas*. Because of this, [he] was named..."

The King of Trees named Nāgārjuna constantly preached the Dharma for the assembly. When he first entered the Buddha-way, for ninety days he contemplated the entirety of the Tathāgata’s teachings throughout his lifetime;
he then cried out in a loud voice, "Who would have thought that the Tathāgata’s teachings were so vast and extensive?
Thereupon, he entered the Dragon Palace and recited the lower version of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in over one hundred thousand verses, which are still transmitted today.
This is the first stage of equal cultivation for those who dwell in the world.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of transformation, employ various functions to support ultimate stillness and subsequently sever afflictions,
these bodhisattvas are said to cultivate samāpatti and śamatha equally, followed by the cultivation of dhyāna.
Sixth is the manifestation of signs through contemplation (*saṃjñā-nimitta-bhāvanā*). Saṃgharakṣita was the teacher of Upagupta.

Having first subdued the arrogance of Upagupta’s disciples by manifesting signs through his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), he subsequently entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and passed into parinirvāṇa.
This was the second turning of the wheel during the Qi period.
If a bodhisattva, by means of the power of transformation, supports the state of cessation and subsequently dwells in pure,
effortless meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this bodhisattva is said to practice *samāpatti* and *dhyāna* simultaneously, followed by the practice of *śamatha*.
The seven great penetrations are the silent contemplation of the Great Penetrating Tathāgata, who is the Buddha himself. First he benefits sentient beings, and subsequently he returns to quiescence;
this corresponds to the third cycle after the Qi period. In each of the subsequent seven cycles, "quiescence" is first designated as the primary focus, while the other two are concurrently included.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation, give rise to supreme tranquility and abide in purity,
such bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated dhyāna and subsequently cultivated śamatha.

Now, first is the contemplation of the Jewel-Bright Ocean of Emptiness. The *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra* (or *Uṣṇīṣa-vijaya-dhāraṇī*) states: "Together they enter the Tathāgata’s Jewel-Bright Ocean of Emptiness.
Here, the contemplation of the numinous mind is the luminosity of original enlightenment, like the jewel-brightness; the subsequent quiet contemplation is like the ocean of emptiness.
Furthermore, the jewel-brightness is wisdom (*prajñā*), while the ocean of emptiness is cultivation (*bhāvanā*); this is the first stage of the cycle.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of quiescence, initiate activity within all objects such that their quiescent function accords with this state,
these bodhisattvas are said to have first cultivated dhyāna and subsequently cultivated samāpatti.

The second is the contemplation of the wondrous function of space. This means that the essence of the numinous mind is like space; when it gives rise to transformations, this is its wondrous function.
This is the second stage, following the first.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of quiescence, abide in meditative concentration with various intrinsic natures and give rise to transformations, [this is the wondrous function].
This Bodhisattva is one who first cultivates *dhyāna*, then cultivates *śamatha* within it, and subsequently cultivates *samāpatti*.

This is the "Śunyata Manifesting the Spirit" contemplation from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; *Śunyata* refers here to the spirit of empty space, which briefly appears when encountered by the reflection of sunlight.
Cultivating this contemplation involves first achieving stillness (*jī*), then serenity (*jìng*), and finally the illusory (*huàn*). This sequence represents the stages of beginning, middle, and end.
This is the first cycle.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of cessation and the unconditioned nature, give rise to functional activity within the pure realm and return to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
such bodhisattvas are said to have previously cultivated *dhyāna* and subsequently cultivated *samāpatti*.
Subsequently, one cultivates *śamatha*.
The fourth is the "Prabhāsa-ābhāsvara" (*Ābhāsvara*) entry into meditative observation; this refers to Mahākāśyapa, also known as Mahā-kūrma.

In the past, he was a goldsmith who was skilled at understanding the nature of gold, making it malleable and pliable so that he could gild it upon the Buddha, thereby attaining a golden complexion through this meditative observation.
First one realizes the essence, next one gives rise to supernormal powers, and finally one returns to meditative concentration; this is the second wheel of the sequence—first, middle, and last.
If bodhisattvas, by the power of quiescence and through various forms of purity, abide in dhyāna and give rise to transformations.
This Bodhisattva is named Xianxiu (First Cultivation of Dhyāna); he practiced śamatha and samāpatti in equal measure.

He manifested fivefold supernormal powers through the observation of many jewels; because the Buddha Prabhūtaratna had previously attained the Way and realized the essence of True Suchness, he subsequently manifested within the stupa from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, appearing as tranquil, illusory, and unimpeded—this is what is meant by "first practicing in equal measure."
This is the first cycle.
If bodhisattvas, by means of the power of cessation (*śamatha*), support ultimate stillness and give rise to transformations,
these bodhisattvas are said to practice *dhyāna* and *śamatha* simultaneously, followed by the practice of *samāpatti*.
The sixth is the transformation-observation ascending from below; this refers to the appearance of sixty thousand bodhisattvas from the lower direction as described in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
This constitutes the second cycle following the Qi period.

If these bodhisattvas, by means of the power of quiescent extinction (*śānti*), augment their transformative manifestations, they give rise to the wisdom of the most tranquil, pure, and luminous realm.
This Bodhisattva is named "One Who Practices Śamatha and Samāpatti Simultaneously, and Subsequently Practices Śamatha.

can still understand through description even when the eyes do not see objects; yet, if [one were blind] while in the womb...
If one is born blind and lacks sight from birth, then when encountering forms, no matter how many various explanations are given, it will ultimately be of no benefit.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "It is like a blind person who does not recognize the color of milk and asks another, 'What is the color of milk like?
The other replies, 'Its color is like a white shell. The blind person asks again, 'Is this color of milk like... [and so on].
He replied, "No. He asked again, "What does the color of the conch resemble? He replied, "It is like rice powder.
He asked again, "Is the color of the milk as soft as rice powder? And what does the rice powder resemble?
He replied, "It is like snow and rain. He further said, "That rice powder is cold like snow and rain."

"What are snow and rain like? He replied, "They are like a person born blind who hears descriptions of these four kinds of analogies but ultimately cannot perceive the true color of milk. Thus, as the poem by Hanshan says:
"The causal conditions are entirely unknown; the blind man asks about the color of milk. In this way, the blind man asks about milk, and the lame man seeks [to know] the path.

The meaning is the same as that of the previous passage. Since the nature of body and mind and so forth are all ignorance, when one attains the ground of the original arising in the preceding Mañjuśrī chapter, then all dharmas practiced are the causes of Buddhahood;
yet now, by employing the original ignorance, all dharmas governed thereby are the karmas of Māra. Furthermore, because the prior awakening was perfectly luminous, the faculties and objects...
The *Pujing* Sūtra states that "all is awakening," yet because ignorance is taken as the root, it is said that "all is ignorance.
This is like using gold to make a thousand vessels—all thousand vessels are gold; it is like using clay to make vessels—all vessels are earthenware.
For example, the phrase "there is no one who does not sever their own life" refers to this clinging to a self.
If one does not perceive, does not know, and cannot sever the [defilements] oneself, one resembles those of lowly and base station in the world;

though they may be utterly debased, lacking in their six sense faculties, with clothing that does not cover their bodies and food that does not fill their mouths, would they ever willingly consent to sever their own lives?
Since they do not so consent, this analogy can also be applied to the subsequent section regarding "attachment to self."
Regarding the statement on "nurturing ignorance," the subsequent section forms a continuous chain of textual logic; thus, it connects with the preceding and following passages.
Therefore, one should know that for those who love me, I accord with them, while toward those who do not accord with me, I give rise to hatred and resentment.
Because one nurtures ignorance through love and hatred, the continuity of seeking the Way fails to achieve fruition.
This single point summarizes the preceding text: from time immemorial, the reason why all who are born here fail to realize the Way is due to the presence of craving.
Regarding the phrase "I and those who accord with me," this refers to the arising of a loving heart toward favorable conditions.

To say that the notion of a self arises toward those who do not comply with one’s wishes and gives rise to hatred and resentment is to explain the existence of a self by means of the arising of a hateful mind toward an adverse object.

This serves to clarify the existence of a self. By means of the aforementioned two minds—hatred and attachment—one nurtures the seeds of ignorance (*avidyā*), both in their latent state and in their active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
What is meant by this is that seeds permeate active manifestations, and active manifestations permeate seeds; it does not go beyond this.
This view does not transcend form, nor does the hearing extend beyond the realm of sound;

the mind arises and follows after objects of perception without ceasing, such that from moment to moment there is hatred and love, from moment to moment there is grasping and rejecting, and from moment to moment they continue in succession. To seek awakening to Perfect Enlightenment and achieve the Buddha-way with such a mind is impossible.
Even if one were to undergo diligent suffering for kalpas, performing various practices, it would be of no avail.
The gateway merely turns and assists in producing ignorance—this is like drilling ice to seek fire, digging earth to find heaven, seeking fish by leaning against wood, or using sand to make rice;
though one exerts oneself with frantic effort, nothing can ever be accomplished.
The preceding scriptural passage provides a general account of the origins of these errors, while the following text specifically explains the four characteristics.
"Good son, what is the mark of self? It refers to that which is realized by the minds of all sentient beings.
The following passage provides a specific explanation of the four marks regarding the bodhisattva’s delusion concerning the realm of wisdom; for now, it inquires:
"How does a bodhisattva fall into the mark of self? The answer states: "The word 'called' (yì) is a term of evaluation."
When Bodhisattvas of great resolve first enter the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*),
they take the seventh consciousness as the means of realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) and the eighth consciousness as the object of realization.

Although one may abandon delusion and realize the truth through the path of cultivation, if this very consciousness that acts as the means of realization remains unextinguished, it is termed [the "defiled mind"].
The aspect of "self" (ātman) belongs to the seventh consciousness, which is the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*), while the eighth consciousness belongs to the image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*).

Indeed, the Sanskrit term *manas* is translated here as "defiled root. The four delusions are self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), and self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Good son, it is like a person whose hundred limbs are in perfect harmony who suddenly forgets his own body;

when the tendons of his four limbs become slack because his nourishment and care have gone astray, he becomes aware of the existence of a self upon the slightest application of acupuncture or moxibustion. Therefore, it is through such realization that the substance of the self manifests itself.

When the strings are too tight, the sound is hurried; when they are too loose, it is slow. These are all manifestations of the limbs being out of tune and the hands and feet failing to maintain their proper measure.
As for the methods [of healing], needles and moxibustion are like the realms of the "contrary" and the "conforming.

As the Sūtra says: "All those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables. It is like people in the world who, when their hundred bones and joints are in harmony and at ease, momentarily forget [their physical burdens].
Regarding the symptoms of tension and relaxation in my limbs and body, this illustrates how, when external conditions neither oppose nor favor one, the perception of a self momentarily vanishes.

As for the methods of regulation and preservation, if one errs in their application—applying heat when cold is required, or cold when heat is required—the symptoms of rigidity and flaccidity in the limbs will manifest quite clearly. One day, a physician arrives and perhaps applies acupuncture.
Or, when one is cauterized with moxa, the limbs feel pain;
this illustrates that when opposing or favorable conditions arise, the arising of a root of joy in the mind is precisely the mark of selfhood (*ātman*). Those who study the Way today are likewise:

whether dwelling in quiet chambers or hiding in deep mountains, they distance themselves from things and abandon people, remaining indolent beyond the realms of fortune and misfortune, their minds ceasing all worldly striving toward external objects.
When one has no longer attachment or aversion, and through long practice in seclusion, their nature is perfected;
when they momentarily attain the forgetting of emotions and are unaware of self or others, they claim, "I have already attained the Way and fully realized the mark of non-self.
Such a person, even if moved by worldly fame, substantial profit, splendor, wealth, wine, beauty, riches, or vital energy, remains unmoved; they can only be praised for this.
When one attains the Dharma or realizes the Dharma, one immediately feels joy; yet when one slanders the Dharma of non-attainment, one immediately feels anger.

This very mind of joy and this mind of anger are precisely the mark of self (*ātman*). One may think for oneself that one has abandoned delusion and realized truth, and for a time there is no sense of self;
yet as soon as others encounter one with circumstances of either adversity or favor, they attempt to grasp at me.
I am as I was before. Good son,
even that mind which realizes the ultimate, thoroughly understood, and pure nirvana of the Tathāgata is still the mark of selfhood.
The preceding passage describes the coarse characteristics; this concluding reference points to the subtle characteristics.
"That mind even up to its realization" refers to the subject (the agent); "the Tathāgata ultimately and fully knows" refers to the object.
Within the object, "the Tathāgata ultimately and fully knows" is the subject, while "pure nirvāṇa" is the object. The intended meaning is that it is not merely a matter of knowing.
The nirvāṇa of the two vehicles is established based on the mark of self;
