even if one were to understand that the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is likewise a mark of self, the nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is merely the void, the perfect illumination, the unconditioned essence of awakening—it is not something else to be realized.
Since one has now attained nirvāṇa yet does not forget the subject-object duality, both are marks of self. Therefore, the ancients...
"Virtuous Cloud, even if one exhausts the matter to the very bottom, one is still wading through wind and waves.

"Noble son, what is meant by 'great signs'? [The Buddha replied: "It refers to those sentient beings whose minds have attained realization. Noble son, one who realizes the existence of a self no longer identifies with 'what belongs to me.
Realizing that which is not-self is likewise so. Having realized this, one has transcended all things."
Those who have attained realization are all characterized by the mark of a person (*pudgala*).
When the mind awakens to this realization, it understands that the "mind" previously realized was not [the true mind]; the single character "not" (*na*) precisely refers to the mark of a person.
This means that sentient beings who have entered the stages (*bhūmi*) awaken once more upon reaching this point, realizing that the "realized mind" from before was not [the ultimate].
Once one has known and realized that the mind is the mark of self, one no longer consents to further conceptualizing or interpreting it as the object of realization;
therefore, it is said that "one no longer recognizes the self.

Yet, when one comes to realize that the mind thus awakened is devoid of the mark of self, one fails to realize that this very mind of awakening remains, as before, nothing other than the self of the human-mark (pudgala-nimitta).
Previously, the various states of mind realized prior to this were coarse consciousness; this awakened mind is subtle consciousness.
Even if one claims that this awakened mind transcends and surpasses all previous states of realization, it cannot yet escape being categorized as the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*).
Why? Because there still remains a mind that can sever and eliminate [delusions].

Good son, if the mind—even to the point of perfectly awakening to nirvana—regards both as "self," and if the mind retains even a slight trace of awakening while claiming to have fully refuted and realized the principle, this is all called the mark of personhood (*pudgala-nimitta*).

Because it does not grasp at subject and object, it is called "perfect awakening"; because there is nothing that is not exhausted [of its conceptualization], it is called "fully refuting. This is the intended meaning.

Sentient beings, by means of the seventh consciousness, do not grasp at the characteristics of subject and object; yet the preceding characteristics of subject and object both involve the notion of self.

Even if one has fully realized the principle of the mind through perfect enlightenment and nirvana, such that no subject or object is grasped, there still remains a slight "mind that can awaken," for it does not forget what preceded it. Therefore, this is called the "mark of personhood" (*pudgala-nimitta*).
Why is this? It is because the wisdom of slight awakening is not a mind of discrimination; therefore, it is called "slight.
Good son, what is meant by the mark of sentient beings? It refers to that which the minds of all sentient beings cannot personally realize or awaken to.

This is further questioned: what is the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*)? It is said that the awareness which previously was the subject capable of awakening is now itself that which is awakened to;

once it has become the object of awakening, it is in turn called the subject. Thus, they revolve endlessly, all becoming both subject and object. Wherever this occurs, it is a state of mutual dependence (*apekṣā*).
Since one realizes there is no fixed nature here, one is free from subject and object. This does not mean, however, that one recklessly asserts that there is nothing beyond them.
To be free from all faults while remaining unaware of this scheme is precisely what is meant by "sentient beings"— the term for those who do not fixate on a single certainty.
When it is said that the mind realized in the preceding proof does not reach this mind, and the mind awakened in the preceding stage likewise does not reach this mind,
the single word "this" (*ci*) is itself the realization of the mind without forgetting.
Good son, it is like a person who says, "I am a sentient being. One should know that when such a person speaks of a "sentient being," it is neither the self nor another.
Why is it not the self? Because if one says "I am a sentient being," then that which is the self is not [the sentient being].
Why is it not another? Because the self is not that sentient being.

This illustration explains and clarifies this section of the text by borrowing the terminology of worldly people to establish its thematic force, thereby revealing the characteristics of sentient beings;
while the underlying principle is ultimately quite simple and accessible, the phrasing is profound and obscure. Now, I shall provide a detailed analysis:
when the World-Honored One, out of compassion, addressed those of pure karma, he said, "Good sons, you must know that sentient beings..."
For example, suppose there were a person in this world who made this statement of his own accord:
"Tell me, how do you speak of 'speaking'? I say that this body of mine is neither Zhang San nor Li Si.
If I were Zhang San, then there would be that Li Si as a counterpart; if I were Li Si, [then there would be Zhang San as a counterpart]."
There is that "Zhang San" who serves as a counterpart;

now, when I realize that I myself am born from the harmonious conjunction of the various conditions of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, I know that what that person calls a "sentient being" is actually what the Buddha taught.
This is because that person has already stated that this body of mine is itself produced through the harmonious conjunction of various conditions.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately knew that those who speak of sentient beings have already realized there is no self;
not only is there no self, but there is also no "other-self. Since one does not grasp at it as "I," there is no dharma of opposition between "self" and "other.
The preceding inquiry and explanation already make this clear. Furthermore, the World-Honored One feared that future generations of beings...
Since the living being will not return, the phrase "neither self nor other" is divided into two sections for clarification and explanation.
First, the two characters "not-self" (非我) are raised as a question: "The preceding text spoke of 'not-self';
how is it 'not-self'? The answer is: "That person who has just arrived said of himself that this body of his is itself a multitude [of elements]."
Since it is said that [the self] arises from the conjunction of conditions, once one says "I am a sentient being," one has already realized there is no self.
Furthermore, regarding the inquiry into the two characters "not that" (*fei bi*), the question is: as stated above, what does "not that" mean? The answer is:
that person who has just arrived said, "This body of mine arises precisely from the conjunction of various conditions. Since he said this...

I am a sentient being; although there is no distinction between self and other, even though both self and other are entirely unapprehended, one should still not harbor a mind that clings to being a sentient being.
"Having no self" means there is no initial mind of realization and no mark of selfhood.
"Having no other" means there is no second mind of awakening and no mark of personhood.
That there are still sentient beings means that this mind capable of discernment does not forget.

Generally speaking, among Buddhist scriptures, there are those where the phrasing is easy but the meaning is difficult, those where the meaning is easy but the phrasing is difficult, and those where both phrasing and meaning are difficult;
this [passage] is one where the phrasing is difficult but the meaning is easy.
Good son, all sentient beings who have attained realization or awakening do so only in terms of "self" and "person";
that which is beyond the reach of the marks of self and person, yet still exists as something realized, is called the mark of sentient beings.

This is a combined analogy for comparative analysis. The meaning is that although sentient beings on the stages (bhūmi) have realized the first "realized mind" as the mark of self (*ātman*), and have also realized the second "awakened mind" as the mark of person (*pudgala*), the fact that they do not forget their realization of the mind is precisely the mark of a sentient being.
The *Liaoshu* states: "If the realization of emptiness is 'I'..."
Furthermore, when one realizes emptiness, if there remains even a single point of a "realizing mind" where the person fails to reach it, is this not the mark of a sentient being?
This is what is meant by "the numinous tortoise dragging its tail": as soon as the trace is brushed away, the trace is born again.
Good son, what is the characteristic of life-span? It refers to that which is perceived by the clear and pure illumination of the minds of all sentient beings and realized through awakening;
it is that which cannot be seen by any karmic wisdom, just like the life-faculty itself.

As soon as there is a mind that realizes, and one does not forget that realizing mind, it is called the mark of self (*ātman*). As soon as there is a mind that awakens, and one does not forget that awakening mind, it is called the mark of person (*pudgala*).
To fully comprehend the mind that realizes and fully comprehend the mind that awakens, yet not forget that comprehending mind, is called the mark of sentient beings (*sattva*).
When these three preceding marks are all exhausted, there is only a single flavor, and the illumination of awareness manifests before one; this is awakening.
The mind not forgetting is called the characteristic of life-span (*āyus-lakṣaṇa*). Now, let us first raise a question: what is this characteristic of life-span?
The answer is: when great-minded sentient beings at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) reach this point of practice, they employ the illumination of the very mind;
this illumination of the very mind is entirely within one's own radiance, free from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and free from...

When the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are not tainted by even a single thread of defilement, one then realizes that all previously held notions of a self, a person, and sentient beings have been entirely exhausted. One thoroughly penetrates the true source;
at all places and at all times, everything is this single awakening, with no second entity. Thus, one intends to cultivate all things through this wisdom of functional activity.

Untainted karma—meaning the functional activity of karma, whether acts for one’s own benefit or for the benefit of others—this wisdom that illuminates it is precisely the subtle defiled consciousness. It is called the "subtlest of the subtle.
Like a person's life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), it constantly continues in succession; it cannot sever itself, nor can it see itself, just as described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

It is said: "Ānanda, this stillness is not the True Suchness (tathatā). It is like a rushing torrent that appears tranquil from afar; because the current is so swift, it is not perceived, yet it is not that there is no flow at all.
The Chan school calls this 'the life-root (jīvamūla) being unsevered.

It has also been called 'not reaching the secure barrier,' or 'the illumination of wisdom manifest before one,' which is still a continuous flow of the permanent and eternal. Furthermore, it is said: "Ten thousand miles away, not a single cloud hangs in the void."
"Empty space is precisely the right time to receive a blow; why is it so? It is simply because, having reached this state, one still has something upon which to rely;

one is still entangled in conceptual elaboration. To call this 'wearing a flower garland to adorn the body' or 'having a jeweled necklace' is to say that one has not yet been able to take a step beyond the hundred-foot pole, nor has one yet cast off the ox at the ten-thousand-fathom precipice."
Because the Buddha-Dharma exists within one's breast, when a monk asked an ancient worthy, "Why did the hundred birds carry flowers for Niutou before he had seen the Fourth Patriarch?
he replied, "When one hears, one is wealthy and noble. He further asked, "After he saw him, why did they no longer carry flowers?
He replied, "After one sees, one is poor. This present characteristic of life is precisely this.
Regarding the time before Ox-head had yet seen the Fourth Patriarch, a monk asked Zhaozhou, "When the bright moon is suspended in the sky, what then?
Zhaozhou said, "It is still a fellow standing on the steps. The monk said, "I pray the Master will grant me an encounter.
Zhaozhou said, "Wait until the moon has fallen, then come and see me. It is just like the ancients who tamed dragons and subdued tigers, and for whom the various heavens sent [offerings].
Those who offer flowers as tribute from the hundred birds are all included within this mark.
Good son, if the mind perceives and sees that all that is awakened is but dust and defilement, for that which awakens and that which is awakened do not depart from dust.

If one uses the wisdom of this dharma-gate to illuminate and perceive that all those previously mentioned three types of awakened ones are merely defiled by the dust of worldly toil, then this very wisdom of the subject that awakens and the object that is awakened—relying as it does on the aforementioned state—is not separate from worldly toil and deluded thought. Why is this?
Because there is still a further wisdom of awakening that has not yet been forgotten; therefore, it is identical to the previous affliction.
What Mencius meant by "laughing at those who have run a hundred paces because one has only run fifty" is that even those who have run fifty paces are nonetheless still running.
It is like the melting of ice: there is no separate ice apart from the melting; one knows the ice is melting simply by its disappearance.
This is illustrated by an analogy: it is like people in the world pouring boiling water over ice;
as the water reaches the ice, the ice immediately melts and becomes one with the water. Although the ice has dissolved, there is still someone capable of recognizing that it was once ice.

Just as saying "it is exhausted" is not actually exhaustion, water is used as a metaphor for the true nature (*tathatā*), while the four marks (*catvāri lakṣaṇāni*) are the metaphor for the boiling water.
This is an analogy for wisdom. As东坡 (Sōngpó) said: "Once the head is severed, there is nothing further that can sever it;
when ice melts, how can one again perceive 'ice'?
To maintain a self and to perceive a self is likewise thus.

Now, although the "I" that exists as the cognizer remains to cognize the three preceding marks that were the objects of cognition, even after these three preceding marks have been eliminated, it is illogical for this "I" as the cognizer to continue to exist independently.
That which exhausts this "I" as the cognizer is precisely the mark of the life-span;
it is like knowing that ice has melted—it would be contrary to reason to further maintain the existence of the ice having dissolved. If one relies upon...
Regarding these four marks explained according to the stages of realization: first, the mark of self (*ātman*) is that which is transgressed by a Bodhisattva of the first stage;
second and third, the mark of person (*pudgala*) and the mark of sentient being (*sattva*) are those transgressed by Bodhisattvas from the second through the tenth stages;
finally, the mark of life-span (*āyus*) is that which is transgressed by a Bodhisattva at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). This [mark of] life-span...
They call this the "flesh-adhering undershirt"; only after finally shedding this one mark does one enter the stage of Sublime Enlightenment and become a Buddha.
Good son, sentient beings in the末法 (mofa) age do not understand these four marks; though they may undergo diligent and painful cultivation of the Way for many kalpas, they [will not attain it].
It is called the "end of the conditioned" because one can never achieve any of the fruits of sainthood; therefore, it is termed the "final age of the True Dharma.
The following passages all clarify the fault of clinging to a self and straying from the Path:

that is to say, if one establishes the mind through cultivation by means of these four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), then every practice will be accompanied by subject and object. Since these are all conditioned phenomena of arising and ceasing, they cannot lead to realization.
The noble fruit is precisely as stated in the *Avataṃsaka*: "If one practices the six perfections for many kalpas, one is not yet called a Bodhisattva.
This implies that not only is the noble fruit not attained, but it is also said that within the true Dharma of the Buddha, during the final age, why is this so?

Now, the True Dharma lasts for one thousand years, the Semblance Dharma for one thousand years, and the Final Dharma for ten thousand years; furthermore, during the time of the True Dharma, people do not grasp [at signs].
If one cultivates by means of signs, all will realize that in this age of the final dharma, people mostly grasp at signs;

now that they are attached to grasping at these realized signs, even though it is the True Dharma (Saddharma), it is the same as the final age. If one encounters this sudden teaching and thoroughly understands the root of the illness, then even in the final age, it is the same as the True Dharma.
As Zhuangzi said: "The world has lost the Way, and the Way has lost the world."
Why is this? This single phrase raises a question,
stating that those who have practiced in the past have already undergone many kalpas and have been diligent in their cultivation.
For what reason does suffering fail to realize the noble fruit?
Because one identifies all forms of self as *nirvāṇa*, there is realization and awakening, which is termed "attainment.
This clarifies that identifying the self as real is the answer; it is said that precisely because one should not identify the self as *nirvāṇa*, [realization does not occur].
Because there is awakening, realization, understanding, and awareness, although one may undergo diligent suffering for many kalpas, it ultimately yields no benefit.
It is like mistaking a dream-body for one's own self; though one exerts oneself in household affairs with various kinds of fatigue, not a single thing benefits one's assets.
For example, it is like a person who mistakes a thief for his son; his family’s wealth and treasures will never be secured.
This illustration serves to clarify the preceding passage in the commentary, which states: "If a thief were outside the house, one might still be able to guard against him;
yet how can one protect and raise him as a son? Furthermore, knowing that a thief is a thief, he poses no threat—yet to recognize him as a son [is to invite disaster]."

The avoidance of ruin is illustrated by the fact that while the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*) can still be restrained when grasping their objects, the deluded self of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is difficult to discern.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Ānanda, the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind now before you—these six act as the intermediaries for thieves, plundering the family's treasures.
From this, the world of sentient beings has arisen since beginningless time."
Because of being bound by the *paryavasthānas*, one cannot transcend the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). Master Shou said:
"To mistake a false thief for a true son is to plunder the family treasures when the kalpa ends; to take fish eyes as dragon pearls is to delude the eye of wisdom. Furthermore, Yongjia said:
"The depletion of Dharma-wealth and the destruction of merit—none arise except from this mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*). Students do not understand this.
By practicing this, one deeply becomes convinced that the thief has been taken for a son. Zhuangzi said:
"There is no greater thief than having a mind intent on virtue, for such a mind possesses eyes. Therefore, the sages abandoned it.

Why is this? Previously, when it was questioned why [the Buddha] did not realize [enlightenment] for many kalpas, the answer was given that it was because he realized it through the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*).
Now, it is further questioned: "Nirvāṇa is the true nature of all phenomena; thus, the essence of the self is also Nirvāṇa. Even if..."
For what reason and by what cause does the recognition of a self and the grasping for realization obstruct the Path?
Those who possess craving for a self also crave *nirvāṇa*, because they take the uprooting of the root of craving for a self as the characteristic of *nirvāṇa*.
Those who harbor hatred toward a self also hate *saṃsāra*; not knowing that craving itself is true *saṃsāra*, they separately hate *saṃsāra* and are thus called "not liberated."
The Commentary states: "Now, the cycle of birth and death fundamentally arises from hatred and attachment; if one seeks liberation, one must exhaust these two sources.

Currently, hating birth and death is likewise a form of fundamental hatred. Although the rejection of suffering and the longing for joy differ in their manifestations, both hatred and attachment are originally habitual tendencies.
If one carries these along while practicing the Path, how could the fruit of Buddhahood ever be achieved? To subdue the root of self-love and take it as Nirvana depends upon cultivation."

Because one suppresses it, a state resembling nirvana arises where the root of craving does not manifest; yet taking this resemblance for reality, one takes this "nirvana" as the fundamental basis for the intention to eliminate the mind of birth-and-death.

Since that very mind is present, how can the root of craving—which is the root of birth-and-death—and its sprout of aversion be called liberation? It is precisely this mind of "nirvana-craving" that is itself the mind of birth-and-death. Furthermore—
Why then do you separately give rise to yet another mind that loathes birth and death?
Since this single mind is employed in two places—using this same mind to loathe birth and death, and using this same mind to love nirvana.
How should one know that dharmas are not liberated?
The single word "dharma" is itself the cause of nirvāṇa. As previously stated, those who crave nirvāṇa are called "unliberated.
This passage further raises the question: if craving for saṃsāra constitutes bondage, then what of realizing that nirvāṇa is tranquility?
By what signs and characteristics can one know that the method of extinguishing the single mind has not led to liberation?
Good son, those beings of the final age who practice for Bodhi take their own slight realization to be personal purity,
because they have not yet exhausted the root of the mark of self (*ātman*).

To take one's own slight realization as being pure is insufficient; the Great Ocean of the Buddha-dharma is immeasurable and inexhaustible, and those who enter it do so gradually, becoming deeper and deeper.
At present, these sentient beings merely know externally that the sense organs and their objects are a provisional combination, and internally they perceive the essence of nature to be quiescent;
they have not yet attained the gateway of great penetration and great awakening, for their root of self-attachment remains.
How is it known that these [defilements] cannot necessarily be completely eliminated? This is understood by examining them through their objects as explained in the following text.

If, moreover, someone praises that dharma and one immediately feels joy and desires to deliver them, or if someone slanders what they have attained and one immediately gives rise to resentment, then one knows that the mark of self (*ātman*) is firmly grasped and lies latent within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
The play of the various faculties has never been interrupted.
It is just as Zhuangzi said: "As for Song Rong’s practice of the Way, though the whole world praised him, it did not increase his encouragement;
though the whole world reviled him, it did not increase his discouragement. Yet these sentient beings have not yet reached such a state.
When encountering praise one rejoices, and when encountering disparagement one becomes angry; by this one may verify that the mark of self (*ātman*) still persists.
Why is this? It is because worldly circumstances—whether adverse or favorable—are coarse and easy to perceive, whereas within the Dharma-gate they are most difficult to detect.
One merely says, "I am practicing for the sake of the Dharma," yet does not realize that this very mind is fundamentally the mark of self. This mark of self is merely...
At that time, it lies hidden and concealed within the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*;
yet when it encounters objects—whether favorable or adverse—it manifests intensely through the gates of the six sense organs, constantly and eternally without interruption or rest.
As the Ancient Sage said: "I shall briefly take up my staff and flick it away; the burning seal is given by hand to the great chiliocosm."
The "□□□□" (various factors) belong to the seeds of the eighth consciousness;
the various sense organs (*indriya*) belong to the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, sixth mental, and seventh *manas* consciousnesses.

Seeds manifest repeatedly, and these active manifestations constantly and uninterruptedly perfume the seeds. If we consider the praise and blame within this context, they pertain to the eighth [consciousness].
"Wind" refers to gain and loss, defamation and praise, censure and flattery, suffering and pleasure.
Good son, those who cultivate the Way do not eliminate the mark of self; therefore, they cannot enter pure awakening.

This concludes the preceding discussion regarding the reason why, due to the persistence of the notion of a self and the loss of the Way, one is unable to attain awakening and enter into pure, perfect *bodhi*.

"Good son, if you know that the self is empty, there is no one who destroys the self; yet because the notion of a self persists, the teaching of the Dharma continues, for the self has not been severed."
The life-force is also like this.

What follows here explains illness as the Dharma; for there is a fear that if one hears the previous Buddha’s teaching and praises it, one will rejoice, but if one disparages it, one will become angry.
As long as anger and joy have not been forgotten, this is the mark of selfhood (*ātman*). Now, in this instance, one intends to endure [the disparagement] without becoming angry.
I employ this because there is no self; for I consider that my present single body is merely formed through the conjunction of various conditions and is ultimately without a self.
Since I have already realized its emptiness, whom do you destroy? Out of pity for your ignorance, I now explain to you in various ways the Dharma of the emptiness of the self.
This very person who perceives existence and non-existence and yet does not destroy [the view of self] is precisely one who has not yet [realized it].
To realize the emptiness of the self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) and yet merely preach the Dharma for others on that basis is precisely not having severed the mark of self (*ātma-nimitta*).

The same applies to the marks of a person (*pudgala*), a sentient being (*sattva*), and a life-span (*jīva*). The Commentary states: "The 'one who reviles' refers to the other, while the 'one who preaches' refers to oneself.
In the scriptural text, stating that the reviler lacks [this realization] is an indirect clarification of his fault; stating that the preacher possesses it is... [the opposite].
This is the fault of following after clarity.
Good son, the sentient beings of the final age who proclaim illness to be the Dharma are therefore called pitiable;
though they exert themselves with diligence, they only increase their various ailments.
This establishes that the fault of clinging to a self and straying from the Way is the reason one cannot awaken to and enter Perfect Enlightenment;
this "sickness" is precisely the four marks [of existence]. If these four marks persist, they are collectively termed "sickness.

Now, all these sentient beings take the sickness of the four marks as the Dharma-gate of the single-minded Perfect Enlightenment of the Buddhas of the ten directions—this is what is called "mistaking a chicken for... [a peacock].

For a phoenix to mistake pebbles for jade is truly pitiable; though its diligence and exertion are great, they only increase its illness—like throwing firewood into a fire while using water to assist the ice.
Therefore, one cannot enter pure awakening.
This obstruction to the Path refers to those who practice the Way and fail to regard the aforementioned afflictions as the Dharma;
consequently, they are unable to realize and enter pure, perfect awakening.

"Good son, the sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age do not understand the four marks (*catur-nimitta*). Taking the understanding and the sphere of practice of the Tathāgata as their own cultivation, they ultimately achieve nothing.
The following passage explains how ordinary persons are conflated with sages; first, it suppresses the sage by equating him with oneself. The commentary states: 'The Buddha...'"

The definitive teachings on the Dharma that accords with principle all state that mind and objects are fundamentally empty, afflictions and karma are fundamentally pure, ordinary beings and sages are not different, and cause and effect are both perfect.
From the perspective of a Buddha, the reality of the principle is indeed thus. Yet, sentient beings have been deluded for a long time;
their habitual tendencies are deeply rooted, such that even if they believe and understand these Dharma gates and employ them in the present, they originally only follow after discursive thoughts.
Using a discriminating mind and consciousness to interpret the unimpeded teachings of others, one claims that even the Buddha’s intention is merely like this;
thus, one praises heaven and earth as being the same while denying cause and effect, having no faith in cultivation or realization.
One who forms such a view is what is called "vast emptiness" (huòdá kōng)—a state of wild, reckless indifference that negates cause and effect and invites calamity.
Furthermore, calamity is like a poor person who counts another's wealth and treasures but possesses not even half a coin of his own;
such a person cannot accomplish the skillful means of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Or there may be sentient beings who have not attained what they claim to have attained, and have not realized what they claim to have realized.
The preceding passage suppressed the Sage to be the same as oneself; this is precisely the matter of employing oneself to equalize with the Sage.

Perhaps there are those who employ themselves to equalize with the Sage, yet have not attained what is called the principle of the Sage—claiming for themselves that they have attained it when they have not.
Or perhaps they claim to have realized the wisdom realized by the Sage when they have not yet realized it.
To claim realization when one has not yet realized it constitutes a grave offense of false speech within the fundamental precepts.

Therefore, at the assembly in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda: "I teach the bhikṣus that in the sanctuary of the straightforward mind, even amidst all actions during the four modes of deportment, there must be no pretense;
how then can you claim for yourself the dharmas of a superior person?"
For example, it is like a poor man who falsely claims to be an emperor and brings about his own execution; how much more so for a Dharma King—how could he falsely usurp [the title]?
Because the ground was not upright, the fruit will be circuitous and crooked. As Zhuangzi said: "This is like setting out for Yue today and arriving there yesterday."
When seeing those who excel and advance, one gives rise to envy in the mind.

The Commentary states: "As for the mental application of a sage, there is no distinction between self and others. Seeing others excel—whether it be through the flourishing of the Dharma or their spiritual progress—one must rejoice in every thought.
By necessarily being able to accord with this, one verifies the inner mind; thus, one may immediately realize [the truth]."

Why is awakening not in vain? Because the Buddhas of the ten directions constantly emit light from the tuft of hair between their brows day and night, awaiting all sentient beings to sever evil and cultivate goodness.
If there is even a single person who gives rise to the bodhicitta and studies the Buddha-dharma, the Buddhas of the ten directions will experience immeasurable joy.
However, if one perceives that one’s own [spiritual] strength is declining while others flourish, then [joy] does not arise.
One who feels joy when their own envy flourishes and others decline, even if they have a profound understanding of the wondrous state,
is merely taking what is an object of the mind and mistakenly claiming it as attainment or realization.
Because those sentient beings have not yet severed their attachment to self, they are unable to enter pure awakening.

This forms an obstruction to the Path; that is to say, it is entirely due to the two classes of beings previously mentioned—those who suppress the noble ones to equate them with themselves, and those who seek to match themselves with the noble ones—who have never severed their attachment to self.
It is because of this attachment to self that they are unable [to attain realization].
To enter into and realize pure *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti* (perfectly pure awakened awareness):

This Bodhisattva Pure Deeds previously asked, "If the nature of this awakened mind is inherently pure, for what reason is it defiled such that all sentient beings are bewildered and distressed, failing to enter it? Now the answer is given:
there are three faults. First, the error of identifying the self (*ātman*) as real, whereby one cannot enter pure awakened awareness. Second, the error of [inappropriate] speech...
To have an illness that prevents one from entering pure awakening— this third point, which confuses the ordinary with the sagely and thus prevents entry into pure awakening—
when considering the meaning of this, whose fault is it?
"Good son, for sentient beings in the final age who hope to achieve the Way, do not allow them to seek awakening merely through increasing their learning,
which only serves to grow their self-view.

This clarifies that those who aspire to the fruition while remaining deluded regarding the cause— those who hope to achieve the Way— are merely pursuing the fruition while only benefiting their excessive learning.
This is precisely the cause of delusion. Generally speaking, the fundamental tenets of the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao) require that one first realize the nature of awakening (*jue-xing*);

only then may one engage in extensive learning to broaden one's wisdom. This is not to say that such study is unhelpful; it is like a dragon finding water or a tiger relying on a mountain. The preface states:

"Of the myriad medicinal formulas, one should select those for specific cures; of the thousand treasures of the sea, one first seeks the wish-fulfilling gem. However, this refers to the ultimate goal.

The people of the world are mostly deluded regarding this meaning; they rely solely on names and phrases, following the text exclusively to pick at branches and gather leaves, without striving for the realization of the mind.
Since the mind is not realized, even if one were to memorize as many scriptures as there are sands in the Ganges, what benefit would that bring to oneself?
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If one does not first eliminate the outflows of desire, then the accumulation of learning will become a source of error. Thus, as for what is seen...
All that has been heard is merely an increase of all manner of evil arguments; it is said that much learning without wisdom is to be ignorant of the true nature (*dharmatā*).

It is like having jewels in the dark but lacking eyes. The various teachings state that śrāvakas contemplate only the fruit and do not contemplate the cause, just as a dog chases a clod of earth rather than the person who threw it, or as in the case of Liezi.
The Way is lost through many paths, and the student perishes through many methods; as Zhuangzi also said: "The Dao should not be sought in multiplicity;
multiplicity leads to confusion, confusion leads to agitation, agitation leads to anxiety, and when there is anxiety, there is no salvation.
All of this is a critique of those who do not first understand the mind before engaging in extensive learning. Liezi (in the "Fuyi" chapter) says: "The neighbor of Yangzi..."
A man lost a sheep and led his own followers while also requesting Yangzi’s servant to join them in the pursuit. Yangzi said, "Alas! When one sheep is lost, why is there such a multitude of pursuers?
A neighbor remarked, "There are many diverging paths. Upon returning, he was asked whether the sheep had been recovered.
He replied, "I have lost it. The neighbor asked, "How did you lose it? He answered, "At the fork in the road, there was another fork within it; I..."
Yangzi did not know the reason for his return. He looked somber and changed countenance;
he did not speak for some time and did not smile for the entire day. His disciples found this strange and asked him, saying, "A sheep is a lowly beast, and moreover, it was not yours.
Why do you diminish your speech and smiles? Yangzi did not answer, and the disciples received no instruction from him. They were brothers in their disappointment.
Zi Mengsunyang went out and told Xinduzi. On another day, Xinduzi entered together with Mengsunyang and asked him, saying:
"Formerly, there were three brothers who traveled between Qi and Lu; they studied under the same teacher and advanced in the Way of benevolence and righteousness.
When they returned to their father, he asked them, 'What is the Way of benevolence and righteousness? The eldest brother replied:"

The elder brother said, "Benevolence and righteousness cause me to cherish my life and only then seek fame. The middle brother said, "Benevolence and righteousness cause me to sacrifice my life to establish my fame.
The younger brother said, "Benevolence and righteousness cause me to preserve both my life and my fame intact.
These three methods are mutually contradictory, yet they all emerge from Confucianism; which is right and which is wrong? Yangzi said: There was once a man living by a river who was accustomed to...
Swimmers are bold in the water; those who row boats and sell ferry-passage provide for a hundred mouths with profit.
Those who pack provisions to become students form a multitude, yet nearly half drown. Originally they learn to swim, not to drown, yet the consequences of their interests are such as these.
If one asks which of these is right and which is wrong, Xin Duzi departed in silence. Mengsun Yang reproached him, saying, "Why?"
"You ask about it in a roundabout way, and I answer you with eccentricity; my confusion grows ever greater. Xinduzi said, "The Great Way loses its sheep because of many paths;
the student loses his life because of many methods. Learning is not fundamentally different, nor is it fundamentally not one—it is only at the end that they diverge so greatly.
Only by returning to the same and reverting to the one can one avoid both loss and gain. Zichang was deeply moved.
It is lamentable that the disciples of the Master study the Way of the Master yet fail to grasp the Master’s true condition. The *Eulogy on the Lotus* says:
"Do not seek the profound mystery through learning and hearing; such study is merely laborious toil and frantic exertion.
How can this compare to non-action, which is leisurely and expansive? In its vast openness and clarity, one spontaneously attains perfect penetration."

One should simply apply oneself with diligence to subdue the afflictions and arouse great valor, so that what has not yet been attained may be attained and what has not yet been severed may be severed.
When greed, hatred, craving, pride, flattery, deceit, jealousy, and the notions of "self" and "other" or "affection" do not arise toward objects,
and all these are completely extinguished— the Buddha says such a person will gradually achieve accomplishment, seek out virtuous friends, and not fall into wrong views.

This exhortation to sever delusions constitutes the true causal condition; its meaning is that the World-Honored One admonishes all sentient beings who wish to achieve the vast and perfect *bodhi* of the Buddhas of the ten directions:

"You should simply act as I have instructed by subduing afflictions and giving rise to a mind of great courage and superior resolve. If you have not yet attained the true realm of perfect *bodhi*," [you must do so].
The meaning of the great light of wisdom that universally illumines the Dharma-realm, the meaning of true and authentic cognition, the meaning of coolness and immutability,
and the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity— all these sublime functions shall be grasped, perfected, and attained. However,
this cannot be achieved as long as one has not severed the greed, anger, craving, pride, flattery, and envy within the inverted states of ordinary beings.
One who is jealous of all obstructive and false dharmas should cause all attachments and endearments to be severed;
when these are entirely empty and quiescent, the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood will be spontaneously accomplished.

Furthermore, one must seek a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to serve as a witness and guide so as not to fall into wrong views. Why is this? The commentary states: "It is like a merchant entering the sea."
One must rely upon a guide; those who study and practice cultivation must certainly depend upon virtuous friends. Therefore, the Chan school says:

"Those who claim to have attained self-awakening without a teacher before King Vairocana (Viyūhaprabha) and those who claim to have attained self-awakening without a teacher after King Vairocana are all celestial māras and heterodox practitioners.
These arise from within the root afflictions—namely, greed, anger, attachment, and pride—and specifically from attachment.
The absence of a distinct nature of greed, as categorized among the mental factors (*caitasika*), namely guile (*śāṭhya*) and envy (*īrṣyā*), constitutes the minor secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
If one gives rise to hatred or attachment toward what is sought, one will be unable to enter the ocean of pure awakening.
The preceding passage was an exegesis in direct order, whereas this passage is an exegesis in reverse order.

It clarifies conversely that by not giving rise to hatred or love, one attains entry into Perfect Enlightenment (*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*). As for "hatred and love," one gives rise to love for oneself and hatred for others; therefore it is said:
"Only do not harbor hatred or love, and you will be luminously clear."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Vimalakarma, you should know: All sentient beings, due to grasping at a self and craving, Have wandered through beginningless delusion;
As long as they have not eliminated the four marks, They cannot achieve Bodhi. Love and hatred arise in the mind, And crookedness persists in their thoughts."

Therefore, those who are greatly deluded and distressed cannot enter the City of Enlightenment; if one can take refuge in the Land of Awakening, first eliminate greed, hatred, and ignorance, and do not harbor the attachment to dharmas within the mind, then one may gradually achieve accomplishment.
My body is fundamentally non-existent; how could love or hate arise?
If this person seeks a virtuous friend, they will never fall into false views; if they seek something else, their mind will become distracted, and in the end, they will not achieve accomplishment.

Regarding the "attainment of awakening," the city serves as a metaphor for awakening; this is a summary that encompasses both the dharma and its metaphor. The city has three meanings: first, it defends against external enemies;

second, it sustains the populace; and third, it opens its gates to attract and guide others. Specifically, when one realizes the nature of the mind, the various delusions cannot enter, which is like defending against external enemies.
When one perceives the boundless merits and the myriad practices increase to perfection, it is like sustaining the populace.
There are no three paths through which one does not pass, drawing in both self and others like opening a gate to welcome them in.

If one can return to awakening, then "kṣetra" (the term for a world-realm) is a Sanskrit word; in this language, it is called a "world. This is like saying that from the borders of the entire realm, there is no land that is not the sovereign's domain.
Once the practitioner has awakened, every phenomenon belongs to that awakening, as it is said: "When a heterodox person speaks the True Dharma, it is still the True Dharma."

The Dharma also becomes either heterodox or orthodox depending on the person; one who preaches heterodox Dharma makes even that heterodox Dharma into orthodox Dharma. That which is loved is itself Nirvana.

As for the statement "my body was originally non-existent," it means that my body is the very root of aversion and attachment. If one wishes to eliminate aversion and attachment, one must not cling to this delusory body.
Since that upon which it depends is empty, how can that which depends upon it remain? It is like when the skin no longer exists, the hair has nowhere to stay.
"To what shall it be attached? Thereupon,
the Bodhisattva Pujue rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

Before the practitioner has eliminated the notion of self (*ātman*), they cannot yet apply their efforts; once they reach this stage, all prior faults have been abandoned. Only when the four notions are removed can one truly cultivate.
Within the mental application of cultivation, there may still be notions of right and wrong; as long as there is right and wrong, awakening remains incomplete.
Therefore, this [text] causes one to rely on a teacher to avoid drowning in the four maladies. Once these are removed, the nature of awakening is without obstruction.
"Xiajue, your awakening is now universal! It is further said that universal awakening encompasses the beginning and the end, the coarse and the subtle, and the shallow and the deep;
therefore, you should inquire further.

Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, you have eloquently explained the maladies of dhyāna, causing the great assembly to attain a state never before experienced, their minds becoming vast and serene."
One attains great peace and stability.
As for "dhyāna-diseases," these refer to the four signs previously mentioned, which are the afflictions encountered by practitioners entering meditative contemplation (*dhyāna-vipaśyanā*).

"Utterly vast" (*tàngrán*) describes the appearance of being as expansive, deep, and far-reaching as water. "Great peace and stability" is contrasted with that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
That Bodhisattvas partially realize, partially sever, and partially awaken is but a minor peace; only when the Buddha fully realizes prajñā is there great peace.

World-Honored One, in the final age, sentient beings will gradually distance themselves from the Buddha, the worthy and holy ones will remain hidden, and false teachings will blaze ever more fiercely, causing all...
"Sentient beings seek such-and-such a person; by relying on such-and-such a Dharma, they practice such-and-such conduct to eliminate such-and-such afflictions.

How may they resolve their minds so that these blind ones do not fall into false views? Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, making this request three times, beginning again and again until it was finished.

This clarifies the intent of the inquiry: just as a person whose child is ill feels particular anxiety, so too does the Bodhisattva’s great compassion first grieve for the fact that in the final age, the worthy and sages have vanished and the True Dharma is about to sink.

While heterodox and false teachings brawny their arms amidst this situation—like a blazing fire spreading through the world—the seeds of the Buddha are in peril, like eggs stacked one atop another, threatening both heaven and earth.

Regarding the point of the injury, I do not yet know what kind of person you intend for all sentient beings to seek out—since you previously mentioned "virtuous friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*), I ask that you clarify this.
Second, by what Dharma do they rely? Third, what practices do they perform? Fourth, what ailments do they eliminate?
May you cause the blind and sightless sentient beings of the末法 (final age) to rely upon these various Dharmas so that they do not fall into the false views of the six heterodox masters.
However, those who are like the "blind in a crowd" are merely people who do not see the Way; they are all termed "the blind in a crowd.
They are like the blind who have had both eyes gouged out and thus cannot see anything at all; even if they were to engage in discourse, it would not be true.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "For example, there was a king who told his ministers: 'Lead an elephant and show it to these blind men. At that time, the high minister received [the command]."
The King then assembled the blind men and showed them the elephant. At that time, each of the blind men touched it with his own hand;
having finished touching it, the minister returned and addressed the King, saying, "I have finished showing the elephant to the group of blind men, Great King.
The King immediately summoned the blind men and questioned each of them individually, saying, "Did you see the elephant? Each of them replied, "I have seen it."
The king asked, "What kind of creature is an elephant? Those who had touched its tusks said, "The shape of an elephant is like a radish root.
Those who had touched its ears said, "An elephant is like a winnowing basket. Those who had touched its head said, "An elephant is like a rock.

Those who had touched its trunk said, "An elephant is like a pestle. Those who had touched its legs said, "An elephant is like a wooden mortar. Those who had touched its back said, "An elephant is..."
It is like describing those who touched the elephant’s belly saying the elephant is like a jar, or those who touched its tail saying the elephant is like a rope;
this is what is meant by "the blind men feeling the elephant and each asserting a different view.

If those blind men were to open their eyes and clearly perceive the object, verifying the true body of the elephant, they would never describe it as having a tail, tusks, or the like. Now, the sutra mentions these blind men precisely for this reason.

[The assembly] asked: "As previously stated, how does this awakening of the mind differ from that [previous] awakening of the mind? [The Buddha] replied: "The former was the awakening of the mind of faith (*śraddhā-citta*);
this is the awakening of the mind of abiding (*vihāra-citta*). Therefore, they are not the same.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Pujue, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! You all..."

"You are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such practice, which can bestow upon all sentient beings of the final age the fearless eye of the Path, enabling those beings to attain the Holy Way. Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Pujue, having received these instructions with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence. "Good son, the sentient beings of the final age..."
Those who, having given rise to the great resolve, seek a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in order to practice, should seek one whose mind possesses all correct knowledge and vision,
whose mind does not dwell on signs, who does not cling to the realms of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, who, though manifesting amidst worldly afflictions, remains ever pure in mind,
who displays the appearance of faults yet praises the holy life (brahmacarya), and who does not cause sentient beings to enter into non-discipline— seek such a person.
The person shall immediately attain the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This answer indicates that one should seek out and serve an enlightened teacher. "Those who are about to give rise to the Great Mind" refers to the exclusion of those of the Two Vehicles who give rise to the Small Mind.
This [seeking] belongs to the direct cause (*hetu*); seeking a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) belongs to the direct condition (*pratyaya*).
However, causes are proximate while conditions are remote; for example, the seed is the cause, whereas earth, water, and so forth are the conditions.
The cause is internal while the conditions are external. Although the seed exists of its own accord, it will not sprout if it does not rely upon earth and water.
Conversely, although earth and water can cause growth, they cannot do so in the absence of a seed.

The same applies to those practitioners today who study the Dharma: although they possess the Buddha-nature within, if it is not opened and guided by the instruction of a teacher, the Buddha-nature cannot be manifested.

Just as earth, wood, tiles, and pebbles originally lack Buddha-nature, yet a teacher can cause them to "have" it [by fashioning them], we know that while the direct cause is intimate, the contributing conditions are remote; such is the nature of this present practice.
When one has already awakened the Great Mind within and seeks out virtuous spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) without, it is because the necessary conditions (pratyaya) are complete;
only when these conditions are fully prepared does the Way of the Buddha (buddhamārga) come to fruition. How is this known? In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Mañjuśrī tells Sudhana:
"To draw near to and make offerings to various virtuous spiritual friends is the primary causal condition for possessing all-encompassing wisdom."
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (The Light Praising the Perfection of Wisdom) says:

"Those who wish to study the six pāramitās should follow true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and should always serve those of right knowledge and vision. One should seek those who possess all-knowledge and vision;
this refers to those who well understand the profound Dharma of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and non-ceasing, and who have thoroughly realized the One."

All phenomena, from their very origin, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of mental objects, and free from the characteristics of subject and object;
they are ultimately equal, indestructible, without karma, without retribution, without cause, and without fruit.

Their nature and characteristics abide in suchness (*tathatā*) within reality. Only after this is removed does one, within ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), unfailingly establish the one in blazing splendor.

To thoroughly understand all dharmas is what is called being a person of right knowledge and vision. That the mind does not dwell upon signs means one has departed from the realm of the afflictions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
That one does not cling to the realm of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas means one has departed from the realm of stagnation in quiescence characteristic of the Two Vehicles.
As the Sūtra says: "One would rather remain in hell for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever give rise to the aspiration of the Two Vehicles."
Regarding this mind, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "If I were to transform others by means of the Lesser Vehicle, I would fall into stinginess and greed;

such a thing is impossible. This refers to one who possesses correct knowledge and vision, who at all times remains constantly far removed from the realms of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles, even while manifesting greed, anger, and delusion within the deep and defiled environments of the three realms.
Yet the mind has never been stained or attached; this is also as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: Vāsukī was loved by water but not drowned;
King Anala was consumed by the fire of anger but not burned; and the Brahmin Jyotipāla was deluded by false ignorance but not confused.
It further states that when a bodhisattva lives at home with wife and children, they have never abandoned the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
He manifests various faults while praising the holy life (*brahmacarya*), saying:

"Because this person of right knowledge and vision, through the power of vows made over immeasurable eons, desires to deliver sentient beings who possess faults, he temporarily employs 'concordant conduct' (*samānārthatā*) to gather and love them, so that their minds do not harbor mutual suspicion and they may become close.
Once their hearts are close, they are then fit to receive the teaching."
In instructing them, one should tell them: "If you give rise to lust, anger, ignorance, and so forth, these are transgressions that lead to falling into the three miserable realms;
if you cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom, these are practices for transcending dreams and illusions, escaping saṃsāra, and attaining true purity.
Thus, by praising the holy life (brahmacarya) in various ways, one should always cause all sentient beings to enter it.
Within the rules and regulations of the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya, one does not allow others to follow the ways of demons, heterodox paths, or ordinary worldlings who lack rules and regulations.
Generally speaking, that which possesses rules and regulations is called the Buddha-Dharma, while that which lacks rules and regulations is the Dharma of the heterodox paths.
Question: Now, I do not yet know what the rules and regulations of the Buddha-Dharma are. Answer: There is the True [Dharma].
This is the dharma of the empty track; this dharma of the track enables the practitioner to sever hindrances, shatter doubts, realize the essence, and give rise to its function.
If one seeks such a person of right knowledge and vision to receive their instruction, one will immediately achieve the accomplishment of unarisen perfect enlightenment.
Sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age who encounter such a person should make offerings to them, not sparing even their own bodies or lives.
This refers to the fact that even that which is most difficult to relinquish—the internal wealth of one's body—should be sacrificed;

that is to say, if one encounters a person of definitive and authentic right view, one should immediately sacrifice this body of one's own, which is as ephemeral and illusory as a bubble, in exchange for a vajra-like, indestructible nature.
Just as one might exchange a clay vessel for a golden jar, so it was with the youth of the Snowy Mountains. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"I recall that in the past, when I was a brahmin practicing the bodhisattva path in the Snowy Mountains, there was neither a Buddha nor the Dharma or Vinaya.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, perceived this and descended to test me, transforming himself into a jackal."

The appearance of the rākṣasa was most terrifying as he stood before the Bodhisattva and spoke half a verse, saying: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are the nature of arising and ceasing.
Upon hearing this verse, the Bodhisattva’s heart was filled with joy. He immediately rose from his seat, lifted up his hair with his hand, and looked in the four directions;
seeing it was indeed the rākṣasa, he went straight to him and asked: "Great Being, where did you obtain [this]?"
"The meaning of this half-verse is the true path of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. The Rākṣasa said, "You need not ask me;
it has been many days since I last ate, and my mind is distracted by the suffering of hunger and thirst, so these words are erroneous and not what I truly know.
The Bodhisattva said, "If you can recite this verse for me in its entirety, I shall serve you for the rest of my life."
"For you, my disciple, I shall declare that your wisdom is far superior [to mine], yet you cherish only your own body and pay no heed to me.
Now, being oppressed by hunger, I truly cannot speak. The Bodhisattva said, "What food do you eat?
He replied, "That which I eat is only the warm flesh and blood of humans. The Bodhisattva said, "Once you have fully recited this verse for me, I..."
“‘I offer my own body as a gift to you, O Kṣāntivādin; who would believe that for the sake of eight words you have abandoned your beloved body?
The Bodhisattva said: ‘Now Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings shall serve as my witnesses. Kṣāntivādin then granted his permission.
Thereupon, [the Bodhisattva] stripped off his skin and used it to fashion a Dharma-seat, saying: ‘O Upādhyāya, please sit upon this seat and teach me well. Kṣāntivādin then sat down.”
He spoke these words: "When birth and death have ceased, nirvana is bliss. Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisattva reflected deeply;
he then inscribed this verse upon stone walls in various places. Once he had finished, he climbed a tall tree and threw himself down.
Before he reached the ground, various sounds issued from the air, and at that moment, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, appeared in person and caught him.
Having taken the bodhisattva and settled him on level ground, he performed repentance, prostrated, and departed.
Within the four modes of conduct, that spiritual friend constantly manifested purity, even manifesting various forms of faults and afflictions,
yet his mind was free from arrogance.
The four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) are walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. "Constantly manifesting purity" refers to the aforementioned forward progression (*anuloma*).
"Various transgressions and afflictions" refers to the aforementioned reverse progression (*pratiloma*). Thus Yongjia said: "Whether it be right or wrong, people do not recognize it;
its reverse and forward progressions are unfathomable even to the heavens. The Commentary states: "Now, the Bodhisattva’s manifestations are provisional..."
The Way is difficult to fathom; rely solely on the Dharma-gate and do not doubt its manifestations.

Do not think that one who acts in accordance with the path is immediately dwelling in sincerity, nor give rise to arrogance upon seeing one who acts contrarily. The Chan school also says: "Simply pluck the fruit without questioning the tree.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Regarding all teachers and venerable ones, conceive of them as the World-Honored One. If there is an exposition of the profound..."
One who resolves doubts through the meaning of the Dharma is beneficial to me; therefore, one should devote one's whole heart to honoring them and not dwell on their other faults.
It is like a worn-out bag containing jewels: one must not refuse to take the jewels because of the filthiness of the bag.

Or it is like traveling at night along a dangerous path where a person holding a torch guides the way: one must not refuse to accept the light because of the person's wickedness. Thus should one regard the Bodhi-mind.
The disciple is also like this: having received the light of wisdom from the teacher, one should not dwell upon their faults;
yet, because the task of being a teacher is difficult and the role of a disciple is not easy, one must not, on account of this warning, mistakenly show disrespect toward a coarse person.

To verify what is true or false, one should proceed as previously described in the process of discernment, and then follow and rely upon them accordingly. Furthermore, this medicine is for treating both disciple and teacher; do not take it incorrectly, but take it as prescribed.
When illness increases and there is no medicine to cure it, it is just as the Sūtra says:

"Whether one has shaved one's head and donned the *kāṣāya*, or whether one upholds the precepts or violates them, gods and humans will always make offerings to them, ensuring they never lack for anything; such offerings to them are called 'making offerings to me.
Furthermore, I say that even monks who have broken the precepts are superior to non-Buddhist practitioners who are diligent in their efforts. This is the secular [view].
If a disciple of the Buddha takes the medicine that ordinary people take, they will immediately fall into hell.
Furthermore, it is said that five hundred great ghosts constantly block the path of one who has broken the precepts and sweep away their footprints;
such a person may not walk upon the ground of a king nor drink the water of a king. It would be better for them to have their body crushed to dust by an iron mallet.
Furthermore, when red-hot iron is wrapped around one's body, one undergoes various sufferings;

having violated the precepts of body and speech, one may not receive the clothing, food, drink, or bedding offered by faithful donors. This is indeed the medicine prescribed for bhikṣus, which laypeople may not take;
even if they were to take it, they would enter hell. Therefore, those of both the monastic and lay communities in future generations should all strive to understand the Buddha’s words well.
How much more so, then, is it easy to relinquish external wealth such as property, wife, and kin?
Regarding the character "搏" (*bó*) [in the phrase "摶財"], Guifeng’s commentary states that this is an abbreviation or error introduced by the translator;
since ancient times in India, spoons and chopsticks were not used, and eating with the hands was called "搏" (*bó*).

Regarding the term "bowl" (tuán): after the meal, the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Tang dynasty maintained that this term for collecting food was not exhaustive, as it did not apply to liquids or moist substances which could not be gathered into a ball.
Consequently, he changed the character "bowl" (tuán) to "portion" (duàn), meaning a single segment of food as used here in this land.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* also employs this character "portion" (duàn); the current sūtra uses the archaic "bowl" (tuán).

This is indeed a corruption and an abbreviation; one should further add the character "food" (shí) so that it reads, "Furthermore, as for morsel food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*)," for in this region [of China] it is not corrupted or abbreviated.
Now, there is only the character "lump" (tuó), which is the abbreviation. There are four kinds of food: first, morsel food;

second, contact food (*sparśa-āhāra*); third, volition food (*manasikāra-āhāra*); and fourth, consciousness food (*vijñāna-āhāra*). Now, morsel food has transformation as its characteristic, while contact food...

Contact has the characteristic of craving; the food of consciousness has the characteristic of aspiration; and the food of volitional formations has the characteristic of intensification—none of these depart from the three aforementioned foods.
"Wealth" refers to money, goods, and silken fabrics; "wife and children" refers to one's closest kin; and "retainers" refers to servants and attendants.
The meaning is that if one encounters the former [conditions], one must know the truth, recognize the delusion, identify the disease, and understand the medicine, thereby attaining correct knowledge.
If one can give even that which is most difficult for oneself to relinquish as an offering when seeing others,
how much more so should one practice giving those things easily abandoned— such as external, limited food, money, silk garments, wives, children, and servants?

If a son of good family does not give rise to evil thoughts toward that spiritual friend, he will be able to ultimately achieve the flower of the mind of perfect enlightenment, its radiance illuminating the lands of the ten directions.
This demonstrates that there is great benefit in drawing near to a spiritual friend; that is to say, whether one encounters adversity or favor toward such a friend, [one should remain steadfast].
One must not give rise to a mind of arrogance; if an evil thought arises, it will immediately create obstructions and coverings that prevent one's own mind from entering the Dharma.
Since ancient times, those who have served as teachers have not received the Dharma casually, for the Dharma is not easily obtained.
As the *Dharmapada* says: "Regarding whatever actions a spiritual friend performs, one should not give rise to even a hair’s breadth of doubt. One must not do so.

In the profound verses on Right Reception (*samyag-samādhi*), it is said that even in the "Fisherman" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*, it is stated: "To encounter one's elders and not show them respect is a failure of propriety;
to see the worthy and not honor them is a lack of benevolence. Unless one is a Perfected Person (*zhiren*), one cannot humble oneself before others;
if one does not humbly serve others with refinement, one will not attain the Truth. Thus, one’s person is harmed. Alas! Among harms to humanity, none is greater than a lack of benevolence.
Once one is thus great and free from the obscuration of evil thoughts, one will gain the joyful guidance and exhortation of virtuous friends toward the unsurpassed, wondrous Way.
Relying upon their teachings, one will ultimately achieve the Dharma-gate and realize the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
This perfect enlightenment is not separate from the one mind; once the awakening mind is clarified, the light of wisdom is revealed and all things are touched.
Abiding in non-attachment, one is luminously clear and bright, like a hundred flowers in full bloom;

throughout the entirety of the worlds of the ten directions, there is nothing it does not illuminate and nothing it does not enlighten. From this point, returning to the root and restoring the source, one transcends the mundane and enters the sacred;
once attained, it is eternal, to be enjoyed without end until the very limit of the future. Thus, one knows that associating with virtuous friends is by no means a minor benefit.
"Good son, the wondrous Dharma realized by that spiritual friend should involve the departure from the four illnesses. What are the four illnesses?
Hereafter, these four illnesses will be analyzed so as to eliminate them: first, the illness of activity; second, the illness of cessation;
third, the illness of indifference; and fourth, the illness of extinction. This first section provides a general introduction, stating: "That spiritual friend..."
The wondrous Dharma that is realized—this Dharma is the very substance upon which one relies—is free from the four maladies of effort, cessation, indifference, and extinction.
Since the maladies of the mind are boundless, these four are essential; if even one of them is present, one is unfit to be a teacher.
Furthermore, the text poses the question: "What are the four maladies? The subsequent passage answers this by identifying and explaining each of their characteristics.
[End of] the Fourth Volume of the Categorized Commentary on the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* (Original Text).
[End of] the Fourth Volume of the Categorized Commentary on the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* (Supplementary Text).

First, the sickness of fabrication: if there is someone who says, "I shall perform various practices within my original mind in order to seek perfect enlightenment," this is called a sickness because the nature of perfect enlightenment cannot be attained through fabrication.
The Commentary states: This refers to those who engage in various activities such as contemplating, speculating, calculating, deliberating, initiating mental effort, and performing actions;

constructing stupas and monasteries; making offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha; reciting mantras and sutras; monks delivering lectures; sitting upright in meditation; practicing various forms of giving;
preaching in the secular world; traveling through the world; and being preoccupied with the anxieties of food and clothing. It is said that these are what must be brought to rest.
Because this path involves conditions, one undergoes hunger and cold, regarding these as meritorious deeds; one contemplates emptiness and existence, cherishing the body and then detesting it.
Among the many gates of practice, one clings to a single one, relying on this solitary practice in an attempt to accord with the awakened mind.

Since this is a product of deliberate effort and gives rise to emotional attachment, how could it conform to the principle of non-action and tranquil illumination? This ailment originates from the illusory contemplations of the past.
That text states that all Bodhisattvas arise from this practice to proceed through the various wheels, all of which involve arising in practice to deliver sentient beings;
now, by losing the meaning of that passage, this [present work] has become a source of affliction.
Second is the illness of indolence. If there are those who say, "We now neither sever birth-and-death nor seek nirvana;

since both nirvana and birth-and-death are without the thought of arising or ceasing, we shall remain indifferent to all things, following the nature and desires of all phenomena while seeking perfect enlightenment," their nature of perfect enlightenment is not something that exists through indolence; therefore, it is called an illness.

The Commentary states: "Previously, one was driven about in search of the Buddha; now, one lets the body and mind go free. This means that since birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is empty, what more is there to sever?
Since *nirvāṇa* is fundamentally quiescent, why rely on cultivation or seeking? Without aversion or delight, there is no effort to cease or maintain thought;
one simply acts with sincerity and spontaneity amidst all phenomena, like heaven being high, earth being deep, and fire being hot.
Hot water, dampness, wind, shaking, earth, stillness, pine trees straight, thorns curved, cranes white, crows black—each of these distinct categories is their nature, spontaneous and natural.
Nowadays, there is a certain class of people who say: "The false follows what others deem false, and the true leaves what others deem true;
each calls it so according to its own mind, so why must one change it? If one acts, let it be as one pleases; if one remains idle, let it be as one pleases."
In leisure, one eats when hungry and puts on clothes when cold; indifferent to good or bad fortune, one acts spontaneously and lives according to conditions.
When sleep comes, one lies down; when alertness arises, one walks. Whether going east, west, south, or north, there is no fixed destination for coming or staying.
To claim that such leisure accords with the Way is not to realize it is actually a sickness; therefore, one must remain in a state of vibrant, harmonious ease.
Shang said: "There is no need for extensive learning or vast erudition; there is no need for eloquence or refined discernment.

One who does not know the size of the months nor heed the intercalary days of the year—when people come to question me, if I am unable to engage them in discussion, I simply eat porridge at dawn and take another meal at the hour of noon. Today, I proceed with effortless spontaneity, bright and clear."

The illness of "idle drifting" (ren-yun) arises because the text in the preceding "Chapter on Discerning Sounds" states: "In the pure, perfect enlightenment, there is fundamentally no cultivation, nor any cultivator.
Failing to grasp the meaning of this passage, one falsely claims to have already attained awakening; thus, why should one engage in illusory practice?
This constitutes the illness of idle drifting.
Third is the illness of cessation: if there is another person who speaks thus, saying, "I shall now cause all thoughts in my own mind to cease forever,
so that I may attain the quiescent equality of all natures and seek perfect enlightenment," then because that nature of perfect enlightenment is not attained through cessation,
it is called an illness.

The Commentary states: Previously, one gave rise to thoughts fearing that it was not so; subsequently, one followed after mental deliberations, fearing loss. Now, one simply brings this delusion to rest.
When delusion is exhausted, there is spontaneous equality, which is itself the truth. What need is there for separate illumination? Because thought is stilled, one is free from marks;
because one is free from marks, one attains the nature. This nature is the nature of the non-nature of all dharmas; it is not, however, identical to the nature of awakening.
This illness arises from prior quietistic contemplation; by mistaking that quiescence for the practice and following the instruction to clarify all thoughts, this illness of cessation is produced.
Fourth is the illness of extinction: if there is another person who speaks thus, "I shall now forever sever all afflictions."
Since body and mind are ultimately empty and non-existent, how much more so are the false realms of the sense organs and their objects? All are forever quiescent.
To seek perfect enlightenment while holding that the nature of perfect enlightenment is not itself the state of quiescence is called a "sickness."

The Commentary states: Previously, one merely ceased mental activity to bring about stillness; here, however, one calculates that the body, mind, sense faculties, and sense objects are fundamentally empty and quiescent.

Furthermore, while previously it was not an obstacle to perceiving the existence of the sense faculties and objects, one did not follow after thoughts of attachment and defilement—hence the term "cessation.
Here, even the sense faculties and objects do not persist; one maintains the aspect of empty quiescence because one perceives their emptiness and non-existence.

Therefore, it is said that "removing and extinguishing" refers to the mind; for the root of afflictions (*kleśa*) is precisely the body and mind. If one clings to the body and mind, how can afflictions be severed?
Thus, the severing of afflictions is indicated by explaining that the body is empty. Furthermore, when afflictions are severed, the body and mind are vacated.

If even the body and mind are empty, what existence can there be for the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*)? Since the body and so forth are fundamentally empty, they are called "eternally quiescent in all marks" (*sarvanimitta-śānta*).
