Having already extinguished the signs of stillness, you now manifest before me intending to seek realization of Perfect Enlightenment with this mind. Yet the essence of enlightenment is numinous and luminous; it is not merely quiescent extinction.
Now that you have extinguished delusions to abide in stillness, how could this possibly correspond? Furthermore, the essence of Perfect Enlightenment is neither moving nor still;
it fuses movement and stillness into a single unity, where its infinite subtle functions are unimpeded and inconceivable. How can a mind abiding in stillness [attain it]?

To claim that being able to harmonize with words is equivalent to approximating the principle is entirely contrary to reason; because it deviates from the principle, it constitutes the "disease of extinction.

This disease arises from the previously mentioned contemplation of quiescence (*śamatha*). Within those various wheels [of teaching], it is everywhere stated that there is "quiescent extinction" and the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*);
yet, by misunderstanding those [teachings], one falls into this [error]. These four diseases all stem from failing to take the holy teachings as the measuring line (*sūtra*).
Taking one's teachers and friends as a guide, one simply raises the mind and forms this intention;
therefore, at the beginning of the sutras, it is always said: "If there be anyone who speaks thus."
"One who is free from the four illnesses knows purity. This refers to one who practices such contemplation as "right contemplation," while any other contemplation is called "erroneous contemplation.

This summarizes the authenticity or falsity of the aforementioned four illnesses. Regarding the phrase "one who is free from the four illnesses knows purity," the commentary states: [The text continues with the explanation of the four illnesses.]
It is said that one should simply take the preceding four gates to examine one's own mind; once the mind falls into any one of them, one knows it is a sickness.

Therefore, it is said that "leaving" [them] means knowing purity. However, these four gates are all praised and encouraged in various sutras, and moreover, the first three contemplations all contain such texts.
That this [particular gate] is now considered a sickness has two meanings. First, the four...
Within these gates, there is none who possesses both contemplative insight and wisdom; they merely follow their own impulses, dwelling one-sidedly in a single practice.

They do not seek out the perfect intent of virtuous friends nor investigate the perfect texts of the Buddha’s teachings. As soon as they realize the meaning of one gate, they cannot long serve an enlightened master;
as soon as they see a sublime passage in a single sutra, they cannot extensively fathom the Sage’s intent. They merely crave the simple.
To eliminate the attachment to "oneness" as being perfect is why the sutra text generally censures it as a sickness. One who practices this contemplation is free from the four sicknesses;
therefore, it is called "right contemplation. If one contemplates otherwise, one grasps at the four sicknesses;
therefore, it is called "erroneous contemplation. A non-Buddhist classic says: "That which accords with the Way of Yao and Shun is the Right Way; that which is not the Way of Yao and Shun is other."
I agree with this point; however, these four gates merely eliminate the disease without eliminating the dharma.
Before one has seen the Way, all four constitute the disease of attachment; after one has seen the Way, all four can be entered as the Way itself.
Thus, throughout the day one acts yet never acts, throughout the day one ceases yet never ceases, throughout the day...
Though extinguished, it has never been extinguished; the Chan school calls this "the person of former times remains unchanged, only their conduct is changed.
It is just as when Śākyamuni was among the monastics expounding the Unsurpassed Way, he was no different from the monastics;
when Vimalakīrti was in the secular world preaching the fruit of liberation, he was no different from the laity; and when the woman Śrīmālā preached the Mahāyāna Dharma.
If one’s physical form does not change when associating with women, how could a bhikṣu who practices the conduct of an icchantika have his monastic characteristics altered?
Furthermore, just as a worldly official may be promoted or transferred to a higher office, yet his appearance does not immediately change nor his robes;
these various explanations merely address the internal mind of attachment—what relevance do they have to the physical body, the male or female appearance, or the clothing?

Is it a matter of beauty and ugliness? If you say that the physical form changes according to realization and the countenance shifts as one attains enlightenment, such that one becomes a sage, then Gautama would have become Śākyamuni only after changing his form, and Vimalakīrti would have become Jinxu (Suvarṇaprabha) only after transforming his appearance.

If one does not comprehend this principle, then even if one treads upon lotus flowers with one's feet, it is no different from acting as a demon. [The Buddha] asked: "Regarding these four ailments, what is their nature?"
Does this teaching concern the Master’s avoidance of the four maladies, or does it concern the student’s own avoidance of the four maladies?

If it concerns the maladies of the Master, why does the inquiry specifically raise them as separate items, and furthermore, conclude by saying, "One who practices this contemplation is said to practice right contemplation"?
If it concerns the maladies of the student, why does the heading state, "That which is realized by the Good Spiritual Friend"?

The Sublime Dharma should be free from the four illnesses. The answer to both [questions] is no different: having heard the sutra and recognized the illnesses, one must seek a teacher who can cure them;
once one has served this teacher, one practices the conduct that cures the illnesses. Whether it be the teacher or the disciple, there is no distinction between their illnesses.
"Good son, those living beings in the final age who wish to practice should, for the remainder of their lives, make offerings to virtuous friends and serve spiritual benefactors (*kalyāṇamitra*).
When those spiritual benefactors come to approach them, they should sever arrogance; if they depart, they should sever resentment.
Whether confronted with adverse or favorable circumstances, they should regard them as being like empty space, realizing that body and mind are ultimately equal."
All sentient beings are of one essence and without difference; practicing in this way, one enters Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
This is the Master’s response from the perspective of accomplishing the task, answering the previous question regarding what practices should be performed and how they are known.
It concludes by stating, "Practicing in this way, one enters Perfect Enlightenment. Furthermore, the *Dharmapada-sūtra* states that there are twenty kinds of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
There are ten kinds of metaphors: first, as parents; second, as eyes; third, as feet; fourth, as a ladder; fifth, as food and drink; sixth, as precious garments; seventh, as a bridge;
eighth, as wealth and treasures; ninth, as the sun and moon; and tenth, as one’s own body and life. It concludes by stating:
"A spiritual friend possesses such immeasurable merits; therefore, I instruct you to draw near to them."
Having heard this, the assembly raised their voices and wailed, thinking to themselves:

"Since the beginningless kalpas, we have always been molded, protected, sheltered, and sustained by our spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Their various acts of kindness and virtue are such that when they wish to come near us, it appears as favorable;
yet if they should distance themselves from us, it appears as adverse. Indeed, the skillful means of a virtuous friend are manifold."
Thus, they humbly accommodate the conditions of things and become intimate with them;

yet when the ignorant, lacking discernment, give rise to hearts of arrogance and indolence, or encounter adverse conditions that cause them to be separated and estranged from one another, they immediately conceive hatred, saying, "He is distant from me," or "He is close to me," speaking of love and speaking of enmity.
Once a single thought of anger arises, ten million obstacles manifest; not only do they lose the Way, but they also fall into ruin.
Regarding the three miserable realms (*tricāṭaka*): the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states, "Those who should be gathered in, one should gather in;
those who should be subdued, one should subdue; thus shall the Buddha-dharma endure for a long time.

This means that sentient beings of the final age who aspire to and desire to cultivate the wondrous practice of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) ought to devote their entire lives to reverently making offerings to, serving, and attending upon [the teacher].

Regarding spiritual friends and good companions: whether those spiritual friends and good companions come to associate with one or distance themselves, these are the signs of present circumstances testing one through adversity and favor.
One must not give rise to arrogance or to a mind of resentment;

how much less so when considering the minds of the Buddhas, who—whether through compassion or majesty, meditative concentration or wisdom—rescue and deliver sentient beings, thereby attaining greatness.
At this time, one’s mental application is like space—tranquil, eternally abiding, vast and impartial, with no further change.
One should, through the wisdom of contemplation, realize that within the body and mind of that spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is present the vast, numinous Buddha-nature;
within this nature, there is such firm penetration and such horizontal pervasiveness.
There is suchness that is eternally constant; there is suchness that leaves no trace; there is suchness that is unchanging; there is suchness that accords with conditions;
there is suchness that pervades heaven and earth; there is suchness that fills all of space.
It is not only within the bodies and minds of virtuous friends that it is thus; rather, it is also present within the bodies and minds of oneself and all sentient beings.
Thus it penetrates vertically; thus it pervades horizontally; thus it is true and eternal; thus it leaves no trace; thus it is unchanging;
thus it accords with conditions; thus it encompasses heaven and earth; thus it fills the ravines and fills the gullies.
One's own self is non-dual; self and other are without difference; they are of the same substance and equal, with no further distinction. This is called "arousing sameness."
Because one embodies the mind of great compassion, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"If there are those who wish to know the realm of the Buddha, they should purify their minds like empty space, remaining far removed from false conceptualizations and all forms of grasping, so that the mind encounters no obstruction wherever it is directed.
Otherwise, even if one knows the Way of Bodhi—which is honored by the world and can be pursued and sought—one [will not attain it].

One who is able to subdue their own pride yet cannot humble themselves to serve a teacher, and who, though knowing that sentient beings (*sattva*) are pitiable, cannot forget their own bodies in the pursuit of the Great Way—against such a person, the World-Honored One has thus given this poignant instruction.

Only if one can rely upon this teaching and cultivate the practices herein described will one be permitted to realize and enter Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vijñāna*). Otherwise, it is not so.
Ming, if one does not practice in this manner, one will be unable to enter Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Good son, that sentient beings in the末法 (final dharma) age fail to achieve the Way is because they possess the seeds of beginningless self and other, and of hatred and love;
therefore, they have not yet attained liberation.

This clarifies the practice for eliminating illness. Regarding "hatred and love toward self and others," although this has been explained repeatedly previously, it is restated here because it is the seed-nature;

that is, it is a subtle illness within the entry into the Path. This means abandoning this and grasping that—hating the false and loving the true—is a manifest activity (*samudācāra*) that is coarse and easy to perceive, whereas the seed-nature is subtle and difficult to clarify; therefore, it is specifically pointed out here.

When there are four against three, the multitude gives rise to delusions of joy and anger; when there is opposition between the wrong and the right, the people of the world compete to give rise to love and hatred—how tragic!
If, moreover, there is someone who regards an enemy as their own parent, with no duality in mind, then all illnesses will be eliminated.

For seven days and nights, one should single-mindedly collect the mind through mindfulness.
This clarifies that for one who uses the mind by remaining detached from signs and collects it through mindfulness, the *Awakening of Faith* states:

"If one practices *śamatha*, one should dwell in a quiet place, sit upright with a correct intention, and even if the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately draw it back and abide in right mindfulness."
One who possesses right mindfulness should know that there is only mind and no external objects.
If, at the beginning of summer, one enters the three-month retreat of the rains, one should dwell as a pure Bodhisattva with a mind detached from the Śrāvakas and without relying on a retinue;
on the day of entering the retreat, one should speak these words before the Buddha:
"Those who dwell as pure bodhisattvas" refers to Mahāyāna bodhisattvas; "śrāvakas" refers to those of the Hīnayāna;
and "retinue" refers to the assembly of the six harmonies (*ṣaḍ-samagra-vastūni*). As for the six harmonies: first, harmony of body;
second, harmony of speech; third, harmony of mind; fourth, harmony of precepts; fifth, harmony of livelihood; and sixth, harmony of view. As the Chan Master Changlu Zhaozuo said in verse:
Be harmonious in body and dwell together; do not depart from those who are virtuous and superior, for they assemble in one place.
Be harmonious in speech and free from contention; do not listen to that which is contrary to propriety. Like-kind spirits seek one another and like-sounds respond to one another;

be harmonious in mind and share the same understanding—do not accept what is expedient or unwholesome, and do not harbor a mind that seeks to deceive. Be harmonious in precepts and practice them together; be careful not to covet, and guard against [transgression].
It is not by merely ceasing evil that one avoids forming enmity; rather, it is through the realization that benefits and knowledge are shared equally that one finds the closest kinship.

If you receive eight taels, I shall accept half a catty; let us work together in harmony and do not harbor contempt for one another. Do not rely on your own strengths; let all live in peace and happiness.
Now, we shall practice according to the Mahāyāna, without needing such a multitude of followers.
I, [Name], a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā, who has mounted the bodhisattva vehicle and cultivates the practice of quiescence, together enter and abide in the pure reality-mark (*dharmatā*).
Taking Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery, I dwell peacefully in body and mind within the wisdom of equality.
Because the self-nature of nirvāṇa is free from all attachments, I now respectfully invoke you, not relying on [any other].

Śrāvakas shall not be bound by their retinues for the three-month summer retreat, as they must dwell together with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas for the sake of cultivating the supreme and wondrous cause of Bodhisattva enlightenment.

In the Sanskrit language, "bhikṣu" has three meanings: first, one who terrifies Māra; second, a mendicant (lit., "beggar"); and third, one of pure precepts. "Bhikṣuṇī" refers to a female practitioner;
"bhikṣuṇī" means a nun, where "nī" signifies woman. "Upāsaka" is translated as "male lay follower" (lit., "one who attends closely"), referring to a male practitioner who studies the Dharma.
"Upāsikā" is translated as "female lay follower" (lit., "one who attends closely"), referring to a female practitioner who studies the Dharma.
Furthermore, while the Hinayana is restricted to the two assemblies [monks and nuns], the Mahayana path is shared by both the clergy and the laity.

"Such-and-such" refers to the individual names [of those present]. "Jū" (踞) means to sit. The term "Bodhisattvayāna" distinguishes it from the sheep and deer carts [of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles].

"Practicing the cultivation of cessation" (寂滅行) distinguishes it from the Four Noble Truths. "Abiding in the true mark" (實相住持) does not refer to abiding in phenomenal characteristics. This is the *gārala* (伽藍).

This is called the "Grove of the Assembly" (*saṃghārāma*), for a grove is a place where an assembly resides; thus, Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) is that upon which the myriad virtues rely.
Regarding this passage, according to Guifeng’s Commentary, the meaning is that the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms.
Question: What are the eight consciousnesses? Answer: The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body constitute the first five consciousnesses. The sixth...
The six consciousnesses, the seventh manas-consciousness, and the eighth ālaya-vijñāna constitute the eight consciousnesses.

Among these, the first five consciousnesses belong to the external, which is their function; the latter three consciousnesses belong to the internal, which is their essence. Furthermore, the first five consciousnesses belong to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), while the latter three consciousnesses belong to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
What are the four wisdoms? The answer is: first, the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
The four wisdoms are: first, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; second, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; third, the Wisdom of Equality; and fourth, the Wisdom of Great Perfect Mirror.

Regarding "now transformed," this refers to a bodhisattva who, upon merely ascending to the first stage (*bhūmi*), transforms and attains the sixth consciousness as the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation.
This wisdom skillfully penetrates all phenomena. Furthermore, within this sixth consciousness, there exists a virtuous nature.
The unwholesome nature and the indeterminate nature—these three natures are used to differentiate all phenomena.
Subsequently, upon entering the second through the tenth stages (*bhūmi*), one transforms and attains the seventh *manas* consciousness as the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*).
This wisdom derives its name from the inversion of its cause; for because it was caused by the grasping at a self that was not equal, it must now be inverted.

However, the manas—here translated as the "defiled faculty"—refers to this consciousness which internally clings to self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), and self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Externally, it clings to the existence of ordinary beings and sages, of the high and the low, and of "that" and "this," being unable to attain equanimity.
As for the aforementioned two consciousnesses, they pertain to the stage of the cause for Bodhisattvas within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Regarding transformation: next, at the level of the two fruits of Equal Enlightenment (*samatā-bodhi*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*pratyavekṣaṇā-bodhi*), one transforms and attains the eighth *ālayavijñāna* as the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). This wisdom is named after its fruit;

however, this eighth consciousness formerly clung to the internal body and external objects—the mountains, rivers, great earth, the sense-faculties, the physical body, the vessel-world, and their seeds. Now, however—
For example, the great round mirror is perfectly full of radiance. Once, the seventeenth patriarch encountered a young boy holding a mirror in his hand.
The patriarch asked, "What does that which you hold in your hand symbolize?
The boy replied, "It represents the Great Round Mirror of all Buddhas, without flaw within or without. Both men were able to see it together; their minds and eyes were identical.

This refers to the transformation at the level of fruition (*phala*). The eighth consciousness becomes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), whereas the first five consciousnesses transform into the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) as a single path at the level of fruition; this wisdom performs all the Buddha-activities.
Therefore, the Patriarch said: "The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure; the Equality Wisdom is a mind free from affliction."

The wisdom of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) is not an achievement of effort; it is identical to the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), the great mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), and the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*).

Regarding the transformation of the fruits and causes of the [sixth] manas and the [seventh] manovijñāna, these are merely conventional designations and lack intrinsic nature. If one does not harbor attachment toward the locus of transformation, then amidst the profusion of activity, one forever abides in the *nāga*-like samādhi.
Although it is said that the sixth and seventh consciousnesses transform within the cause, while the fifth and eighth are perfected upon the fruit, this is merely a transformation of their names.

It is not that their essence is transformed; rather, the present tranquility of the body is the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom), and the tranquility of the mind is the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wonderfully observing wisdom).

Previously, these were associated with the four afflictions and falsely conceptualized the *ālayavijñāna* as one's own internal self, giving rise to views of inequality within the principle of equality.
Now, since the nature of the objects of perception (*ālambana*) is quiescent, the seven evolving consciousnesses [are likewise stilled].

Because they are identical in their nature as suchness (*tathatā*), they constitute the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). Next, "Great Perfect Enlightenment" (*mahāpariniṣpanna-avabodha*) is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
Have you not seen how Puyong addressed the assembly, saying: "When Deshan entered the gate, he immediately held up [his staff]"?
Is this not the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Must Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*)? Furthermore, when Xuansha and Tianlong were wandering the mountains and saw a tiger—[is this not the same?]
Is this not the Wisdom of Equality? Linji addressed the assembly, saying: "There is a true person of no station who enters and exits through the gate of your faces;
those of you who have not yet realized this, look! Look! Is this not the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation?
Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying: "In my place, it is like an ancient mirror: if a barbarian comes, he appears as a barbarian."
The manifestation of the Han [consciousness] coming from the Han [realm] and manifesting here—is this not the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom?
The meaning is that by taking one *pariniṣpanna* (perfectly realized) *bodhi* as my single dwelling place, all cognitive natures (*vijñāna*) are entirely transformed into the wisdom of *bodhi*.
This is precisely the fundamental source of birth-and-death and the very nature of *nirvāṇa* for the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The self-nature of this nirvana accords with principle; thus, it penetrates the six directions and opens up the four quarters.
Whether great or small, subtle or coarse, its operation is nowhere absent. It has no specific location to which it can be attached, unlike the Hinayana, which is attached to specific locations.
"Great Bodhisattvas" refers to Mahayana bodhisattvas on the stages. "Great causes and conditions" refers to... [text ends]
This refers to the minor joints.
Good son, this is called the Bodhisattva’s manifestation of completing the three-month period of the summer retreat and proceeding thereafter without obstruction.

Although the three-month period at the site of enlightenment has concluded, the summer limit for those of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) has not yet ended; for [the Bodhisattva] fundamentally does not observe the Small Vehicle’s summer retreat.
Therefore, there is no hindrance to proceeding wherever one goes without obstruction.
Good son, those sentient beings practicing in the final age who seek the Bodhisattva path and enter the three periods of cultivation must never grasp at any of the realms they hear of.
This is a general indication that within the objects of application and the objects realized therein, one must truly observe that one cannot grasp at or become attached to erroneous states;
thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Māra can enter the minds of all sentient beings, causing them to take refuge in his faction;
even if one's body were smeared with lacquer, or one's hands and arms were severed, it would not pose a difficulty for him, for the power of Māra is such that all people believe in it."
Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Deeply attached to false and illusory dharmas, they firmly grasp them and cannot relinquish them.
These are all not what is heard or seen within the state of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

As for faith, understanding, practice, and realization, although their stages differ, the dharmas that are believed, understood, practiced, and realized remain fundamentally no different from beginning to end. This would not be the case unless it were from the very outset.
The three stages of the causal ground for the fundamental realization of *bodhicitta* should not be grasped with attachment; that is to say, when understanding, one understands what is believed;
when practicing, one practices what has been understood; and when realizing, one realizes what has been practiced.
The three contemplations—quiescence (*śamatha*), illusion (*māyā*), and cessation (*śānti*)—are enumerated below.
Good son, if sentient beings practice *śamatha*, they first grasp at ultimate stillness and do not give rise to thoughts;
when stillness reaches its peak, they become aware of it. Thus, this initial stillness extends from a single body to a single world, and their awareness is likewise so.
Since the world of sentient beings has already fully attained awakening and all sentient beings are entirely within that awakening, every thought that arises is thoroughly understood.
It is like a shadow entering a mirror—the mirror reflects it without omission; or like a reflection entering a vase—the vase responds to it without confusion.
It is not that all objects heard by them can ultimately never be grasped;

this is a warning against grasping at improper objects. The Tiantai teachings state: "Whenever one is in meditative concentration, if one sees auspicious signs, they should be verified by means of three methods:
first, polish them with concentration; second, cultivate and rectify them according to the original practice; third, verify them with wisdom."
Observing with wisdom is like people in the world who wish to test the authenticity of gold by three methods:
first, by burning it; second, by striking it; and third, by rubbing it. As stated in the *Lengyan jiao*: "In the past, there was a Chan master sitting in meditation in the mountains.
Suddenly, he saw a filial son carrying a corpse toward him; having placed it before the master, the son began to weep, saying:"
"How can he kill my mother? The master knew this was Māra; he thought, "This is a demonic realm. I shall take my axe and chop it away.
He might not have attained liberation had he not done so. He then took his axe from the staff and struck once.
The filial son fled, but later realized his robe was wet. Upon looking at it, he saw blood flowing out; he had unexpectedly cut himself as well.
There was a Zen master who, while sitting in meditation, suddenly saw a pig come before him.

Thinking it was a demon, he seized the pig by its snout and cried out, "Bring a torch! When his junior disciples came to look, they saw that it was the Master himself holding his own snout and crying out.
This was entirely because, while sitting in right meditation, a vision had arisen in his mind, which subsequently manifested.
This is why external māras enter; it is for this reason that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* speaks of fifty kinds of māras in relation to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
"Good son, if sentient beings cultivate samāpatti, they should first bring to mind the Tathāgatas of the ten directions."

All Bodhisattvas in the worlds of the ten directions rely on various gateways to gradually practice the samādhi of diligent effort, extensively making great vows to cultivate seeds through self-infusion.

This is the contemplation of illusion (*māyā-vipaśyanā*). Whereas the preceding stage of the contemplation of stillness did not depend on external conditions, within this gateway of the contemplation of illusion, one must...
Relying on the majestic power of the sacred realm, the chapter on "Illusory Contemplation" concerns transformation through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);
however, within this present site of practice, one first disciplines oneself in cultivation, and thus it concerns seeking Buddhahood through great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*).

As for "making a vow," it means exerting and directing the mind to initiate [the aspiration], while "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) refers to the longing and desire for attainment; that is, since beginningless time, sentient beings have harbored such longing in every moment of thought.

Since one has now fully realized that the objects of the five sensory realms are to be sought [only as mental constructs], one resolves to cultivate the mind in every thought-moment, delighting in the objects of compassion,
wisdom, and the six perfections so that they may permeate the mind and form habitual tendencies.
It is not that all those realms one hears of are ultimately ungraspable.
This admonishes against grasping at improper objects.

Good son, if sentient beings practice *dhyāna*, they first take up the method of counting; within the mind, they clearly understand the distinctions and the number of thoughts as they arise, abide, and cease.
Thus, throughout all four modes of deportment, they distinguish and count these thoughts without exception.

This is the gate of counting within the practice of tranquil observation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). "Counting" (*shù*) is pronounced with a rising tone; this refers specifically to the meditation on counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*).

It means to harmonize the inhalation and exhalation so that they are neither too tight nor too loose. If one counts, one proceeds from one to ten, maintaining the thought that the mind is present [therein].

Counting prevents the mind from racing and scattering; this is truly due to the practice of counting the breaths. When the breath is regulated, the mind becomes pure, and one subsequently attains thorough penetration and realization.

One comes to know the four phases—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—within the mind, as well as the coarse and subtle, the beginning and end, the boundaries and the sequence, and the numerical quantity of deluded thoughts;
there is nothing that is not known. Why is this? It is because when the mind is still, it perceives movement. Now...

The phrase "no different characters" (*wú yì zì*) in the Sūtra means to omit or abbreviate. According to what is explained in the Śāstra: the ordinary person of the ten stages of faith (*shí xìn*) awakens to the characteristic of cessation (*miè xiàng*);

the three levels of worthies (*sān xián*) awaken to the characteristic of difference (*yì xiàng*); and those in the ten stages (*shí dì*) awaken to the characteristic of abiding (*zhù xiàng*). When the position is fulfilled, one awakens to the characteristic of arising (*shēng xiàng*).

As for the "characteristic of arising," all movement of thought has utterly ceased, and there is only the single mind (*yī xīn*). The preceding passage, however, refers to the wisdom of awakening during the time of sitting meditation.

Only while sitting does one realize that this is illusory; then, within the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—one simultaneously knows the coarse and subtle, the beginning and end, the origins and details, and the measure of the four marks of perception. Once known, there is no affliction.
It is like a malevolent spirit wishing to possess a person: if one knows its name, it naturally vanishes. This is what is meant by "knowing."
The thief is indeed a thief; no one can act as such. These several gates constitute one among the five methods of cessation and contemplation (*pañca-vinodana*). What are these five?

First, for sentient beings with excessive greed, the Buddha causes them to enter the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Second, for sentient beings with excessive hatred, they enter the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*).
Third, for sentient beings with excessive distraction, they enter the contemplation of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*). Fourth, for sentient beings with excessive delusion...
Having entered the contemplation on causes and conditions, they enter the contemplation on the Buddha for those sentient beings who possess many obstacles;
gradually progressing further, they eventually come to know even a single drop of rain in hundreds of thousands of worlds as clearly as if seeing it with their own eyes,
just like the objects they employ.
This means that the pure mind is the very essence of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), and the world is fundamentally contained within it.

When contemplative practice is perfected, one is entirely in accord with the root source; thus, knowing the number of raindrops is naturally appropriate to one's fundamental capacity. It is not only raindrops—it is the same for all things.
To cite one example to illustrate many, we have here specifically mentioned raindrops. Nevertheless, those of the class of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are deluded regarding this true mind.
Because one follows after what is known, its function is lost. Even Xunzi spoke of the "gentleman" (*junzi*):

"The subtle point of unity and the perilous point of unity—the mechanism of the perilous and the subtle—the gentleman is able to know it. The *Book of Documents* says: "The human heart is perilous; the Way-heart is subtle.
Only through refinement and unity may one truly hold fast to the center. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of the Dragon King.
If Varṣākāra knew the number of drops of the Maheśvara [rain], how much more so would a practitioner who has entered meditative observation?

If one were to reach the ultimate, only upon attaining the stage of Buddhahood would one know it; however, because wondrous wisdom is generated within the context of observation, we allow that what is seen therein is identical to that of a Buddha.
That which is heard by them—the entire range of objective realms—is ultimately ungraspable; this is called the preliminary expedient of the three contemplations.

Regarding what is called "the preliminary expedient of the three contemplations," the Bodhisattva Perfect Enlightenment previously asked: "Of the three kinds of pure contemplations, which is to be taken as the beginning?
This is the concluding answer, stating that practicing stillness (*śamatha*), illusion (*māyā*), and tranquility (*śānti*) alone is the initial expedient.
It is so. If all sentient beings universally practice these three modes of diligent application and spiritual progress, this is called the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world.
This is "universal cultivation. What is meant by universal cultivation? It refers to the complete cultivation of the three types of contemplation: stillness, illusion, and quiescence.

This is truly because the three contemplations are complete and the myriad practices are perfected; thus, from the perspective of this practitioner, it is as if the Buddhas have appeared in the world.
Furthermore, when this person’s fundamental enlightenment (benjue) is free from deluded thought, it is called the appearance of a Buddha;
"Buddha" has the meaning of "awakening. Guifeng said: "My own mind is fundamentally equal to the Buddha-mind; I have merely been submerged in samsara for kalpas because of delusion."
"Bodhisattva" is a term from the Sanskrit language; in the Tang language, it means "awakened. An awakened mind that is tranquil and illuminating is precisely *bodhi*.
If, in a future age of decline, sentient beings of dull faculties desire to seek the Way but fail to achieve realization, [they shall rely on this].

The following section concerns mutual cultivation, which is to say, returning to cultivation. Herein, first it clarifies that for a person of dull faculties, the cultivation of contemplation has not yet been perfected.

Due to karmic obstructions from the past, one should diligently practice repentance and constantly give rise to aspiration; first, one must sever hatred and love, as well as jealousy, envy, flattery, and crookedness.
Seeking the supreme mind, one makes this solemn vow with firm resolve to realize [enlightenment], exerting effort and rousing the will to repent of karma and sever delusions.
One should practice one of the three types of pure contemplations; once this contemplation is attained, one must not revert to practicing the other two, nor ever let the mind abandon them.

"Gradually seeking realization" clearly explains the mutual cultivation [of the two truths]. The Preface states that "practicing the specific, the pervasive, and their mutual integration" refers to this and the preceding passage.

The Commentary states: "There are those who are hindered by material forms; for them, the contemplation of emptiness and stillness is difficult to accomplish. They first contemplate the illusory nature of form."

When illusion is entirely empty, quiescent contemplation is perfected; yet if one further clings to fixed, substantial form, it obstructs the mind-consciousness and makes the contemplation of illusion difficult to cultivate.
First knowing that its essence is fundamentally non-existent, yet not hindering the perception of its appearances, one then perfects the provisional illusion.

Furthermore, there is the difficulty of cultivating the Middle Way when it is absolute; first knowing that the provisional is entirely empty, yet without [the duality of] provisional and empty, and empty and provisional, [one realizes the Middle].
When both emptiness and emptiness-of-emptiness are absent as mere designations, and all oppositions are severed, only then is quiescence realized.

Within this, there are those who directly perceive the source of the mind and thereby know that all phenomena are empty because they are identical to their nature, yet provisional because they do not destroy their characteristics;

or that they are provisional because they manifest from nature, and empty because there is nothing else manifested apart from it. If one intends to cultivate the practice of tranquil contemplation, one must not fail to attain this.
If one is permitted to practice the contemplation of illusion (*māyā-darśana*) but does not attain it, one is then permitted to practice the contemplation of stillness (*śamatha-darśana*).
If one does not attain either of these two contemplations, one is then permitted to practice the contemplation of quiescence (*śānti-darśana*). This is just as the Tiantai teachings state:

"In destroying all delusions, nothing is more profound than emptiness (*śūnyatā*); in establishing all phenomena, nothing is more profound than the provisional (*prajñapti*); and for the ultimate realization of all things..."
In nature, nothing is more profound than the Middle; therefore, when all is empty, there is no provisional and no middle, and nothing that is not empty.

When all is provisional, there is no emptiness and no middle, and nothing that is not provisional. When all is the Middle, there is no provisional and no emptiness, and nothing that is not the Middle.
This principle may be applied analogously to other concepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Perfect Enlightenment, you should know: All sentient beings who wish to seek the unsurpassed path Should first undertake a three-period retreat for repentance of karma from beginningless time.
After passing twenty-one days, they may then engage in correct contemplation; It is not an object within the realm of what they have previously heard."
Ultimately, one cannot grasp the gate of the clear enumeration of *śamatha*, the ultimate stillness of *samādhi*, and the correct mindfulness of *dhyāna*;
this is called the "Threefold Pure Contemplation. If one can diligently practice it, this is called the appearance of a Buddha in the world.

For those of dull faculties who have not yet achieved success, they should always diligently apply their minds to repenting all sins from beginningless time; once all obstacles are extinguished, the realm of the Buddha will manifest before them.
The preceding eleven chapters of the sutra text constitute the section on the orthodox teaching (śāsanamūla). Regarding sudden and gradual awakening and cultivation:
the chapter on Mañjuśrī constitutes sudden awakening through understanding; the chapter on the Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus) constitutes sudden awakening through realization;
the various wheels of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) constitute gradual awakening through realization; and the chapter on the *Caryāmaṇḍala* constitutes gradual [cultivation].
Xiuwu once examined the meaning of the two phrases used by the Chan school: first, the "initial phrase," and second, the "final phrase.
The initial phrase refers to the first moment of awakening; however, one must obtain the final phrase before reaching the secure barrier. This sutra is likewise so:
the sudden realization and awakening in the opening chapter on Mañjuśrī constitutes the initial phrase. [The chapter on] Puxian...
The realization attained through the completion of contemplation is the "final word"; it is like the meaning being identical whether Sudhana first sees Mañjuśrī or sees him again later.

The third part, the section on circulation (*parivarta*), refers to the desire to extensively benefit others now that the teachings and meanings within the section on the true principle (*saddharma*) have been fully expounded.
Because it will spread far and wide to future generations, circulating and permeating boundlessly, it comes with this specific portion.
If there were no one at all to transmit it, it would not flow; yet because it flows, it does not abide and does not stagnate.
Or, if its transmission encounters obstacles and difficulties, it is not "unpenetrated"; rather, it is not obstructed and not blocked, flowing like water without hindrance.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Worthy" refers to the three worthies prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), whose rank is that of the ten sages (*ārya*)—namely, the Bodhisattvas on the stages.

"Virtuous" means conforming to principle; it is the foremost, the head. Thus, one desires that all myriad virtues may simultaneously accord with the true principle, thereby becoming the cause for attaining the position of the true fruit.
Those who seek the subsequent fruits of sainthood must rely upon the circulation of the scriptures and teachings; the circulation of the scriptures and teachings [is essential].
Since he is the foremost among the virtuous and excellent, it is appropriate that this section on the dissemination of the teaching corresponds to the questions posed by this Bodhisattva.
The World-Honored One of Great Compassion has extensively expounded for us and for the sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age such inconceivable matters as these, so as to bring about their awakening.
The "Inconceivable Matters" refers to the near celebration of the *Dōjō* (Place of Practice) and the far celebration of the *Ippu* (One Section).

This means that within this one section of the sutra, the World-Honored One reveals the contemplation of the two emptinesses for those of superior faculties, reveals the various wheels of the three contemplations for those of middling faculties, and reveals the preparatory practices of the *dōjō* for those of inferior faculties;
thus, these various dharma-gates are distinct [from other teachings].
Transcending the realm of the refined and the coarse, emerging beyond form and substance, and detaching from the limits of words and thought, it is therefore called an inconceivable matter.
Even the Confucian classics state that "the Way of the Master rises above the heights of heaven and descends below the depths of the earth; one looks for it in front and suddenly it is behind."
It cannot be sought through physical form, nor can it be grasped through intellect or wisdom; this is the same principle as the inconceivable.
World-Honored One, what are the names of this Mahāyāna teaching, and how should it be upheld? What will sentient beings attain by practicing it?
"How may you, O Meritorious One, cause me to protect and uphold those who transmit this sutra, so that this teaching may reach its ultimate destination?
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, making this request three times, beginning again from the end.
However, within the section on the main doctrine (*śāstramūla*), although the explained meanings and principles are already complete and perfect, the ordinary mind finds it difficult to sustain them.
While listening, one may comprehend them clearly, yet there is fear that they will be forgotten later; therefore, it is necessary to uphold the teachings and penetrate the text.
Since the words must not be omitted, one should interpret the meaning according to the text and give rise to contemplation based on that meaning; only then will true realization be achieved.
Because it concerns the practice [of the Dharma], this question asks for the name of the sutra. What does "how should it be upheld" mean?

Although it was already stated previously that this refers to upholding the Dharma, what is asked here refers to upholding the teaching—meaning to personally observe and practice it oneself, and to uphold and explain it for others.
To disseminate this teaching means to perform these ten types of Dharma-practice; that is to say, if a person is single-mindedly...
Regarding this definitive sutra teaching, through making offerings, transcribing, bestowing as gifts, hearing, receiving, reciting, explaining, contemplating, and practicing it—
thus distributing and propagating it in the final age— one does not yet know to what ultimate stage this person’s wisdom and merit will reach:
will it be the stage of a bodhisattva or the stage of a buddha?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

That you are able, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, to ask the Tathāgata about such teachings of the sūtra, its merits, and its name—listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you. Then, the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha joyfully received these instructions.
Ānanda and the great assembly listened in silence. "Good son, this sutra has been spoken by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of ten thousand million *koṭis* of Ganges Rivers;
it is protected by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, taken as refuge in by the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, and is the pure eye among the twelve divisions of the scriptures."

Regarding this sutra, since the Buddha who speaks it is the true body (dharmakāya), which is unimpeded and of one essence with all dharmas as numerous as motes of dust, the teaching of one is the teaching of all.
Thus, the three true bodies teach simultaneously; there is no teaching, yet nothing is not taught. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"I do not see any buddha-land where this sutra is not taught. If one does not understand this definitive teaching (nītārtha), then...
It is taught according to circumstances, whether it is spoken or not; it is that which is protected by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"We Buddhas shall protect and uphold this Dharma so that all Bodhisattvas in future ages who have not yet heard it may all hear it";
and it is that to which the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions take refuge, meaning the practice of the causal path.
Within this [text], there is nothing that does not lead one to Buddhahood through this Dharma; it is the pure eye of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

This is truly because it investigates the root of delusion and illuminates the source of awakening. Thus, its principle permeates all the scriptures, and its meaning leaves nothing unexhausted herein.
If one understands it, then all the teachings will become clearly visible, as if pointing at something in the palm of one's hand. As for "the eye," it is like...

Just as a person with eyes can clearly perceive all objects within their field of vision, so too are the twelve divisions of the scriptures known as the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*):

first, the Sūtra; second, the Geya (Verses); third, the Vyākaraṇa (Prophecies); fourth, the Gāthā (Chanted Verses); fifth, the Nidāna (Causes and Conditions); sixth, the Upadeśa (Direct Instructions);

seventh, the Itivṛttaka (Past Events); eighth, the Jātaka (Birth Stories); ninth, the Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings); tenth, the Adbhutadharma (Marvelous Occurrences); eleventh, [the Avadāna (Parables)]; and twelfth, [the Upadeśa (Treatises)].
The twelve categories of discourses (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) are what are called the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-sūtra*).
This present scripture belongs to the two divisions of *sūtra* (discourse) and *vaipulya* (extensive teaching).

That which was previously taught by all Buddhas—the Tathāgata’s protection and refuge for Bodhisattvas—is precisely the dharma of the perfection of *bodhi* (Awakening); it is the eye of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.

This seal is definitively the core principle (*mūla*) of all sūtras; thus, the preface states that "the method of sealing and determining is the core principle of all sūtras," which refers precisely to this text.
Question: Does this sūtra correspond to the teachings of the three periods or five periods? Answer:
The sudden teaching (*tongjiao*) does not concern itself with sequence, time, or location; it is taught whenever a person of sudden capacity (*donji*) is encountered.
Therefore, it does not correspond to the teachings of the three periods or five periods. Furthermore, an objection is raised:

"Since it does not correspond to those teachings, how can one explain the passage in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* which states that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is protected by the supernatural powers (*ṛddhibala*) of all Buddhas?
The answer is: That which is protected by the supernatural powers of all Buddhas in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* belongs to the Main Teaching (*samyak-artha*). This scripture...

The protection by the Buddhas belongs to the section on dissemination (*pravartana*). If that protection of the sutra were part of the section on dissemination, it would be permissible not to exclude it;
however, since it belongs to the section on the main teaching (*samyak-artha*), one knows that they are not the same.

This sutra is titled "The Great Vaipulya Perfect Enlightenment Dharani," and it is also titled "The Sutra of Definitive Meaning," "The King of Secret Samadhis," "The Definitive Realm of the Tathagata," and "The Distinctions of the Self-Nature of the Tathagatagarbha.
You should uphold it with reverence.
The previous question asked: "What are the names of this Mahāyāna teaching, and how should it be upheld? This is answered by stating that there are five names.
Furthermore, these titles of the sutras were established by the Buddha himself. Generally, there are seven ways in which sutras receive their names:

either by way of essence (*svabhāva*), or function (*karman*), or result (*phala*), or by naming after a person (*pudgala*), or by naming after a dharma (*dharma*), or by naming after a request (*adhyeṣaṇā*).

The various distinctions among dharmas—such as those between dharma and metaphor, essence and function, fruit and cause, the signifier and the signified, the real and the false, or the object and the wisdom—are sometimes combined and sometimes presented singly, differing from one another. Now, the five names of this sutra already encompass these many types:
"Great" (*mahā*) refers to its essence; "Vaipulya" (*fangguang*) refers to its function; "Perfect Enlightenment" (*yuanjue*) refers to its fruit; and "Secret" (*mi*)... [refers to its cause].
"Secret" (*guhya*) refers to the cause; "king" (*rāja*) is a metaphor; "samādhi" refers to the Dharma;

and "the definitive meaning of the sūtras" (*sūtra-nītārtha*) is a praise of the expressive medium (*vyañjana*). All others are the expressed meaning (*artha*). The Tathāgata is the person who realizes [it];
the "definitive realm" (*niyata-viṣaya*) is the object realized. The "Tathāgatagarbha" belongs to the general category and is a name for that which is still enmeshed in afflictions (*saṃkliṣṭa*).
This is the union of the true and the false. Furthermore, the self-nature (*svabhāva*) is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, while its differentiation is the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Thus, both person and phenomena are fully revealed; both the dharma and the parable are presented; both substance and function are complete; both fruit and cause are present;
and both the expressed meaning and the title are provided. Only when the true and the false are both manifested can one find a title for a sutra as comprehensive as this.
The title of this definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is thus clearly established; yet the World-Honored One further commanded that one should uphold the Dharma according to this very name.
Those who claim to have realized it and uphold it—those who have awakened to and clarified the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*)—are such that the nature of words is itself liberation;
they may fill entire pages with radiance while upholding it. This is not the case for those who have not awakened to and clarified the mind-ground.

When one is deluded regarding the true nature of all phenomena and gives rise to views based on characters by grasping at phenomena as being external to the mind, those very views must be countered by using characters to reveal their original nature.

This is like using sound to stop sound, using a wedge to extract a wedge, using a trap to seize a trap, or using poison to counteract poison; it does not involve departing from characters, but rather practicing according to what has been taught.
This is practicing while upholding the meaning.
Good son, this sutra reveals exclusively the realm of the Tathāgata; only a Buddha, a Tathāgata, can fully proclaim it.
As previously stated, "this is the ground of pure awakening for all sentient beings," and it was further said that ignorance, craving, and the four illnesses constitute the four... [omitted].
Regarding the statement that "the marks now manifest only the realm of the Tathāgata":

since it is said that they manifest only the inconceivable realm of the Buddha’s wondrous enlightenment, and that only a Buddha alone can fully exhaust what is taught—what, then, is that which is taught?

It refers to the teaching that the ignorance of sentient beings is entirely non-existent; this is solely the realm of the Buddha. If the realm of the Buddha were not manifested, [this would not be possible].

How could sentient beings all arise from emptiness? If they were not empty, how could they ever penetrate the ground of awakening? Thus, the stages of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* are themselves the realm of the Buddha;
this is precisely the meaning [of this teaching]. Later generations, however, possessed those of shallow knowledge and inferior understanding who claimed that the Buddha-dharma ends here.
This was merely their own interpretation of what was said.
If all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age practice according to this, they will gradually advance until reaching the stage of Buddhahood.
To the previous question regarding the extent to which this teaching shall be disseminated, the answer is now given: it is because this sutra exclusively reveals...

Because it is the realm of the Buddha, those who cultivate these ten dharma-practices will necessarily reach the stage of Buddhahood; the stage of Buddhahood is precisely the rank of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

This is what is meant by not lingering at the "transformed city" (*nirmita-pura*) but immediately ascending to the "jeweled palace" (*ratna-gṛha*); in the Chan school, this is called "an ordinary person remaining unmoved while ascending to the rank of Buddha."

"Good son, this sutra is titled the 'Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna. Sentient beings with sudden faculties attain awakening through it, and it also encompasses all classes of beings who practice the gradual path.
National Preceptor Xianshou categorized the profound and shallow meanings of the entire Tripitaka into five teachings."
First, the Hīnayāna teachings, which are the four Āgamas; second, the Initial Mahāyāna teachings, which are the eight divisions of the Prajñāpāramitā;
third, the Final Mahāyāna teachings, which include the Śūraṅgama-samādhi, the Nirvāṇa, the Ratnakūṭa, and others;
fourth, the Sudden Mahāyāna teachings, which include the Awakening of Faith and the Laṅkāvatāra; and fifth, the Perfect Mahāyāna teachings, which is the Avataṃsaka.

This present sutra belongs to the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*) and is intended exclusively for sentient beings of sudden capacity; within those of sudden capacity, it is further divided into three levels of faculties:
superior, middling, and inferior. The Commentary states: "The Gate of the Patriarchs (Ch'an) is the Sudden Teaching, yet its contents include the Gradual Gate (*jian-men*).

Since it encompasses both the Sudden and the Gradual, it benefits those who are slow as well as those who are quick; whether one attains realization or not, whether one enters or does not enter, all may remain [in the teaching].
Regarding the reason for cultivating the mind, Master Shanzhu said: "Whether one understands it as something most extraordinary or does not understand it at all, I grant my approval.
It is like the great ocean, which does not refuse even small streams; even when mosquitoes, gadflies, or asuras drink from its waters, they all obtain their fill."

This provides an analogy: the great ocean represents the sudden teaching (dun-jiao), the small stream represents the gradual teaching (jian-jiao), mosquitoes and gnats represent the two vehicles (er-sheng), and the asuras represent the bodhisattvas.
"Drinking its water" and so forth represents how those of the two vehicles who uphold this sutra all attain awakening and entry.
The commentary (*shu*) states: "The great ocean contains immeasurable waters, yet those who drink from it..."

Regarding the measure of one’s own capacity, whether great or small, there are boundless Dharma-gates of Perfect Enlightenment to be received and upheld; according to the vessel, these are either sudden or gradual.
Good son, suppose there were someone who filled the three-thousandfold world system entirely with the seven treasures.
To practice giving is not as meritorious as for someone to hear the name of this sutra or even a single phrase of its meaning;

this reveals the nature of merit. Once the assembly had concluded, [the Buddha] spoke of the three capacities—superior, middling, and inferior—and further discussed the principles of cause and effect.
Fearing that sentient beings of future generations might lack faith and fail to cultivate such causes to bring about such results, he then...
Within this section on the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*), the merit of a single path is weighed and praised so that future generations may give rise to faith and joy.
This is similar to the meaning of the two layers of cause and effect and the threefold weighing found in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

In Sanskrit, *dānapāramitā* is translated here as "generosity" (*bushī*). This means that to extend the mind broadly is called "dispersal" (*bu*), while to withhold from oneself and bestow upon others is called "giving" (*shi*).
It is said that by practicing this *dāna-pāramitā*, all other practices are subsumed. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of ten *pāramitās*:

first, *dāna*, which refers to the giving of wealth, the Dharma, and fearlessness—there is nothing that is not relinquished; second, *śīla*, which refers to guarding against what is improper and ceasing evil, so that there is no flaw within or without;

third, *kṣānti*, which means that neither the adverse nor the favorable disturb one, but rather one investigates with discernment and accepts with patience; fourth, *vīrya*, which is to be free from...
1. Body and mind are like all phenomena; by increasing cultivation of the five dhyānas, discursive thoughts are entirely forgotten, and one abides peacefully in the realm of principle.

2. The six pāramitās are free from discrimination; one skillfully realizes the emptiness of the mind. 3. Through expedient means, one engages with existence while remaining constantly empty; in all actions and deeds, there is no attachment. 4.

With the power of vows, one seeks the supreme above and transforms those below, exhausting the limits of the future. 5. With the power of strength, through reflection and cultivation, success is achieved.
The myriad objects do not move; through the ten wisdoms, one decisively severs delusion, realizes the Dharma, and nourishes the spirit.
Now, by means of the single perfection of giving, one compares it with the merit of the sutras. As for the meaning of a single phrase, this reveals its superiority over the seven treasures.
The intent is that even if one were to use jewels such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and red pearls, one would not seek personal peace and happiness thereby.
Therefore, to universally bestow [merit] upon all sentient beings is a cause of conditioned and out-flowing (sāsrava) existence that evokes the retribution of human and celestial realms;
it is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void: when its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down, bringing about an unfavorable rebirth in the future.
If one now hears even a single phrase of this sutra that accords with the truth and practices according to what is taught, [one shall not fall].
Severing delusions and dispelling doubts is the supreme cause for the untainted (*anāsrava*) state;

it enables one to transcend the dream-like and illusionary nature of existence, emerge from saṃsāra, and proceed directly toward the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi. Therefore, this merit surpasses the merit of the previous seven types of precious material offerings.
The Commentary states: "Worldly treasures may fill the entire universe, yet they can only serve as jewels that lead to tainted results; the wondrous Dharma, however, [is otherwise]."
The character [for "one"] necessarily receives the retribution of Bodhi. The Chan school also says:

"If you recognize one phrase, the work of a lifetime of study is finished. In the Exoteric Teachings it is said: "Of the thousands of characters in the scriptures, a single mind can penetrate them all.

In the Book of Poetry it is said: "Of the three hundred poems, a single word can encompass them all. In the Records it is said: "Master one thing, and ten thousand matters are finished. This is what is meant by "explanation."
It is said, "My Way is one and runs through all. An ancient poem says: "Though learning may not be much, it can bring about perfect stillness.
If this is so, then returning to the same source is returning to the One. Once a single point is penetrated, thousands and tens of thousands of points are simultaneously liberated.
Therefore it is said: "When a single leaf falls, autumn comes to the world; when a single speck of dust rises, the great earth is gathered up; when a single flower blooms, the world [awakens]."
The meaning of this phrase is identical to the principle that "one thing is quiescent and the myriad dharmas are true.
Good son, suppose there were someone who taught as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in a hundred Ganges Rivers to attain the fruit of Arhatship.
This reveals inferior wisdom. In the Sanskrit language, "Arhat" has three meanings: non-arising, worthy of offerings, and free from thieves.
As for the Ganges River, it is forty *li* square; its sand is as fine as flour.

Even if one were to take as many people as there are grains of sand in a hundred such Ganges Rivers and ensure they all attained the realization of the holy ones of the small fruit (*śrāmaṇaphala*), [it would still be inferior].
The merit of such a person is not ultimate and is therefore inferior.
It is not equal to that of someone who proclaims this sutra and explains even half a verse.

The preceding passage cited the inferior; this [passage] reveals the superior. The intended meaning is that it would cause as many sentient beings as the sands of a hundred Ganges Rivers to attain Arhatship.
The merit obtained from the fruit of Arhatship is not equal to the merit of someone who, on behalf of the Buddha, proclaims even half a verse of this sutra.
The commentary states: "Generally, a 'full verse' refers to four lines. There are two kinds of lines: first, lines of text; second, lines of meaning.
If one relies on lines of text, then two lines constitute half a verse; if one relies on lines of meaning..."
"To say that all dharmas are originally empty and quiescent is half a verse; to reveal that the essence of emptiness is not empty is the full verse.
Furthermore, O son of good family, if there should be anyone who hears the name of this sutra and their faith is free from delusion..."

This clarifies hearing and believing. "Not being deluded" means being free from doubt and confusion. However, throughout immeasurable kalpas, the teachings of the Mahāyāna have been difficult to see and difficult to hear;
there have even been those who, having heard them at times, did not believe, did not comply, did not awaken to them, and did not enter into them.
Thus, the *Lunyu* says: "If a person lacks trustworthiness, one does not know what can be expected of them. Now, as for the *Yuanjue* (Perfect Enlightenment)...
The profound purport is the wondrous gate of the One Mind; it cannot be contemplated without great wisdom, nor can it be believed without great faculties.
Contemplation is precisely the raising of the Buddha-wisdom, and belief is precisely the entry into Perfect Enlightenment.
It requires only a sincere resolve free from doubt to ensure its successful accomplishment.
It should be known that such persons have not planted roots of merit and wisdom under one or two Buddhas,
but rather have planted all such roots of goodness under as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River upon hearing this scriptural teaching.
This verifies their past causes. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "One should know that such persons have planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas;

having already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable thousands of myriads of Buddhas, upon hearing these passages, they give rise to pure faith for even a single thought-moment. As for these "various roots of goodness," they are not... [incomplete].
Beyond this, the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion give rise to the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Now, those who believe in the central tenet of this sutra must possess a faith that is simultaneous with understanding; such faith encompasses the ocean of fruition and is no small matter.
Therefore, one may verify that their past causes involved the accumulation of seeds of faith.

"You, son of good family, should protect those practitioners in the final age so that evil Māras and various heterodox teachers do not afflict their bodies and minds, causing them to fall into despondency and retreat.
To your previous question regarding how to provide protection and support, I now reply: simply ensure that evil Māras and heterodox teachers do not afflict their bodies."

The "mind" (citta) here refers to the act of upholding and protecting. Recently, someone composed verses and inserted them into the sutra, likely unaware that this section belongs to the *parīndanā* (concluding transmission).
May readers not harbor any doubts regarding this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Bhadrapāla, you should know that this sutra was spoken by all Buddhas and is well-protected by the Tathāgatas.
It is the eye of the twelve divisions of scripture, named the Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-cakra-vajra-dhāraṇī, which manifests the realm of the Tathāgata. Those who practice in reliance upon it..."
Advancing until reaching the stage of Buddhahood is like a small stream flowing into the ocean, which satisfies all who drink from it;
yet even if one were to give away seven precious jewels filling the three thousandfold world system, it would not equal hearing this sutra.

Even if one were to transform beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges so that they all attain arhatship, it would not equal proclaiming half a verse. Therefore, in future ages, you must protect those who proclaim and uphold this, ensuring they do not fall into despondency.
At that time, within the assembly, there were eighty thousand Vajras—including Agnīśikhara-vajra, Vajra-pramardana, and Nīlambā-vajra—along with their retinues.
They rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, if in the future final age there are sentient beings who are able to uphold this definitive Mahāyāna, we shall protect them.”
We shall protect [this place] as we would our own eyes, even unto the site of enlightenment or wherever one practices;
we, the Vajras, leading our own retinues, will guard it morning and evening so that one does not regress. In that household, there shall be no calamities or obstacles forever;
epidemics shall be extinguished, and wealth and treasures shall abound, never lacking.

From here below is the section on receiving the command to provide external protection for the propagation [of the teachings]. As for "Fire-Head" (Agnimukha), this deity has flames upon his head and holds a vajra in his hand.
At that time, the Great Brahmā King, the twenty-eight Heavenly Kings, Sumeru Mountain King, the Guardian Kings of the Nation, and others...
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him three times to the right, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I too shall protect those who uphold this sutra, constantly ensuring they remain peaceful and secure, and that their minds never regress."
The Great Brahmā King is the Lord of the First Dhyāna Heaven; the King of the Twenty-eight Heavens is the Lord of the Three Realms;
the King of Mount Sumeru is Śakra; and the Kings of the Heavenly Protectors of the Nation specifically refer to the Four Heavenly Kings.

At that time, a great powerful ghost-king named Kumbhāṇḍa, together with one hundred thousand ghost-kings, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, I too shall protect those who uphold this sutra, attending them morning and night so that they may not fall back or be discouraged.
Within a distance of one yojana of where such a person dwells, if there should be...”
"If spirits and deities invade his territory, I shall cause them to be shattered like fine dust.
As for the Kumbhāṇḍas—Kumbhāṇḍas are spirits that consume the vital essence of humans, moving as swiftly as the wind;
they range through forests and wilds. A 'yojana' refers to forty *li*."

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, all the bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and the eight classes of followers, as well as the various heavenly kings, the Brahma kings, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Commentary states: This is truly because the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* explains that there are three kinds of meanings for which one should joyfully accept and practice:

first, the purity of the speaker, who does not grasp at fame or profit due to being untainted by them; second, the purity of the Dharma taught, because of knowing the essence of phenomena as they truly are;
and third, the purity of the attainment of the fruit, which refers to the benefit of the teaching. [Question: Regarding the beginning of the sutra...
Question: Is this accomplishment of faith the same as or different from the preceding faith? Answer: The former faith is shallow; this faith is deep. How is this known?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Thus have I heard" gives rise to faith; "faithfully accepting and practicing" gives rise to wisdom.
Faith is that which enables entry, while wisdom is that which enables transcendence. It further states: "Faith is the beginning of entering the Dharma."
Wisdom is the ultimate and most essential requirement; although there are differences in depth and shallowness, if wisdom and faith are unified, there is no distinction.
*Yuanjue jing lüejie*, Scroll Four, End (Conclusion).

I, Yingchen, have humbly heard that the nature of all beings is uniform and one, fundamentally without interruption; yet, because consciousness is clouded by the six sense objects, delusion and awakening become divided.

Fortunately, there is the ocean-like nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), which clarifies where the sudden and gradual approaches converge. Through this vehicle of definitive meaning, the true Dharma, the boundary between sages and ordinary beings is unified.
It points out the essential path for sentient beings and reveals the true source of all Buddhas. Therefore, all sentient beings...
I have heard what I had never heard before and attained what I had never attained before. Yet, when principle is hidden in obscurity, the hearer remains in darkness;

when the subtle enters the profound, the attainer finds it difficult. Thus it is said that although Perfect Enlightenment has always been Perfect Enlightenment, responding to the times requires discerning its divisions.
My own nature is dull and ignorant, yet I have once perused the subtle words of Guifeng, which surged like a great ocean, and I have gained [understanding].

The *Fù'ān zhī lèi jiě* (Classified Explanations of the Fù'ān) clears the mist and reveals the bright sky; I respectfully and diligently transcribe these various editions, hoping to propagate their transmission widely.

May those who recite them orally and behold them with their eyes attain awakening of the mind and the opening of the heart, all dwelling together in the Great Radiant Treasury (*Mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*) and ascending collectively to the Sublime Site of Perfect Enlightenment (*Samyak-saṃbodhi*).
With sincere aspirations for sublime benefit, I reverently pray for the boundless longevity of the Two Palaces [the Emperor and Empress], and to repay the infinite kindness of my parents.
The ultimate grace has caused all who have seen or heard of it to receive its residual moisture.

On the day of the winter solstice in the year of Jǐnhài, the Year of Purity and Tranquility, Lěn Yìngchén, a recipient of the rank of Chéngxìn, respectfully records this with prostrations before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha: "May the power of this transcription [bring about such merit]."
Universally delivering all beings, first repaying the kindness of deceased kin, and recompensing the virtue of teachers and masters,
may we universally succor all classes of sentient beings and together realize the wisdom of all modes.
